THE MAN WHO NETER ADVERTISES. Sing, business muse, the dark and doleful fate Of him who lthours but. that he may wait : The piles of goods heaped up within his btore, Which can't. be less, and never may be more; The man whose life has lost all fortune's prizes: In tact the man who never advertises. Sing of his start, his great ambitious scope. The ctpital that gave him cause to hope, His credit large, his full and ample stock, His bank account as solid ass rock; Then fe,l the doom to which the man was fitted Who never advertised, but simply waited. So simply. and so vainly! Splendid signs Which basement art Irradiates and refines; Plate gissa show windows, elegantly dressed; Such lovely clerks, cashiers, and all the rest. Served ray to show him how the public sizes The style of him who never advertises. Ire waited. and all waited; clerks, c tshiers, Salesmen and sake wornen—such detightful dears-- Impatient waited all the season through, With precious little for the cr -twd to do. The pubtic saw the tact there's no denying— But passed the store without a thought of buying. Bus nest& was dull, but salaries and rent Went on tit' cash and credit both were spent; The silly merchant hotted his luck would tuts:, Until the she if closhd the whole concern. Now, at a pittance which his soul despises. He works for one who always advertises.

_so Better to have loved a short girl than never to have loved a tall. An auctioneer, by birth a native of the Green Isle, caused to be printed on his handbill at a recent sale, "Every article sold goes to the highest bidder, unless it so happens that some gentleman bids more." An innocent old farmer weighed the butter he sold to his grocer with pound bars of soap that he bought of him, and it turned out that the butter fell short three ounces to the pound; but the grocer didn't make a pablic row about it. A poor man once came to a miser, and said, "I have a favour to ask." "So have I," said the miser; "grant mine first, then I will comply with thine. "Agreed." "My re- quest is," said the miser, "that you ask me for nothing." Do not wade far out into the dangerous sea of this world's comfort. Take what the good God provides you, but say of it, "It passeth away; for indeed it is but a temporary supply for a temporary need." Never suffer your goods to become your God.—Spurgeon. "CORNS REMOVED WITHOUT PAIN." "Two shillings, if you please," the chiropodist said, With the sweetest of smiles and a nod of his head. "Arrah, now," says Biddy, "what's that ye are sayin'? I thought ye removed thim without any payin'." "Strange," remarked Mrs. Brown, "I have rung at Mrs. Smith's door three times this week, and I didn't succeed in raising any one. I suppose the family is out of town." " Possibly," replied Mrs. Jones, "but Mrs. Smith toli me just now that she could tell your ring among a thousaffd." At the time there was so much excitement about ironclad vessels, the father of a family who was carving one day at dinner a piece of mutton, remarked—" This mutton seems to be very tough." Little Walter, a six-year-old, looked up, and said—" Father, I guess it came off our ironclad ram!" "Mr. Jones, I think I will have to raise your board," said a One Hundred and Twenty-ninth-street boarding-house keeper to a gentleman whose appetite seemed to increase every day. " Ah, I thank you very mach for your kindness in raising my board. I have been unable to raise it myself for some time." At a certain party a gentleman in the midst of an angry dispute' threw a bottle at his opponent's head by the way of emphasising his argument. Foote, who was present, immediately picked the missile up and laid it on the table, "saying, Friends, if you pass the bottle as quickly as that you wont' be able to stand out the evening.' Sir Fletcher Norton whose want of courtesy was no- torious, happened, while pleading before Lord Mansfield on some question of manorial right, to say—" My lord, I can illustrate the point in an instant in my own person. I my- self have too little manors." "We all know it,Sir Fletcher," the judge interposed, with one of his blandest smiles. Men must prepare in youth and in middle age the means of enjoying old age pleasantly and happily. These cen be nothing more distressing than to see an old man who has spent the greater part of his life in well-paid-for labour re- , duced to the necessity of begging for bread, ate' relying , entirely on the commiseration of his neighbours, or upon the bounty of strangers. Augustus was told of an extravagant Roman knight who had wasted all his property. When his goods were sold by auction, Augustus commissioned a person to bid for his pil- low. Being asked why he wished to have this article of furniture in particular, he replied—" Such a pillow must be i very desirable upon whicllea man so deep in debt could sleep so soundly." A dragoon was tried in Dublin for desertion, and for car- lying off his horse and accoutrements at the same time. When on his trial, an officer asked him what could induce him to take his horse away; to which Pat promptly replied, "He ran away with nee, your honour." "But whv," said thenEficer, "did you do with that money you got for him?" "That, plase your honour," said the fellow, with the utmost indifference, " ran away too." Mrs. Whalley is a character in our villatre. She is now an old woman, and lives in a small cottage off the main street. A few days ago she met a lad drivins a fine load of hay to market. She stopped him, inquired the quality and price of the hay, and, after much deliberation, ordered the boy to drive his horses into her yard. The place was rather strait for the waggon to enter, but lie finally managed to drive in, and prepared to unload. Looking up to the lad— who, pitchfork in hand, was about to toss off the hay—she said, with great simplicity—" You may give me about enough for a hen's nest: I've been wanting it for some time !"—Horper's Monthly. THE SEARCH FOR BEAUTY.—" Surely there is no other view like this in the world!" exclaimed an English noble- man in one of the mountain passes in Switzerland. The guide had heard that there was but one, naming a view in Scotland. "Why," retorted his lordship, "that is on my own estate, and I have never seen it !" Historically the narrative is open to doubt, but the idea intended to be con- veyed is strictly true. Englishmen, as a rale, know com- paratively little of their own country from a holiday point of view. To the gentle, kind-hearted Goldsmith, "a shoe- maker's holiday,' which consisted of a walk through the fields to Highbury, or Hampton, and back, was the supremest enjoyment of his life, but such was "not for the fashion of the times." The love of the picturesque is deeply engrained in the nature of the tired dweller in smoke- begrimed cities, as seen in the fact that dramatic action de- pends largely for success upon scenic effect; but in the love of scenery there are two kinds of pleasure, that of familiarity and that of strangeness, the latter being by far the most in- fluential. It is this modern mania for the novel and strange that induces the hard-worked toiler in town and city to pre- fer the harrassing distractions of the Continent to the lovely scenery and sequestered retreats of his own country. You are nasre likely to run against a familiar friend at Paris— where according to Thackeray, "very small London people become very great ones, if they've money"—or at the Rigi Kulm, than at Windermere, or Ben Lomond, or at the Isle of Wight.—Holiday .litmler of " Family Maya- rine." _ _ _

THE STouv OF A MASTEIIPIECE.—WheII Antokolsky con- ceived his "Ivan the Terrible" he was still starving on a pound a month. It would have been mere midsummer mad- ness to think of a studio of his own. He tried to get one in the Academy; but he tried in vain. He then asked per- mission to work there during the vacation in the sculptors' class-rooms; and after a great deal of circumlocution the required permission was granted (1870) on condition that In return for it he mended all the broken noses and maimed hands and lame legs of the battered old bas-reliefs which had been sent in on account of the Academy gold medal. He began to work at his "Ivan the Terrible" with the passionate and indefatigable unrest peculiar to him. He wanted to finish it out of hand, under the impulse of a unique, unbroken inspiration. The incessant labour, the old unending hardships and privations, the miserable cir- cumstances under which he lived and wrought, combined to make him seriously ill. He took a horrible cough, and began to suffer violently from pulmonary haemorrhage. He was obliged to leave his work, and go home and rest. In a month he was back-again in St. Petersburg. There a new grief was in store for him. The class-room in which his znodel stood, by order of the academical authorities, had been appropriated to other uses, and the terrible Tzar had been parcelled out in fragments, and stowed away in a lumber room under the roof. Antokolsky kept up his heart. He was worn to a shadow with hardship and illness; he had no light to work in, and no room; he was faint and giddy and tired; but he laboured on. And at last "The Terrible" was finished. Naturally enough, the artist's first idea was to show his work te his professors. He was a young man, however; and none of them were interested in his work. Had it been a veteran's, like Piraenoff or Baron Bloat, it would have been another pair of shoes. But it was only Antokolsky's; and they declined to look at it. So the artist went and called on Prince Gagarin, the President of the Academy, and asked inspection of him. The President was vgy civil, told him that he had long had his eye on him, affd that he would be delighted to come and see. He came ; he saw ;he was conquered. No such work bad come from a Russian artist; and he knew it, and was enchanted with the knowledge. Next day he returned with the Grand Duchess Maria Paulovna ; she was every whit as much astonished and impressed as the President. "The Emperor must see your work !" she said in her ecstasy. But to make this pos- sible another sacrifice was required of the artist. lie was still under the tiles; at such a height the Emperor and he were practically ten thousand miles apart ; and. he was requested to cut up his work, and get it carried piecemeal downstairs and set up in a bigger room on the ground floor. This he positively refused to do. The President was per- suasive ; the Grand Duchess was benevolently imperious ; but the sculptor stood firm. Then, at a sign from her Im- perial Highness, a miracle was operated in the little garret. The floor became covered with exquisite tapestry; fair windows appeared in its walls; it grew glorious with costly furniture and silken hangings; and one evening at six o'clock there was a strange and awful jingle of spurs on the narrow stairs, and in came the Tzar. He looked affably at the majestic presentment of his predecessor ; and he honoured the artist with a "gracious conversation "—"Who: are you? "—" Antokolsky."—" Where from ?"—" Wilno " " Very good, very good !" With that there was another strange and awful jingle of spurs, and the Tzar had vanished. ----The Magazine of Art.

LORD TOLLEMACHE AND THE PRODUCTION OF ENSILAGE. —Lord Tollemache, in order to test the value of ensilage as a cattle food, particularly for Cheshire milking stock during the winter, has just completed the construction of three capacious silos at Peckfort, which now await filling. The crops to be utilised—probably Italian rye-grass—will first be chopped small and then tipped into the silo, with heavy superincumbent weights to exclude air. A Cumlous CatermeatioN.—Each head of clover contains about 60 distinct flower tubes, each of which contains a portion of sugar not exceeding the 500th part of a grain. The proboscis of the bee must therefore be inserted into 500 clover tubes before one grain of sugar can be obtained. There are 7,000 grains in a pound, and as honey contains three-fourths of its weight of dry sugar, each pound of honey represents 2,500,000 clover tubes sucked by bees. A sale of Jersey cattle and other animals bred by Ld. Bray- brooke took place at Andley End, Saffron Walden, on Fri- day last, by Mr. John Thornton. The sale was a succsesful one. Twenty Jersey cows and heifers realised £631 128.6 d., or an average of £3l lie. 7d.; five bulls £142 165., or an average of £2B us. 3d. Seven rams, out of 10 offered, made £47 55., or an average of £6 158.; and 31 pigs made £B4 6s. The -total amount realised by the sale was £905 193. 6d. WHEAT EARS.--Mr. Saunders Spencer, of Holywell Manor, St. Ives, writes :—I have pleasure in forwarding you. one of the first ears which I have this year found growing in a field of wheat; variety, Scholey's Square head, grown on mixed soil with a gravelly sub-soil;• cultivation, one ploughing as soon as a heavy crop of winter beans was carted off; beans grown with a good dressing of pigs' manure; wheat no muck, but six stones of nitrate of soda per acre applied in March. The wheat was drilled the third week in October; seed, six pecks per acre; present prospect of crop, good.—Mark Lane Express. EXPERIMENTS ON FOOT AND MOUTH DlSEASE.—Profes- sor Robertson's report on the experiments being carried out in connection with foot and mouth disease at the Royal Veterinary College, read before the recent meeting of the Royal Agricultural Society, is to the effect that in cases where the disease had been communicated by inoculation the animals were not susceptible to a second attack. But Professor Robertson points out that although it is possible to induce foot and mouth disease "of a more moderate type by intra-venous injection of a variously-charged fluid, it is not at all probable that the disease so induced will afford • protection for a longer period against a second attack than • obtained by its development in the natural form." ' FARM PRODUCE FROM NEW ZEALAND.—The Canterbury Times (New Zealand) publishes an account of the first annual meeting of the Canterbury Frozen Meat Company, held in March last. From this it appears that the total cost to date had been £14,792 17s. id., and that arrange- ments have been made for the carriage of five cargoes of frozen meat to London by the New Zealand Shipping Com- pany's steamers; shipments to be despatched from Lyttel- ton every alternate month from March till the end of Jan., 1884. As provision has been made for the cool storage and preparation for export of cheese and butter, it was hoped that the shareholders would avail themselves of the oppor- tunity thus afforded for securing a regular and profitable outlet for their produce in the English market. AGRICULTURAL EDVCATION.—At the recent monthly ; Council of the Royal Agricultural Society, Lord Moreton, M.P. (chairman), reported that 26 candidates entered their names for examination for the Society's senior prizes and certificates, and of these 19 presented themselves on the 9th •of May and four succeeding days. The result of the exa- mination was that the following gentlemen, placed in order of merit, obtained first-class certificates and the life mem- , bership of the society, the first four also qualified for prizes: ' —Girischandra Bose, Royal Agricultural College, Ciren- cester, £25; Henry Blair Mayne and Arthur Herbert Kerr, College of Agriculture, Downton, Salisbury, £10; Edward Charles Ozanne £5, John Henry Tiffen, and James Henry Dugdale, Royal Agricultural College, Cirencester. AGRICULTURAL EXPERIMENT AT WOW:MS.—OD Thursday week a party of agriculturists, numbering upwards of fifty, principally members of the Royal Agricultural Society of England, proceeded from London to Woburn, for the pur- pose of viewing the field and feeding experiments which are being conducted there (through the kindness of the Duke of Bedford. K.G.) one of the special objects being to observe 1 the effects of the different manures on the various crops. , The exeursionkts. who were accompanied by the Society's , chemist, Dr. Voelcker, F.R.S., assembled from nearly all , parts of the kingdom. An area of 27 acres is devoted to ; the field experiments, and, in addition to this, his Grace has , set apart Crawley Mill Farm, comprising about 90 acres, for the purposes in view. The visitors„were greatly in- !t r..Aed in Dr. Voelcker's observations in elucidation of the experiments, regarding which elaborate reports are made public from time to time; and the farm manager was com- plimented on the remarkable freedom from weeds which , characterised the land.

ENSIL kGE EXPERIMENTS BY TICE HIGHLAND AGRICUL- Turut SOCIETY.—Dr. Aitken reported, at a recent meeting, } that, in the absence of Mr. Mackenzie, of Portmore, Mr. Mylne and he had recently inspected the silo being con- structed for the society at Portmore, and gave a description of the experiment. The silo, which is now nearly corn- ' pleted, is a rectangular chamber 30ft. long, 13ft deep, and 12ft. wide. It is partly dug out of is dry bank adjoining the steading, and is constructed of concrete, consisting of seven parts gravel got in the neighbourhood and one part Portland cement. The capacity of the silo is such as to contain, when full, about 100 tons of ensilage, and it is ex- pected that the cost will not exceed 13s. per ton of capacity. , The crops—consisting of grass, oats, maelin, and tares—are to be cut about the tin-.e of flowering, and stored irrespec- ' five of weather. Mr. Mackenzie is constructing a silo of similar capacity at another steading to receive the produce of about 12 acres meadow grass and about 8 acres clover grass. In addition to these a silo of about 15 tons capacity will be dug on the hill farm in the form of a trench 15ft. long, 5. feet wide, and sft. deep, to be tilled with bog grass for the feeding of sheep. It will be simply a hole in the solid earth, dug as smoothly as possible without lining of any kind, arid when it has been tilled and trodden the earth which has been taken out will be heaped on the top, to give the weight required to keep the ensilage in good condition. HAv-ereatxo.—The. bad hay-making seasons of the past half-dozen years were what in reality led to the inquiries after the Neilson system of stack-cooling, which may still be considered on its trial, although the Royal judges were in such over-haste to condemn it at Reading. The artificial drying system of Mr. W. A. Gibbs has in it also the germs of much excellence, and we regard with the greatest satis- faction the fact that both originators of these improved methods are busily employed in endeavouring to do away with their alleged imperfections. The chief objection made last summer to the Neilson system was the settling down of the stack into such a close, impervious mass at the base that the fan could not draw air through, which led to the engen- Oertnent of must. Mr. Neilson has never experienced this very much himself, because he is accustomed to condition . his hay in cocks longer than most people who have adopted • this system; but, perceiving the rock on which they flounder, he has improvised a new stack-foundation, having a brickwork framing with semi-apertures sft. high, and en- closing a considerable space round the aperture at the centre, through which the suction from the fan works. This, with a small chimney carried a few feet higher, absolutely pre- vents the evil of the too close compression complained of, and renders the circulation of air through the stack when the fan is set in motion to be very even and far more effective. The leading objection against the Gibbs' method has always been the great cost of the apparatus, and that the original inventor hopes soon to lessen most =Aerially. The Royal judges had the bad taste to nickname Mr. Gibbs' drying machine and heat generator "Jumbo" and "Alice," because they seemed so very cumbrous, but Mr. Gibbs some time before the Reading trials had seen the necessity of sim- plifying and contracting the size of his artificial dryer, which can now be procured for one-third the cost formerly.
Live within your income. It's terribly hard work to live without it.
It takes a girl twice as long to wash the front windows of a house as the back windows.

No place, no company, no age, no person is temptation , free. Let no man boast that he was never tempted. Let ' him be high-minded, but fear, for he may be surprised in that very instant wherein he boasteth that he was never tempted at all. For in life's paths of honour and of duty Each day fulfils the promise of the last ; He best may hope to win the future's beauty Who best has kept the treasures of the past. —Mrs. Mary E. Blake. A young city gent, dressed in a faultless suit and a pair of shoes which tapered to a point in the most modern style, was visiting in a rural district. A bright little four-year- old boy looked him all over until his eyes rested on those shoes. He looked at his own chubby feet and then at his visitor's, and then looking up, said, "Mister, is your toes all cutted off but one ?"

A little fellow, some four or five years old, and who had never seen a negro, was greatly perplexed one day when one came by where he and his father were. The youngster eyed the stranger suspiciously till he had passed, and then asked his father—" Pa, who painted that man all blaqk so?" —"God did, my son," replied the father.—" Well," said the littiv one, still looking after the negro, "I shouldn't have thought he'd Mlle held still." Chatting with one of her neighbours not long since, she related her experience when converted, many years ago, as follows :—" I used to be very gay, and fond of the world and all its fashions till the Lord showed me my folly. I liked silks and ribbons and laces and feathers, but I found they were dragging me down to hell—so I gave them all to ny sister!"—Harper's Monthly. Rector (whose curate has lately left the parish), visiting old woman: "Well, Betty, I expect you will miss Mr. Robinson a good deal?" Betty: "Oh, yes, sir! He were a beautiful young man, air!" Rector: "Well, he was a very good man, Betty; but I don't know about his being exactly beautiful.'" Betty: "Oh, he weren't much to look at in the face, I know; but, lor, sir, his innards was lovely."

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

As soon as we have rain the cottager must attend to the transplanting of the various crops, such as cabbages, cauli- flowers, broccoli, &c. As the plants are being drawn up they should be closely examined, both hearts and roots. Many of the cauliflower class will be found what gardeners term "blind," which means that they will not produce the desired flower heads in any shape whatever; and dry weather, such as we have experienced, seems highly favour- al:a to the production of such an undesirable result, as all plants so affected are worthless. On the roots of many of ' the Brassica tribe will be found protuberances called club- bing. These plants should be discarded, as they rarely do any good. The cause of clubbing has not been satisfactorily demonstrated. Some attribute it to insect agency, others maintain that the insect's presence is an accidental result. We have cut some hundreds of the protuberances and have not discovered insects in them. One writer, or rather lec- turer, some months back alleged that heavy wet soil was favourable to clubbing. We have found it more prevalent on light dry soils. Many other causes are assigned which are purely speculative. Where there is such diversity of opinion the suggested remedies will be corresponding nume- rous, so we offer none. We have not the twentieth part of clubbing that we had had a few years ago. We have pur- sued a vigorous liberal policy in the way of frequent visits to the muck heap, combined with constantly working the ground. So soon as a piece of ground is vacant, upside down is its fate, and without any apology in the shape of sundry pats on the back, we leave it to the elements to deal with. _ _

CELERY.—There should now be no delay in preparing the trenches for this and if all is in readiness -16 y the time we have rain, much labour will be saved in watering. At the same time it is highly. important to give it one good water- ing immediately after planting for the purpose of setting the soil round the roots. The rain must be unusually heavy to do this as effectually as careful watering. TURNIPS may still be sown at this time and after. We confine ourselves to Veitch's Red Globe and another, the American Red Top (which is similar), also the White Stone. Our earliest, the Early Purple-top Munich, is now fit for use, having formed bottoms from 2in. to 3in. in diameter. It is quite three weeks in advance of two other early sorts, and, unlike early sown ones, it does not show any tendency to "bolt" or run to seed. _ _

.... ~..._ ........_ ..... ___,.... Lurrum.—The long period of dry weather will have caused advanced crops of these to "bolt," consequently their season will be very short. A sowing made at the pre- sent time might prove of more service than all previous ones.

GOOSEBERRIES.—Where the crop is heavy it should be reduced to one-half. The fruit from the lower branches or any likely to touch the earth should be gathered entirely, for they will only get gritty from the splashing of the rain, as well as occasional friction with the soil in windy weather. The fruit left on the trees will grow much finer. There is also much less strain on the energies of the trees in conse- quence of early thinning. The caterpillar has commenced its cruel work of denuding the trees of their foliage. The best preventive is hellebore and powdered alum, in propor- tion by weight of one of the former to two of the latter, covered over with sufficient water to thoroughly mix them. To every ounce of hellebore add one gallon of water, which, with a syringe or fine-rose watering pot, will do about a dozen ordinary sized trees. Elder leaves boiled in as much water as will cover them, adding one ounce of tobacco to every gallon of water, is said to be effectual. Dusting the trees when wet with road dust or lime and soot, in about equal parts, is said to check their progress. Hellebore, &c., being such a drastic remedy, we fly to it at once. TILE FRONT GARDEN.—The grass-plots that were allowed to grow six inches to twelve inches long, and then cut, ap- peared a fortnight ago as if affected with jaundice, and at present they look more like a patch of fustian spread in front of the dwelling than a piece of green grass. Timely cutting would have made all the difference. Frequent waterings in dry weather will greatly improve it. Staking and tying such as peonies, delphiniums (or larkspurs), dahlias, and other tall growing and heavy topped plants should not be neglected. It is ruinous to some plants when the shoots break at the bottom. No secondary growth is made that season, and the plant is further weakened for the following year. Roses seldom get through the season with- out being attacked with greenfly. Fortunately it is easily got rid of in the following manner :—ln a quart of warm water dissolve a piece of soft soap the size of a walnut ; squeeze the juice out of a quarter of an ounce of tobacco. An easy way to accomplish this is to put it in a rag. By dipping the hand in this mixture and drawing it in a grasp- ing way over each shoot, a little of the liquid will go a long way, and whatever is left can be preserved in a bottle until required for a future time. TIIE WINDOW.—This may be made highly attractive on the outside if a box is made to tit it and filled with plants. There should be ample provision made in the bottom for the free passage of water. The usual method is to make sundry holes in the wood forming the bottom. I maintain this weakens each board considerably, as well as hastens decay. I prefer to allow from half an inch to three-quarters of an inch of space between each board. I scarcely need state that the pieces should be fixed crossways, and their width may vary from four inches to eight inches. Pieces of crocks should be laid over the chinks, and the whole of the bottom covered with pieces of turf and rough leaf soil. The soil for planting should be fresh and rich.

div.head: INDEPENDENT METHODISTS.
div.p: INDEPENDENT METHODISTS.

The 78th annual assembly of the lnpopendent Methodist and Free Gospel Churches was brought to a close at Sunder- land on Wednesday evening.. The public services oom- menced on Saturday evening, and were continued on Sunday. The attendances were very large, and appropriate references were made to the sad calamity at the Victoria Hall, which occurred just as the majority of the representatives arrived in the town. The assembly met for business on Monday morning in Bahany Chapel. Allusion was first made to the 'sad event at the Victoria Hall, and on the proposal of Mr. W. Brimelow (Bolton), a resolution of sympathy with the bereaved parents was adopted, and this was immediately followed, or. the motion of Mr. J. Settle (Bolton), by a sub- scription of £5O to aid in the interment of the children whose parents were unable to bear the expense. The following were re-elected : President, Mr. M. Kennedy, Oldham ; vice-president and editcr,• Mr. W. Brimelow, Bolton; setretary, Mr. A. Roscoe, Pemberton ; vice-secretary, Mr. J. Wild, Oldham. Mr. T. Makin, Urmston, was ap- pointed treasurer. The Connexional Committee was con- stituted as follows : Messrs. J. Hudlass (Bolton), 'F. Lush (Burnley), J. Knowles (Warrington), J. Pros (Wigan), J. W. Gardner (Manchester)' and W. Jackson (o!dhatn). The reports of the Book-room Committee and the Evangelistic Committee were approved, the reported increase of 300 in the membership giving much satisfaction. Several churches, including Horwich were received into the Union. On Tuesday a scheme foe district repr-sentation on the Con- nexional Committee was submitted and adopted, and rees- lutions were passed approving of Sunday Closing, Mr. Richard's Cemeteries Bill, and the movement for putting Nonconformists on an equal footing with the Established Church with respect to the registration of marriages.—On the Monday evening, on the invitation of the Mayor of Sunderland, the representatives had tea at the Masonic Hall, and his Worship in welcoming them to the town acknowledged the practical sympathy the assembly had shown with those bereaved by the Victoria Hall disaster.— On the Tuesday evening a peblic meeting, at which about 1.500 people were present, was held and presided over by the Mayor. Addresses were given by Messrs. M. Kennedy (Old- • haml, W. Sanderson (Liverpool ), and W. Brimelow (Bolton); Messrs. J. Hudlass (Bolton). J. Knowles (Warrington), M. Pinkerton (Glasgow), and IV. Branfoot (Sunderland), also . took part in what proved to be a highly successful gather- ing. The proceedings closed on Wednesday evening by a , public temperance meeting.
The man who tried to get up a concert with the band of a hat is the same genius who a few weeks since played upon the affections of his grandmother.

AN OLD CLOTHES STORE !—The toad has a funny way of getting rid of its old clothes. Once in a while the skin begins to split down the back, like an old coat, and a new skin is seen underneath. When the toad finds this out it begins to undress itself; it pulls and pushes at the old skin until it gets it off its head and legs and body, and then it does something funnier still—it takes the old skin, rolls it up into a little round mass, and swallows it like a pill! "What a methodical fellow you are Brown," said Filkins, who had stepped into Brown's office during the latter's ab- sence. "Why, what do you mean?" asked Brown, who had just entered. "Mean ?" echoed Filkins; "to think that you should lock all your drawers up when you are only going out for five minutes! 'Tisn't likely that anybody would meddle with your papers." "Of course not," replied Brown, "but how did you find out that the drawers were locked ?"

THE REPUBLIC or LETTERS.—The field of Letters is called a Republic; but I do not know why, because in a Republic all the men are equal, whereas in literature they are all unequal. Perhaps the name is taken from some fancied re- semblance to a South American Republic, where the Presi- dent, or Publisher, whatever he is called, is changed once a quarter with a new Pronouncement. The so-called Republic lies in a flat country without any hills, streams, dykes, or eminences; it is circular in shape, and is bounded on all sides by circles of stone seats rising one above the other to a dizzy height. The citizens of the Republic are always strutting about on the arena trying to attract as much atten- tion as possible from the people in the seats, and hoping to see a great crowd assemble, with prodigious shouting,s, directly they begin to play their parts; when they are not playing, they are standing aside and criticizing their fellow actors. Some there are whom no one reg,ardeth at all ; when they come on the seats are swiftly emptied; these play for their brethren alone, who look on and jeer; and there are a very few—a happy few—at whose appearance the seats are crammed. Yet all the citizens in this Republic pretend to be of equal strength and give themselves the same airs.—Good Words.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 23, 1883 PANIC IN A PUBLIC HALL.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 23, 1883 PANIC IN A PUBLIC HALL.

183 DEATHS. Sunderland web on Saturday the scene of one of the most appalling disasters in connection with places of public entertainment which has ever occurred in England, and one which, with the exception of the Ring Theatre tragedy at Vienna and the circus burning in Russia, is perhaps without equal within living memory. On Saturday afternoon the Victoria Hall—the largest building of its kind in the town— was filled by an audience almost entirely composed of children, who had been invited to witness a special conjur- ing performance by the Messrs. Fay. The usual legerdemain performance was varied by the announcement that prizes would be distributed to the holders of certain tickets, and as school children were admitted at the specially reduced price of one penny each the attendance was naturally enormous, the gallery alone being packed with at least a jhousand little ones. Everything proceeded satisfactorily until the close of the performance, when it was announced that the prizes would be distributed in the pit or area of the hall, whereupon the little occupants of the gallery, many of whom held prize tickets, became excited ; and some, not wishing to miss this, the crowning item in an interesting programme, began to make their way down from the gallery to the area, and almost immediately nearly all of those in the gallery were on their way downstairs. The staircase is a winding one, and about three-parts of the way down there is a doorway through which those wishing to reach the area must pass. It was at this spot that a terrible block occurred. The first censers, in their natural eagerness to get through, in some way or other jammed the door in such a way that a bolt caught in the ground and held it firmly just ajar. Before the children in front could get the door open the steadily growing pres- sure from those behind, who, owing to the winding of the staircase, could see nothing of what was going on, caused a block; and, as the downward stream was still unchecked, there ensued a fearful crush, and ere long the staircase, only seven feet wide, and the narrow lobby was one indiscriminate mass of struggling, fainting, and shrieking children. Thus far none of the officials of the building and none of the audience in the body of the hall seem to be aware that anything was wrong, and the terrible struggle in the narrow staircase must have been going on for some time when Gra- ham, the hall-keeper, apparently strolling in that direction quite by chance, was attracted to the fatal door by the groans and cries of the poor little sufferers behind it. He saw that the belt had caught in such a way that the door could neither be opened nor shut entirely, and through the aper- ture, about two feet wide, thus formed, he caught sight of a writhing mass of human forms. He made one frenzied but futile effort to force back the door, and then rushed upstairs by another way into the dress circle, from which position, by strenuous efforts he succeeded in stopping the further flow of children to the staircase. He then hurried back to the door, where he saw at once that theonly means of rescue was to pull the bodies one by one through the two-feet aper- ture already mentioned, and with th 3 assistance of a man named Frank Rain, residing at 4, Howick-street, who was passing the hall at the time, and who williugly gave his ser- vices, the ghastly task was commenced. Graham says there must have been at least two hundred bodies behind the dcor, and as they were hauled out, there was some danger of delaying the work of rescue, by block- ing with the little corpses the passage or lobby between the outer doer and the door which had caused the awful catas- trophe. But further help fortunately arrived in the person of Dr. Waterson and others, and as soon as a body was pulled out by Graham, it was rapidly examined, and if dead laid out in the area or dress circle. If the little sufferer still lived—and the signs of vitality were often difficult to detect—he was at once conveyed to the Infirmary er the Palatine Hotel, and other houses in the vicinity, where their injuries were tenderly cared for by Dr. Beattie, Dr. Murphy, Dr. Dixon, Dr. Wilford, and other physicians, who were promptly on the spot, and devoted themselves ungrudgingly to the work of mercy. The conduct of the cabmen of the town was also beyond all praise. They flocked to the hall with their vehicles, and rendered valuable help in conveying the injured to the Infirmary and elsewhere. Ere long Graham had completed his work, and it was ascertained that some 166 little corpses lay in pitiful array in the dress circle and area of the building, which had so recently been ringing with their childish laughter. Meanwhile the dreadful news had spread like wildfire through the town, and the hall was soon besieged by thousands. The excitement was indescribable, mothers screaming for their children, and fathers fiercely striving to force their, way into the building It was, however, deemed prudent not to admit anyone until the work of rescue had been completed, but the gentlemen, all of them full of sympathy and compassion, who volunteered to assist in the necessary but unthankful work of keeping beck the e,x- cited crowds, found it a most difflault task, especially at the lower door in the Borough-road. When at length Graham had completed his mournful labours, in the perfermance of which his energy and nerve were beyond all praise, thole claiming to be the parents of missing children or of children who attended the perfor- mance at the hall were admitted in batches And conducted to the area and dresa circle, where ensued heartrending scenes which will be indelibly impressed upon the memory of all whose painful duty it was to witness them. There was a continuous wailing and sobbing from scores of men and women as they picked their w 4 amongst the rows of corpses seeking to identify missing ones, and now and then a louder outburst of grief served to show that the face of a loved one had been recognised. If unsuccessful in the area the searchers were conducted to the dress circle. Many women repeatedly fainted, and all were almost completely overcome with grief. One affecting case was that of a poor woman whom Councillor Erringtan was sympathetically aesisting in her search. As she accidentally touched a corpse with her dress a man said to her, perhaps somewhat roughly, "Don't stand upon them." She replied, "Good God, I have too many of my own to stand upon them." The tin- fortunate woman a few minutes afterwards discovered three of her own children amongst the dead, and fainted. A boy named Alfred Dixon, one of the rescued, said that when he got into the crush the feeling which came over him was like going to sleep until someone caught hold of him and pulled him out of the heap of bodies. He then heard hi a little brother Charley say, " Don't let go of my hand, as someone is standing upon my face." He was pulled aeray, however, and the brother was subsequently found among the dead. Outside the hall such a sight has never h,fore been pre- sented. A few years ago, at the pit, after the Seaham colliery explosion, the sight was appalling, but hero to- night men were to be seen in the public streets carrying away in their arms the dead bodies of their children with a white cloth over their faces. The children had been ex, amined and found lifeless before they were given up to their parents or relatives at the front entrance of the ball. Every few minutes a parent or a friend carried out a dead body and got into a cab, which drove them to their reaidence. As they left the door orthe hall in the cab, the fathers with dead children upon their knees showed signs of great grief, and in cases where the methers had identified their little ones, the spectacle was heartrending. Some cried and implored to he allowed inside the building, and the police endeavoured in the kindest manner to help those seeking their children. The Victoria Hall, in which the sad cataeirophe occurred, has a double frontage facing the Tower-road and Murton- street, the gable overhanging the Borough-road. The building is a very capacious one, being the largest in Sun- derland. About live years ago a great, though unsuccessful, effort was made to obtain it for a town hall. The interior of the structure is divided into three parts—the hod of the hall, which seats about 1,000 pereons, the gallery, which has sitting accommodation for 1,100 adults, and the dress circle, which is elegantly upholstered, will seat COO or 700. It was not occupied to any extent, but the gallery and the body of the hall were crowded mostly with children. At the close of the conjuring en- tertainment, when the distribution of prizes took place, there was much excitement on the part of the children in all parts of the building. As already stated toys had been given away downstairs, and those in the gallery were on the way down to participate In the dis- tribution. From the top of the gallery down to the street there are four flights of stairs with passages intervening. Leaving the gallery the steps are approached through fold- ing doors, which open outwards, upon which plan, in fact, all the doors from the various perts of the hall are arranged. It was'at the bottom of the third flight of steps where the sad catastrophe happened. There are about a dozen steps, at the foot of which is a doer, which opens inwardly, not outwards. Unfortunately the door was almost closed, as al- ready stated, being, we understand, from 20 to 24 inches. From the jamb there was a hole into which the door was bolted so that only one person could pass through at a time, and an arrangement suitable for checking those going in, but a tremendous barrier to a crowd making its exit. On Monday morning the following mesrage was re- ceived from the Queen:—" From Sir Henry Pensonby Balmoral, to the Mayor of Sunderland.—The Queen is ter-. ribly shocked at this awful calamity, and her heart bleeds for the many poor, bereaved parents. She prays that God may support them. Her Majesty is most anxious to hear how the injured children are.' The Mayor at once replied as follows :—" To Sir Henry Ponsonbv.—Will you please express to the Queen my heartfelt thanks for her very kind expressions of sympathy. The calamity is almost without a parallel, and the town is deeply affected. Will forward newspaper for her Majesty's perusal." Many pathetic instances are told of the losses to families. One poor woman' a Mrs. Mills, lost four, and it has caused such a shock to her system that it was feared she would have died. A rumour gained currency to that effect; upon inquiry, however, it was ascertained that, although still very weak, hopes were entertained that Mrs. Mills would recover. Some children who bad been delayed in the home coming by the disaster, on being questioned as to vi hat kept them so long, innocently replied, "Oh, ma, we all fell asleep on the stabs." One man was seen emerging from the Victoria Hall with a little girl in his arms; the child's long hair floating over her face, and her pallid cheek showed that death bad claimed its victim, and the f Aber passionately kissed the cold face and bewailed his bereavement in tones that deeply moved the bystanders Among the many diatressing features in connection with this dreadful affair, that of mistaken identity was not the least agonising. A number of children taken away in the excitement of the moment were afterwards returned to the ball, the poor people having been misled as to the identity of the shapeless little 111:19FPA of humanity they had carried away with them. In one particular case a father took home a little boy by mistalee. and af‘er arriving there, found it was the body of a neighbour's child. In the meantime his own boy had been recovered alive, and was treated with all the care and skill possible, but the little fellow died in the

morning. Anothar touching incident related to one of the unfortunate victims, Barbara Blakey, ten years. Prior to going to the hall her last words to her father were "Be sure and get me a nice flower on Sunday to say my piece in at the anniversary." The flower was got, and adorns the lifeless form of the child.

Inquests upon the bodies were opened during Monday. In the evening a great town's meeting took place, about 2,000 persons being present. The Mayor presided. A reso- lution was passed placing on record an expression of heart- felt sorrow at the fearful calamity which had taken place at the Victorial Hall, and of deep sympathy with the grief- stricken parents and relatives of the deceased children. A subscription fund was instituted for the purpose of rendering assistance to any who might require aid under the distress- ing circumstances, and to mark the event by some suitable memorial to be hereafter decided upon. r Mr. Fay, the conjuror, has made a statement denying that he left the hall without hearing of the accident. He says he remained in Sunderland through the night. He was, he states, attending to his apparatus on the stage when his assistant came running to him in a fainting condition, and said, "Oh, dear, they are all slipped down, and some are dead; and lam nearly killed." Mr. Fay goes on to say that he then rushed to the dress circle lobby, where he saw two children lying appirently unconscious, and three men amongst the children near at hand. He did not think the two little boys were dead, so he rushed off to get a doctor. He met one in the street, and took him to the hall door. BY that time some hundreds of people were there, and he went off again in search of policemen to keep order. The assistant has since told Mr. Fay that the children came quietly out of the gallery, and that he called to them, "Pass on, pass on." For a time they seemed to leave the hall by the stairs all right, but then he noticed a block, and in going amongst the children saw that a crush was taking place. Nearly one-half of the children must have got safely down the gallery stairs and out of the hall before the block took place. An im- pression has got abroad that tho first of the children that left the gallery caused the block, but that was not so. Mr. Fay conjectures that some of the children, in passing down the stairs, pulled the folding doors from the wall, and that the bolt then dropped into the socket.

A statement hii also been made by Mr. Fay's manager, who says an assistant went to the gAllery to give the pre- sents to the children. He believes that the stock of presents must have become exhausted, and that turning to leave the gallery for more, the children rushed after him down to the landing, when the crush occurred. Then, continues the manager, he believes that some of them must have got be- hind the door and gradually pushed it forward until it came over the hole ii which the bolt was fixed. It was a loose bolt, and he thinks there is no doubt that it fell into the hole and so the crusla occurred.

The interment of nearly 90 of tie victims took place on Tuesday in the three cemeteries which are connected with the town. The greatest number of bodies, 53, were interred in the Bishopwearmouth cemetery, situated about two miles from the town. Throughout the whole route the reads were lined with vast crowds of people, who were most respectful and sympathetic in their demeanour. Most of•the houses and shops had drawn blinds, and the flags on the churches and public buildings were hoisted half-mast high. The shipyards and other works were for the most part closed, and workpeople crowded the main thoroughfares to wateh the hearses and mourning coaches, of which there was a constant procession throughout the afternoon. At one of the cemeteries an address was delivered by the Rev. W. A. McGonigle, who referred to the common sympathy which had been shown from the Queen on her throne to the lowest in the land for those who had Buffered in the terrible calamity which had come upon the town. At Ryhope cemetery there were eleven interments.

div.head: LATER DETAILS.
div.p: LATER DETAILS.

By the identifications which have taken place, and a death which occurred on Tuesday night, it is now ascertained al- most beyond doubt that the number killed by the Victoria Hall disaster is 182. The reason that larger numbers have bekn given is that the names of some children were reported twice.

Charles HasseDina, Mr. Fay's assistant, has made a state- ment, in which be denies the truth of the boy Wilson's story about his closing and bolting the door which caused the accident. He says he gave the presents away at the top of the stairs, but was forced down by the rush of the children, and the door, which had been wide open when he went up, was partially closed. He sip if the dress circle had not been locked not a fraction of the loss of life would have occurred.

Her Majesty the Queen sent, through Sir Henry Ponson- by, on Wednesday morning, the following telegram to the Mayor of Sunderland :—The Queen wished to send a gentle- man of the Royal Household to represent Her Majesty at the funeral, but understands there will he no public funeral. Please inform me if there will be any public ceremony or manifestation of feeling at the sad -event." To this his worship replied, stating that through unavoidable circum- stances no public funeral could be held. Her Majesty's gracious sympathy was fully appreciated. The work of interring the bodies of those killed was con- tinued on Wednesday, ninety-one burials taking place at the three cemeteries in that town. Among the expressions of sympathy received by the Mayor is one from the " Presi- dent pro. tern, of the Irish Republic," who generously de- clines to allow political animosities to interfere with his offer of condolence and sympathy with the bereaved. The Mayor of Sunderland has set an excellent example. If it be agreeable to the subscribers, he is prepared to himself erect a monument commemorative of tho disaster, and so leave all other subscriptions free to be applied to the erection of a memorial charitable institution. Whether this idea be carried out or not, it is clear that the public sub- scriptions will he large, and will result in the establishment of a valuable public institution. Although the excitement consequent upon the sad disaster is gradually abatiug, it still continues the su',)ject of conver- sation in the town. The Mayor received a telegram on Thursday from Sir H. Pensonhy, Balmoral, stating th.e Empress of Germany had expressed to the Queen her d

sympathy with the families of the sufferers. - Messages of sympathy were also sent by the Mayors of Middlesborough and Huddersfield. William Robinson, keeper of the Argo Fcigite Inn, died on Thursday morning from apoplexy, sup- posed to have been induced by excitement in his efforts to save life at the hall. Only eight bodies were interred at Bishopwearmouth Cemetery on Thursday, and three at Ryhope-road Cemetery. Some scores of Sunday school children followed the remains of a brother and sister, named. James Oliver Elliott and Elizabeth Watt Elliott. Dr. Mor- deg Douglas, senior physician of Sunderland Hospital for Sick Children, has received a letter from the Dowager Lady Wilford, enclosing a cheque for five guineas for the benefit of a little girl in hospital, named Mary Elizabeth Fox, which happens to be Lady Wilford's own maiden name. Dr. Douglas has replied that he will hand the donation to the ladies' committee for the purpose specified.

1 The removal of an Earlesto vn man to Rainbill ; Asylum on Saturday last has given rise to a great deal of conversation about his amusing and peculiar ; movements during the last week or two. The unfortunate person who has thus obtained an unenviable notoriety has been out of work for over two years. This ' fact appears to have preyed upon his mind, and the poor 1 fellow—who is married, and has a wife and some children— has latterly been low-spirited and in a deeponding state of ; mind. During the past fortnight he had given evidence that 1 his intellect was becoming deranged. From his recent I actions it would seem that he suffered under the ' delusion that he had been suddenly transformed into a wealthy lord or a person of some considerable means. One of the methods by which he proceeded to put his " ideas " into execution was to visit tradesmen of the town and give orders for various articles and work to be done, while oc- casionally he would enter some of the public-houses and call for a glass of beer. After being served with the liquor he would drink it, and when asked for the money he would contemptuously demand to know if they wished to insult him. It would be ascertained that he was without money, and he would then leave the house apparently under the impression that his " dignity " had been offended. Accerding to the many statements made respecting his strange proceed- ings, it would appear that he went to the residence of a builder in the town, and gate an order for a lam) number of houses and property to he erected. He afterwards visited the place of business of a master painter and paper-hanger, and stated that he was building eight new houses and he engaged him to paint and paper them; while a prominent upholsterer and furniture dealer received an order to completely furnish the houses with costly furniture. Not very long afterwards he turned up at a well known "store," and stated that he wanted two sacks of flour, a flitch of bacon, and a ton of sugar sending to his house directly and without a moment's delay; while in another department of the same business premises he ordered a large number of articles, including furniture and brushes, and some of the latter, it is said, he even took with him. As the goods were not forthcoming as soon as he apparently wished them, he again visited the stores, and enquired why they had not been sent. At the house of a well- known publican in the same street he gave ap order for a barrel of beer to be forwarded to his residence. It would seem that this satisfied every- thing with the exception of his personal appearance, which he apparently did not forget. As befitted such a person of his "elevated position," he visited one of the principal clothing and outfitting shops in the town and 'wanted measuring for clothing amounting in value to many pounds, and not content with this he entered another business estab- lishment and ordered six new white shirts. It is stated that his conduct at home was far from echat it ought to have been and hikwife at times has been much afraid that he would commit some rash act. For his own benefit and the safety of others it was deemed advisable to remove him to , an institution where he would be properly looked after and attended to, and this was carried into effect, as previously stated, on Friday last.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL SCHEME.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL SCHEME.

The Select Committee of the House of Commons con'', tinned its consideration of the Manchester Ship Canal Bil' on Monday, Sir Joseph Bailey presiding. Mr. Henry Law, C.E., called on behalf of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, considered the estimate of Mr. Lyster of the cost of the works contemplated in the Mersey was certainly not over estimated; if anything, it was a liitle under the mark, especially in the item of repairs. He believed that the training walls could not be made on the sand. The only way of making the channel would be to dredge it at the moment of making it, and to let down the stone for the training walls as the dredging proceeded, so that the walls would rest in the first instance on the bed of the river, instead of having been lowered down on drifting sand. The promoters recalled Mr. Messent, engineer, to give rebutting evidence in regard to the cost of dredging. —Mr. Rodwell, Q C., then addressed the committee on be- half ef the Mersey Dock Board. Physically he admitted that the undertaking could be carried ont, but financially he did not. Considering the vague, indefinite nature of the scheme, he felt sure the committee would not for one moment put Liverpool in jeopardy, more especially as he appeared net for any private interests, but on behalf of the public. He thought it had been shown that the works in the Mersey would be most dangerous and attended with great risk to Liverpool, and he challenged the promoters to show, as had been stated, that similar works had been suc- cessfully carried ont on other rivers.—The learned coun- sel hid not concluded his address when the committee adjourned.

On Tuesday, Mr. Rodwell, Q C., resumed his address. Whatever the result of the inquiry might be, many doubted whether the scheme could be carried to a practical con- clusion under the powers of the Mersey Conservancy Act. Mader these circumstances he asked the committee not to give their assent to a scheme brought before them in such a crude and questionable shape. The promoters had failed to satisfy the committee that they could carry out the works in accordance with any plans recognised by engineers or men of science, and that they would not be able to raise the money necessary to carry out the scheme supposing they had the legal power, and he asked the committee, in the interests of Liverpool and Birkenhead, not to imperil the grand estuary of the Mersey or the magnificent docks at those two places, as it was a question of national con- cern, in order to satisfy what might be the folly, or perhaps jealousy or cupidity, of the Manchester people promoting this bill.—Mr. John Davies agent of Mr. Henry Vyner, the owner of Wallasey Pool and a large adjoining estate of 1,000 acre, said his employer's property had been " nursed " for many years as intended dock estate. Some £19,000 had been expended upon it, and if anything were done to the river that prevented its being made into docks, that money would be thrown away.—Mr. Henry Robertson, M.P., C.E., fromerly engineer to the Birkenhead Railways, and Mr. Vyner's engineering adviser, also gave evidence.—The case of the Birkenhead Corporation was next proceeded with. —Mr. John Laird, ex-Mayor of Birkenhead, stated that the Corporation were the owners of Woodside Ferry. Great difficulty had been caused on the Liverpool side by the Pluckingharn .74ank, and the Woodside Ferry traffic at low- water had been moved northwards: but if a similar state of things occurred 'at Woodside the same arrangement could not be carried out, owing to the small size of the landing- 'stage there.—Mr. Higgins then addressed the committee on behalf of the Birkenhead Corporation, and the committee adjourned. Cue committee met again on Wednesday. Mr. Dudgale, Q.C., opened the else for the Shropshire Union Railway and Canal Company, and said that the canals of the com- pany were over 200 miles in length, and they had Ellesmere Port as their port of import and export. Their trade con- sisted of all sorts of merchandise carried in coasters varying from 130 to 400 tons, the majority of which cline from the South of Englandlwith china clay, or from ports in Cum- berland and Lancashire with iron ore. They had a great trade with Liverpool, Runcorn, and Garston, and imported a large quantity of grain, exporting a large quantity of manu- factured iron good's from the Midland districts and the black country. The result was that the traffic going in and.out of Ellesmere Port was something over 300,000 tons in 1882, and he believed it had been rapidly increasing since. The company had three river steamers, seven canal steamtugs, over 100 flats, and nearly 400 ordinary canal boats. In view of the general policy of the country to keep open the canal system, it was right that nothing should be done to prevent the company obtaining that access to the sea which they now enjoyed. There was a branch channel connecting El- lesmere Port with the main channel, and this enabled coasters ;to enter and leave Ellesmere Port at certain timee of the tide. It was obvious that if the channel of the river was inter- fered with as was proposed by the promoters of the bill, the branch channel from Ellesmere Pert would not be left as it was now, but would silt up.—Mr. G. R. Jebb, engineer to the Shropehire Union Railway and Canal Company, gave evi- dence in support of Mr. Dugdale's statement. Sir W. B. Forwood was called, and stated that he had made calcula- tions of the cost of 100 bales of cotton from Now Orleans to Liverpool, and of 100 bales from New Or- leans to Manchester by the ship canal. The coat to Manchester would hi £lOl 19s 61, and the ' cost delivered at a railway station in Liverpoel would be £9B Os lid. The total saving on 100 bales of cotton would, therefore, be £3 18s 74, but that would be swallowed up by the railway transit between Liverpool and Manchester. Only a small portion of the cotton consumed in Lancashire was consumed 4,...Manchester. In the course of a year 50,000 tons of cotton went to Manchester, se that that amount of cotton would benefit to the amount of the difference between the cost of carriage and £3 185 7d per 100 bales. The total number of spindles in the United ' Kingdom was 41,000,000, of which 32000,000 were in Lan- cashire, 3,500,0G0 in Cheshire, principally at Stockport, 4,500,000 in Yorkshire, and 1,000,000 in Scotland. He had taken the published returns of 1879 as to the Number of spindles, and added 5 per cent. The number of epindles which would be benefited by the canal would be 23,500,000. Taking all the charges, there would practically be no ad- 'vantage to Blackburn by sending cotton by the canal to Manchester. There was a difference in favour of Liverpool in the sending of cotten to Blackburn . and Oldham, Wigan, Chorley,Tyldesley, Stockport, Bolton. Leigh and Bedford. Oldham was the largest manufacturing' ' centre in Lancashire, but he thought that Manchester would receive the largest amount of benefit, because there would be no railway carriage. At Oldhan9 about 3.000 tons par week were worked, or about 15,000 bales. The result )! taking a ship to Manchester was to increase the ocean ' freight by five per cent, and the insurances per cent. There would be a saving to certain districts engaged in the , cotton trade of £41,400 a year. but they must strike off against that the Liverpool balance of .£14,000 odd, so that the net saving for the whole cotton trade of Lancashire would not be more than £26,894. According to his calcula- tion, taking 15 per cent. extra freight to Manchester and , per cent. extra insurance, the result of sending ocean steamers to Manchester would be that there would be no profit at all.—Mr. Pereber asked witness several questions as to cost between Liverpool and Manchester, and, after several calculations, it woe agreed that the committee should be furnished with the figures on the following day in the form of an analysed statement. If 100 bales of cotton were sent from Liverpool to Manchester by rail, the cost would ,be 8s per ton, and, 100 bales weighing 2211. tons, the total amount would be £8 18s Bd. To this had to be added cart- age, which would make the cot at the mill at Manchester £lOB 13s id, against £lOl Les 64 if sent by the canal. The £248, the cost of going to Manchester by the canal, in- cluded £l3O for the use of the canal, £l5 for a steemtug, and £B3 for demurrage. Ire considered th at the railway , rates were excessive, but did not think that making the canal was the way to cure that.—The Chairman said that he wished to attend the quarter sessions next week, and it was agreed that the com:nittee should adjourn on Monday Inext till the following Thursday.

At Thursday's sitting of the Canal Committee, Mr. Pem- ber, counsel for the promoters, intimated that an agreement had been arrived at with the Mersey and Jrwell and Budge- water Navigation Companies, whose undertakings would be purchased by the Canal Company.—Mr. Aspinall, for the Corporation of Liverpool, then addressed the Committee, contending that if the powers sought were granted Liver- pool and its trade would be at the mercy of the acting Mer- sey Conservator, Admiral Spratt, and Mr. Leader Williams. Subsequently the Committee heard evidence from a ferry owner at Tranmere, The bill proposes to acquire the Man- chester Racecourse, which Mr. Mark Price, the secretary, described as the property of a company with a capital of £40,000, of which £28,000 was paid up. The present price of their £lOO shares was £550, and he considered that the sum of £171,000, set apart for compensating the Company and three other landowners, was not sufficient to satisfy their own reasonable claims. Evidence was given in behalf of other landowners, the case of Sir Humphrey de 1 rafford being under consideration when the Committee adjourned.

LORD R. CHURCHILL AND MR. GLADSTONR.—The text of the communications which have passed between Lord Ran- dolph Churchill and Mr. Gladstone respecting the real authors of the massacres at Alexandria on the 11th June, 1882, has been published. On the 12th inst. Lord Randdph wrote to Mr. Gladstone asking whether, if a full statement and the evidence upon which he relied were placed in the Premier's hands, it would be impartially examined with the view to furher independent inquiry either in Egypt or by hearing evidence in this country. On the 16th inst. Mr. Gladstone replied that in any steps the Government take they would have due regard to-the position of the Khedive as ruler of Egypt, and to the responsibilities under which they lay with reference to the peace and welfare of that country. Lord Randolph Churchill wrote on the same day accepting this "as indicating that the Government were fully alive to the odious possibility of maintaining on the throne of Egypt a man who could be proved guilty of having successfully plotted tbe massacre of a number of the Queen's subjects " in order that he might thereby more effectually compass the ruin of a popular Minister. He accordingly promises within the next few days to supply a circumstan- tial indictment against the Khedive, and to bring forward witnesses to establish its truth.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

Sir Rutherford Alcock, chairman of the British North Borneo Company, writes discrediting the telegram announ- gin the massacre of the company's servants in Borneo. t•-- The Duchess of Connaught distributed the prizes at the Military College, Oxford, on Saturday, and the students -.Were subsequently addressed by the Duke of Connaught. On Monday, Mr. J. V. Jones, principal of Firth -College, Sheffield, was elected principal of the new South Wales '‘College, at a salary of £7soa year. A 'meeting, attended by about fifty workingmen, has reeolved to invite Mr. James Samuelson to becotue a labour candidate for Liverpool at the next Parliamentary vacancy. Mr. Errington, M.P., writes from Paris to contradict the statement that the republication by the Propaganda of the " Apostolic Acts" relating to Ireland was owing to his aggestien, or in any way his act or due to him. Mr. William Simpson, who had been a prominent man in Liverpool public life for many many years, died suddenly on Saturday. Mr. Simpson was at various times a candidate !or Liverpool. He also contested Preston in the labour - interest. The divorce case, Howarth v. Howarth, in which Mrs. Zowarth sued for a divorce on account of her husband's ernelty and adultery, concluded on Monday in a verdict for the petitioner, a decree nisi being granted with costs and the Custody of the child. . An unusually large amount was raised on Sunday by the annual school sermons at St. George's Church, Bolton. The Collections for years have continued to increase, and at Present show no signs of going backward. The scholars number 1,800, and the collections during the day realised over £350, exceeding last year by about £B. •The Home Secretary has appointed Mr. Henry Fielding -Dickens of the South-Eastern Circuit (second son of the late Charles Dickens), to the Recordership of Deal, *vacant by the recent appointment of. Mr. Dixon, Q.C. as a metropolitan Polka magistrate. Mr. Dickens was called to the Bar at the Inner Temple in 1873. Mr. Sergeant Wheeler, judge of the Brompion County Court, and formerly well known as a solicitor, and then bar- rister, in Manchester, died on Friday evening at his London residence, Holland Park Terrace. He was educated at the Manchester Grammar School, and afterwards proceeded to Cambridge.- For some time he was judge of the Salford Hun- dred Court of Record, and in 1873 succeeded to his last ()facial position. DREADFUL DEATH or A MINER —An inquest was held on Monday, at Halesoveen, respecting the death of a miner named Weston, who was killed at Manor Colliery, near Rai esowen. The deceased had occasion, early on Saturday, morning, to go down an incline in the pit, and, in con- sequence of his either falling asleep or stumbling, he was knocked down by six trucks and was disembowleeand par- tially decapitated. The occurrence was believed to be a Pare accident. _ _

_ Cheerful accounts continue to be given of harvest pros- Picts. In England and France the backwardness consequent on the coldness of the spring has been nearly overcome; in Germany the wheat plant is described as healthy; in Austria and Hungary the prospect is more hopeful than was recently thought; and though the condition of whearin the United States is not now so good as at this time last year, the area Of spring wheat is larger, and the Canadian harvest will give a much increased yield. On the whole, there need be no fear of dearer bread, and though the English hay crop Will probably be light, its quality is highly spoken of. LORD CARNARVON ON ENGLISH AND A M SILICAN AGRICULTURE. —Lord Carnarvon, speaking at the dinner of the Marlborough and Pewsey Vale Agricultural Association, Newbury, on Tuesday, referred to the improved aspect of agriculture after a lengthened depression caused by bad seasons and American competition. America had, be said, nuns, advantages in breeding cattle, in climate, and space; but in several kinds of stock the English were decidedly superior to the Americans. In poultry, also, England ex- celled. He considered something more was needed to pre- vent the importation of contagions diseases with animals, and improvements should be made in the incidence of the rates and the railway charges. George Atkins and Caroline Atkins, husband and wife, Were charged at Oldham' on Saturday, with neglect of their Children. The prisoners had three children, the oldest aged 81; whom they left in a house in Morton-street by them- selves and then decamped. A neighbour took them in Charge, and the children were afterwards conveyed to the Workhouse: They were in a dirty and squalid condition. at. Evans, relieving officer, stated that thelemale came to he workhouse on Thursday, and said she f'as a "friend" sj. the children, pretending that she VMS not their mother. The husband accused his wife of drunkennessand habitually. Pawning the children's clothing. The prisoners were sent to gaol for two months with hard labour.

THE PHCENIX PARK TRAGEDY: WANTON DESTRI7CTION Intsumnie.--For tome few weeks past a prominent feature in Alsop's waxworks exhibition, Liverpool, has been life-size wax flgore4 of Lord F. Cavendish and Mr. Burke being attacked in the Pkenix Park by the Invincibles. On Saturday night four young Irishmen, apparently sober, entered the room set apart for these figures. One jumped Over the brass rail and deliberately knocked down the figure of Cavendish, trampling it under foot, whilst the other three demolished the wax figures of the Invincibles, junep- Ling on the debris. Three of the four were secured, and ....4atuled to the police, and they have been brought up at the 3/44terpool police court and committed for trial. Point of considerable interest to managers of elementary ,eohools has been raised by the managers of St. Peter's 40tnan Catholic School, Liverpool, who wrote to the Educa- tion Department to know whether "if a child be persist- entiv. habitually, end inexcusably irregular " in attendance at school, they would be justified in refusing admission. The department replies, no, "the scholars should be at once lePorted to the School Board, whose duty it is to make them attend regularly." To the school managers this reply Means that they must continue to keep on the rolls children vtho will never earn the G ,veniment grant; and to the, 801100 l Board it means that an officer must be kept to attend ecially-to each Wilful amid persistent truant player. The -.Liverpool truant school system ought, however, to help nesth managers and the hoard out of this difficulty. „ LORD R. CHURCHILL AND MANCHESTER.— It was men- some days ago that Lord B.
