div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 23, 1883
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 23, 1883

r An explosion occurred on Tuesday at the tar distillery of Mr. Ellison, of Steavor Bottoms, near Rochdale, doing much damage, but no personal injury. The Exchequer returns from June Ist to June 16th shows —Receipts, £17,693,084; expenditure, £16,458,022: bal- ances, £7,423,898. Corresponding period of last year— Receipts, £16,963,681; expenditure, £16,198,759; balances, £6.280,021. Mr. Irving Bishop has written declining Mr. Labouchere's new offer to test his powers of thought-reading until the hon. dumber has paid the bet which, iii Mr. Bishop's opinion he lost in the early part of the week. It is quite certain that Mr LabOnchere will not pay the money. There is, therefore, no prospect that this second test will be applied. Mr. Justice Chitty, in the Chancery Division, on Monday, dismissed the petition in reference to the custody of the young Jewess Rose Rosenberg, it being admitted that the girl was now beyond the jurisdiction of the court; but his lordship made no order as to costs, as it appeared from the evidence that it was through Miss Burke Mr. Rosenberg lost the custody of the child.

On Monday afternoon a gentleman precipitated himself from the Great Eastern express near Chelmsford, and was instantaneously killed. He had upon him a card bearing the address Mr. J. F. Skipper, Pump Court, Temple. The body was removed to the mortuary. On Tuesday a Lon- don correspondent was informed that the body was that of Mr. Skipper, who for some time has been in a desponding state of mind. DROWNING ACCIDENT.—STRANGS CONDUCT OF A BRO. THER.—An inquest was held at Tipton, on Friday, on Alfred Curtis, who was drowned in the presence of his brother and another spectator. The brother said he was so troubled that he went to tell his mother, and so did nothing to res- cue his brother. The other adult said he had brain fever, apd could not enter water. Tke coroner censured the brother.

Lord Salisbury, acknowledging a resolution passed by the Glssgow East-end. Conservatives, says he is gratified to receive the kind assurance of their continued confidence and support, and helhinks they will not abate their efforts to promote the spread of Conservative opinions in Scotland, Sir Stafford -Northcote, acknowledging the same resolu- tion, says he will do his best to encourage some of his Conservative friends to go to Glasgow whenever it can be managed. _ .

THE FIRE ON I TRAINING SHIP.—It has now been dis- covered that the fire which occurred on board the training ship Mars, stationed in the Tay, off Dundee, about three weeks ago, and by which damage to the extent of £4,000 was sustained, was due to incendiarism. The Procurator Fiscal for Fifeshire, who has been prosecuting inquiries, has dis- covered that three boys on board set the ship on fire, out of revenge, it is stated, for some punishment they had received. The result cf the investigation has been reported to the Crown authorities in Edinburgh. SAD FATALITIES AT RIIABON.—On Tuesday night, a man named John Eveson, employed at the Plasmodoc stone quarries, met with a terrible death. He had fixed the tips of the crane to a huge stone which was-being lifted from a stack, when the stack rolled upon him, cutting his body in a shocking manner, and almost decapitatine. him.—On Tues- day .morning, a man named Evan Evans was terribly mutilated and killed at Wynnestay collieries. He was tak- ing a" stretcher" out of the roadway in the mine when a heavy fall of roof came down, death being instantaneous. THE COBDEN CLUB.—Lord Ampthill, Lord Arthur Rus- sell, M.P., Lord Moreton, MX., Mr. Goschen, M.P., Mr. Dandas, M.P., Mr. R. Creyke, M.P., Mr. Cartwright, M.P., and, it is said, other members of the Cobden Club, ,have resigned their connection with that institution. The cause, according to The Times, is "the admission as honorary members of one or two foreign politicians of an advanced, not to say revolutionary character, and an apprehended tendency of the club to depart from its original purpose of the dissemination of sound principles in political economy." ' ASSASSINATION BY A SOLDIER.—A communication just received from Ramleh narrates a deplorable tragedy. Two privates of the Duke of Cornwall's Light Infantry,quartered in Ramleh Barracks, were drinking at the canteen, and quarrelled. One, an Irishman, was called by the other, an Englishman, an "Irish Invincible." and a fight ensued but their comrades persuaded them to shake hands, and "hey went to the barrack room. The Englishman left shortly afterwards, and, on returning, was shot dead by the Irish- man who was immediately seized and awaits his trial for murder. No provocatian beyond what is stated above is known.

A SERGEANT DISMISSED AT A VOLUNTEER INSPECTION. —At the annual Government inspection of the First Volun- teer Battalion of the Queen's Royal West Surrey Regiment at Croydon, on Saturday afternoon, while an officer was giving instructions for the men to fsrm into companies, Sergeant Ward made use of some insulting observation, which, as it turned out, reached the ears of the officer. He at once reported the matter to Lieutenant Colonel Robinson, the commanding offwer, who, after consulting Col. Lloyd, the inspecting officer, ordered Ward to stand out of the ranks. A drummer then divested him of all his accoutre- ments, and he was dismissed the regiment, being ordered to leave the field forthwith.

_ THE RITUALISTIC DISPUTE AT SHEFFIELD.—Mr. Walter Wynn, the people's warden of St. Matthew's, Sheffi4d, has written to the Archbishop of York directing his Grace's at- tention to a sermon preached by the Rev. G. C. Ommanney on the anniversary of his coming to the parish. Mr. Wynn complains that the Archbishop, having ordered Mr. Om- malarkey by monition to make obedience, does not follow up his monition by compelling obedience ; and with regard to the Rev. Mr. Griffin, who assists Mr. Ommanney, Mr. Wynn says he is becoming increasingly insolent, and as he is not licensed to St. Matthew's it will be necessary to deal very summarily with him unless his Grace interferes to re- dress the grievances. VANDALISM AT BEAUMARIS CHURCIL—A circumstance of a very discreditable, and at present mysterious, character has occurred at Beaumaris Parish Church. Prominent in the chancel were the family paws of Sir Richard Bulkeley (the patron of the living) and of Colonel Hampton Lewis, both of which were last week demolished by some undis- covered vandal. At Tuesday's meeting of the Town Council, Mr. Watkins, the people's warden, after an allu- sion to a certain charity distributed by the rector, said that he and his fellow churchwarden (Mr. John Jones) wished publicly to disavow all knowledge of the demolition of the pews, and to express their regret at such an unseemly oc- currence. The pews had teen smashed to pieces, and who- ever bad done it had been guilty of most disgraceful con- duct. (Hear; hear.) Mr. T. Pritchard expressed his satis- faction at hearing such an emphatic denunciation of a most discreditable affair.

SUICIDE OF A YOUNG LADY.—AU inquest has been held at East Harnham, Wiltshire, on the body of Cerena Florence Hale, 20, a lady pupil at the Salisbury Diocesan Training College. About 10 o'clock on Monday morning the body was seen in the river by Mr. Russell, of Brighton, a gentle- man staying at Canon Gordon's, and who was fishing at the time. A medical man was at once called in when the corpse was removed from the water, but all efforts to restore animation were fruitless. Evidence was given to the effect that the deceased had gone into a garden near the river to gather woodruffe. and that she was not afterwards seen alive. Miss Rod Well, lady superintendent at the training school, said the parents of the deceased resided in London. The following letter was found in the desk of the deceased: Dear Ma,—l am deeply grieved to tell you that 1 have given way to temptation. You will hear all from Miss Rod- well, our lady superintendent. She has been kind to me throughout all, oh, so very kind. At the time I write this I feel out of mind. What to do Ido not know. I feel cer- tain that I shall be dismissed from the college, and rather than bring disgrace upon you and my vicar I will get rid of ;myself. I feel that I have done more than I can expect forgiveness for." A verdict of temporary insanity was the finding of the jury. REVIEW OF THE RESERVE SQUADRON. The reserve squadron was on Tuesday reviewed at Spithead by the Lords of the Admiralty. The ships were moored in two lines, the weather line being led by the flagship of Admiral Hoskins, and the lee line headed by the Hercules, late flagship of the Duke of Edinburgh. The Belleisle, guard- ship at Kingstown, was expected to have joined the sqnad- ron, but has been ordered to take up the post of guardship at Cowes while the Queen is at Osborne. The Admiralty were represented by the First Lord, Earl Northbrook; Sir A. C. Rey, Senior Sea Lord; Lord Alcester, Sir Thomas Brassey, and Captain Codrington ; and Mr. Campbell- Bannermann, secretary, who were met on board by the Com- mander-in-Chief, Admiral Hornby, and Flag-Captain Rowley. Their lordships proceeded on the Admiralty yacht Enchantress, a salute of 19 guns being fired from the Duke of Wellington, flagship of the harbour squadron, to Spithead, where a similar salute was fired from the Lord Warden, all the ships at anchor manning yards. No manceuvres were executed, the programme being rather an inspection than a review. Their lordships first boarded the Defence, where the men were put through drill and the vessel's equipment and condition inspected. Each ship was visited in succession. The inspection lasted from 11 a.m. to five p.m. The vessels sailed on Wednesday, the cruise extending as far as Norway and concluding on the 25th of next month.

A BURGLAR CAUGHT IN A CHIAINEY.—A burglar who was I caught in the chimney of a pawnbroker's shop in Padding- ton, Liverpool, has had an experience which will probably prevent him from ever again attempting to enter premises by so perilous a route as a flue. He went about his business very methodically. Failing to gain admittance by cutting the panel of a door, be left his boots and chisel at the rear of the premises, got upon the roof, put off his hat and coatsand having removed a chimney-pot, went down the chimney. But when he got a little way down he stuck fast, and could neither move upwards nor downwards. He had a chisel in his trousers pocket, and if he could have got his hand down to it he might have worked his way out. But this he could not do. He kicked his boots and stockings off, got rid of his trousers and underclothing, and then attempted to get the chisel out of his pocket with his foot, hut his Lfforts were in vain. Literally naked and in prison he now cried aloud for a deliverer, but as the chimney was bricked up at the bottom he could not he heard, and in this predicament he remained for airteen hours. Meanwhile his boots and chisel, left in the yard, bad been found, and further investi- , gation led to the discovery of his coat and hat on the roof. Then, looking down the chimney, the police saw the man himself, and were saluted with an imprecation at their slow- ness in arriving. The burglar was then hauled up by a rope, and on Tuesday was committed for trial at the sessions. Stveral other charges, however, have yet to be made against him.

A MAN WORRIED BY A SOW.—On Friday, while M. Durkan, the servant of a farmer, in the neighbourhood of Bangor. tried to extricate a young pig from some railings, he was attacked and worried in the hands and face by a sow which stood near.

TETE PREMIER AND LORD ROSEBERY.—Acknowledging resolution from the committee of the Scottish Liberal Club in reference to the resignation of Lord Rosebery, Mr. Glad- stone writes that he fully shares the regrets expressed bv I the committee, and joins in the hope that Lord Rosebery's abilities may ere long be again turned to account in active public service. MOVEMENTS IN TEE CIVIL SERVICE.—Eacise : Mr. C. Masson, Wigan second district, Warrington, to Abergavenny district, Hereford; Mr. J. Fox, Stornoway district, Inver- ness, to Wigan second district, Warrington; Mr. R. Hepen- stall, Wigan third ride, Warrington, to Swaffkam ride, Lynn; Mr. T. W. Daly, Main Preventive ride, Stirling. to Wigan third ride, Warrington. A brutal murder took place at midnight, on Tuesday, in Sunderland. Sergeant Carter, while going his rounds at Ayres Quay, saw a group of people and heard a man threaten- ing to kick another who was lying on the ground in an un- conscious state. The assailant proved to be a man named Marrs, and had kicked his brother George, aged thirty, severely. On medical assistance arriving, George was found dead.

THE SKYE CROFTERS' GRIEVANCES.—Mr. Fraser Mac- kintosh, M.P., opened the Inverness Free Library on Satur- day. Alluding to his escape, with other Royal Commis- sioners on the Skye Crofters grievances, from the wreck of the Lively, Mr. Mackintosh attributed it to the ability and sagacity of the officers and crew of the Lively. The Royal Commissioners had found, he said, that cruel wrongs had been inflicted on a noble people, whom no Government should neglect. ALLEGED MURDER BY AN HERBALIST.—An inquest was held at Chippenhana, Wilts, on Tuesday, on the body, of Mary Ann Salter, servant girl, who died last Saturday. The de- ceased had been in service several years in London, and re- turned home enciente. She was attended by Harriet Wig- more, herbalist, who administered drugs to procure abortion. After hearing medical and other evidence, the jary returned a verdict of murder against the woman Wigmore, and the coroner committed her for trial. A SLEEPING W/ITCHMAN.—Mr. Warton has narrowly escaped enforced imprisonment in the House of Commons through the night. In prospect of his appointed task of watching the orders through, the hon. gentleman took up his position in a quiet corner behind the Speaker's chair. Here he fell asleep, and remained in that condition till the whole Of the orders were disposed of, the Speaker had left the chair, and members had departed. He was fortunately discovered by one of the attendants after the ghs had been partially extinguished and the doors were about to be lecked. SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT.—As Mr. Bernard Charles Molloy, member for King's County, was passing through Leicester-square, London, late on Fri- day night, on his way to his chambers in the Temple, a heavy coping stone fell from one of the buildings in coarse of erection, cutting him severely about the head. He was at once conveyed to the Charing Cross Hospital, where his wounds were dressed, and he was subsequently removed to his chambers, where he now lies. The same medical gentle- man who attended him at the hospital saw him again on Saturday evening, and he reports that he is progressing as satisfactorily as could be expected, though he will probably be confined to his room for some days.

A NIGHT ADVENTURE IN A LIVERPOOL HOTEL.—At an early 11,4ur on Friday morning a police officer on duty near the Walker Art Gallery observed from the windows of a temperance hotel on Islington-flags several sheets and other bedclothes evidently intended for the purpose of getting out of the premises. On arousing the inmates he learned that one of the gentlemen staying in the house had been relieved of his silver watch and £1 in meney by a woman who had accompanied him to the place on the previous evening. Wqilst he was sound asleep he quietly rose from bel, and, after rifling his pockets, stealthily entered an adjoining chamber, which was unoccupied. Quickly divesting the bed of the sheets and blankets, she tied them in a rope, and having secured one end to the post she lowered herself down from the window, and managed to get away with her booty unperceived. SWEDENBORG SoarrY.—The seventy-third annual meet- ing of this society was held at 36, Bloomsbury-street London, W.C., on Tuesday, the 19th inst. Major Bevington presided. The following resolutions were submitted tqi the meeting:—" That in the opinion of this meeting it is or the utmost importance that all who desire to be freed from the thraldom of merely sensuous thought, and to believe in a personal Creator who has revealed Himself to men, should become acquainted with the theological writinge of Emanuel Swedenborg, in which the true doctrine of the One God, the Divinity of the Sacred Scriptures, the nature and laws of the Eternal World, and its connection with this, are un- folded to the rational understanding of men." "That the wide-spread indifference to religion which exists among the working classes may be most effectually combated by the diffusion among them of the doctrine of Use or Charity contained in the writings of Emanuel Swedenborg, and this meeting suggests that the new committee should issue one of the small works dealing with this subject at a price which will bring it within the reach of all."

COURT-MARTIAL ON Two NAVAL OFFICERS.—A court- martial was held on board Her 'Majesty's ship Victory, in Portsmouth Harbour, on Wednesday, for the trial of Sub- Lieutenant the Hon. Philip Bourchier Tyrwhitt and Seib- Lieutenant William James, who were charged with, being guilty of conduct unbecoming officers and using insulting language and behaving in a scandalous manner to occu- pants of a ship's galley in Mill Bay, on the 14th instant; behaving with contempt to Captain Adeane; making false statements in reply to Captain Adeane, of H.M.S. Shannon, as to what ship they belonged to. The inquiry lasted all day. The defence was that the accused did not know Captain Adeane was on board the galley, and that they had indulged in chaff towards the occupants on account of the crew causing them five minutes delay before they could board the boat. They had stated they belonged to the Shannon in a chaffing tone, thinking they had no right to be asked the question. The court, after long deliberation, dismissed the prisoners from the service. This c)urse was rendered imperative by the 28th section of the Naval Discipline Act. Wercetertarr IN ENGLAND.—A correspondent of the Times says—" There is no need to go to West Prussia for witch- craft towards the end of the 19th century. In a parish near where the counties of Devon, Dorset, and Somerset meet, a young man, being afflicted with scrofula, which caused at times contraction of the muscles of the right thighband very consideraMe pain, formed the idea that a poor, delicate! woman living next door, wife of a labourer, and mother of several children, had bewitched him, and one day, in his ; agony, rushed into her room with a large sewing-needle,- I and before the poor woman had time to think, scratched her severely in the neck, and in four places on her bare arm, drawing blood in each instance, then rubbed his hand on the blood and ran off. The poor woman came to me to complain, showing the scratches, and I advised her to take out a sum- mons before the the justices; but time passed. The young mau, as usual, felt relieved of his pains for a time, and his mother, a widow occupying a few acres of land with cows I and pigs tried to assure me that drawing the blood cured her son, pigs, she considered the other woman bad "overlooked" him. This happened some months ago, and I need hardly add that the young man has been several times since perio- dically similarly afflicted." • EXTRAORDINARY OUTRAGE BY GIRLS.—On Wednesday, at the Preston Police Court, Nancy and Sarah Ellen Isher- wood, aged respectively 10 and 12 years, the daughters of a labourer living in Bouverie-street, were charged with having committed an aggravated atliault upon Elizabeth Jolly, aged five years, the daughter of an operative cotton- spinner, living in Inkerman-street. Mr. Blackhurst con- ducted the prosecution; the prisoners were undefended.— On the evening of the 7th inst. the prisoners took the child Jolly, when she was returning from school, and walked about with her till dusk, when they went to an untenanted shop in Bouverie-street, and entering the yard by the, back doer they washed the child in a pool of dirty water, then undressed her and put her in the cellar under the shop, where she remained till next day, when she was accidentally discovered. Mrs. Jolly, the mother of the child, stated that when she did not come home they gave information to the police of the loss of the child. She was sent for next day to Mr. Nightingale's shop, at the corner of Bouverie-street, where she fond her daughter. She looked cold and exhausted, her eyes were closed up, and she was very ill. Seven hours passed before they coeld get the child warm, and she had been ill ever since. Mr. Walmsley, surgeon, said the child had received a very severe shock to the system, and had been in a very precarious state, but was now recevering. The Bench de- cided that the prisoners must he sent to an industrial school, and remanded them to the viorkhonse till the necessary ar- rangements were made. TEE LABOUR MAIMET.—The labour market, although in some localities still unsettled, is on the whole satisfac- tory. Building operations are active and on railway works especially the demand for men is gelid. In colliery districts labour is active, especially on the Wear and the Tyne, as most of the collieries are working fnll time. The colliers' strike in North Staffordshire continues, although to some extent it is not so brisk, many men having resumed work. Tin-plate industry is improving in the West; most of the works are fairly supplied with orders which will last some 'ime. At Sunderland, the bricklayers have struck for id

per hoar advance, but the masters refuse more than id, and the men remain idle. The bottle-making industry in that district is reviving rapidly; many of the old works have been re-started. A strike amcngst engineers is anticipated. The iron trade may be (rioted more active." Shipbuilders and marine engineers are busy in all districts. At Birming- ham all branches of trade are well employed, the supply of workpeople not being equal to the demand. At Sheffield workers at many of the workshops are extremely busy, and the strike in the file trade, which has lasted nearly three months, terminated on the 18th inst. by the men giving in to the 10 per cent. reduction. The teitile trades are not generally very active, although at Leicester hosiery weavers are well employed; while at Nottingham the hosiery machinery is barely kept going ; and in the lace trade some makers are restricting production as much as convenient. At Halifax the spinners of botanies are very busy; and at Leeds machinery is fully employed. At Kidderminster the carpet looms are well employed. The boot and shoe trade is quiet, production in some districts being curtailed. Haymaking and other agricultural pursuits are very brisk. Emigration continues good.—.tabour News. The most notorious eavesClropper ever known is—Rain. The international chess tournament is rapidly drawing to a close. The second prip (4175) was on luesday won by Steinitz.

The forty-sixth anniversary of the Quem's accession to the throne was celebrated throughout the country on Wed- nesday. The foundation stone was laid on Wednesday of a new dock which is being constructed at Cardiff by the Marquis of Bute, at a cost of L 500,000.

Mr. Murray, the Conervative member for Hastings, has announced his intention of reigning his seat in Parliament for reasons of a personal and private nature. Early on Wednesday morning, a man unknown was found dead at the bottom of a flight of stairs at the New Inn, Falsgrave, Scarborough. A review of all the troops in Portsmouth garrison was held on Wednesday in honour of the visit of Prince Mein- ingefi to Prince Edward of Saxe Weimar.

A despatch from Paris Boulogne says that L'Hoak will soon make a fourth attempt to cross the Channel, an it is proposed to start a subscription to defray the expenses. The Lord Mayor of Dublin has received a cablegram from Messrs. Redmond and Walsh, intimating that Aus- tralia guarantees £l,OOO to the Parnell tribute. It is believed that the Liverpool firm, which was to be- come a competitor for carrying the Irish mail between Holy- head and Kingstown, has retired, leaving the contest between the Irish Company and the London and North- Western Company. A labourer, named James Egan, living in Ormrod-street, was before the &Ron borough magistrates, on Wednesday. He was creating a row in the street, and on a sister attempt- ing to stop him fighting with a man he knocked her down and brutally kicked her, also knocking down his mother. He was an old offender, and was sent to prison for two months.

A child uamed Emma Waring, three years of age, daugh- ter of a coach builder in Richard Birch-street, Bury, was on Tuesday evening drowned in a dolly tub. The child was playing in the kitchen while washing was going on, and on the return of Mrs. Ashworth, the washerwoman, from hang- ing clothes in the yard, she found the deceased head first in the tub, which was half full of water. Between nine and ten o'clock on Wednesday morming, Benjamin Cornish, aged 60, employed at the Ash Inn Brewery, Heaton Norris, near Stockport, stabbed himself about six times in the region of the stomach with a penknife and afterwards threw himself into a vat of beer. Deceased had been off his work for over a week, but he returned on Monday last. In connection with the hearing of a charge of disorderly conduct against a private in the Lancashire Fusiliers at Bury, on Tuesday, it was stated that, under an order from the War Office, soldiers were allowed leave from Saturday night until Monday morning. The police superintendent informed the magistrates that, in Bury at least, the soldiers were a "great nuisance." There were strong objections against the men being let loose upon the town, and he in- tended to ask for the cancelling of the order. A exciting chase after an escaped prisoner is reported from Bolton-by-Bowland. John Baxendale, a navvy, who was committed for two months for larceny, escaped from custody at the Bolton=by-Bowland Police Court. Aa alarm was raised by a constable, and several police officers gave chase. The escaped prisoner leaped fences and crossed several fields, closely followed by the officers. The prisoner, however, was ultimately captured while he was in the act of climbing a gate, and he was safely landed in the police cell.

John Carroll, one of the most famous jockeys on the English turf 25 or 30 years ago, appeared on Wednesday morning in the Birmingham Police Court, without a coat to his back, ragged, and of dissolute appearance, charged with begging. Carroll has won many of the chief races, notably the Great Metropolitan Stakes two years in succes- sion—in 1852-3 ; the Lincolnshire Handicap in 1865, and others. It is stated that at one time he was worth many thousands of pounds. A week ago he was charged with mendicancy in the same court, and was discharged. He was now sent to gaol for one month, though he begged hard to be sent to the workhouse. He made a ramblingspeeck to the magistrate, interlarded with broken French, and by his incoherence evidently showed that his miral has been affected by his long dissipation. Met. GLADSTONE AND MIDLOTHIAN.—Mr. Gladstone has written a letter to his constituents in which his opponents will find no sign of despondency. The Premier refers to the circumstances under which he was unable to fulfil his promise to visit Midlothian in winter, and holds out a hope that he may yet be able to redeena his pledge, and at the same time be able to say, as he can say now, that he sees no sign of the disintegrating forces which were visibly at work before the break up of his last Administration, nor any rea- son to suppose that the country has at all changed its opinion since the general election. Tory critics fondly imagine that a great revulsion of feeling has passed over the country since 1880, but should Mr. Gladstone be able to go upon another Midlothian campaign, the enthusiasm which his visit to tcotland will arouse will go far to unde- ceive them.

SCOTCH LANDOWNERS AND THE Du KE OF BUCCLEUCH.— A preliminary meeting, composed of peers' members of Parliament, landowners, &c., connected with Scotland, was held, on Wednesday, at the Duke of Richmond's town re- sidence, when it was resolved that an opportunity should be given to the people of Scotland of recognising in some public manner their sense of the long and honourable career of the Duke of Buccleuch, and of the estimation in which he is held by all classes of the Scottish nation. Among those who were present, or intimated their concur- rence in the objects of the meeting, were the Dukes of Rich- mond, Argyle, and Roxburghe, the Marquises of Tweed- dale and Lothian, Earls of Stair, Wemyss, Haddingten, Rosebery, and Aberdeen, Lords Elphinstone, Saltoun, and Tweedmouth, Sir H. Maxwell, M.P., and Mr. Robert Jardine, M.P. A committee was appointed to carry out the prelimi- nary arrangements. . .

. - HANDEL'S "MESSIAH " IN 1784.—While so much has been done by "additional accompaniments" to bring Han- ders works down to the times ih which we live, we cannot ignore the fact that they were conceived under conditions totally different from those to which we are accustomed. The organ played a much more important part in the accom- paniments than it does now, and the orchestra of Handel's time was constituted in a manner altogether different from that in modern use. At the first Handel commemoration in 1784, for example, the band consisted of two hundred and fifty instruments, which included no fewer than twenty-six oboes and twenty-six bassoons. This number fairly repre- sents the proportion of these instruments in the bands of Handers time, and when we reflect that our modern orches- tras usually contain only two oboes and two bassoons, we shall have difficulty in realising the effect which must have been produced by such an excessive preponderance of reed- tone.—The Quiver for June. DEATH OF BISHOP COLENSO. A Durban telegram of Wednesday lasr announces the death of Dr. Colenso, first Bishop of Natal, in the seventieth year of his age. It was in 1853 that he-was appointed to his bishopric, and up to that time he was chiefly known as the author of standard treatises on arithmetic and alg,bra. In 1861, however, he began the publication of his fatuous work on the Pentateuch, in which he questioned the accuracy and Mosaic authorship of the first five books of the Bible, and so brought upon himself a charge of heterodoxy, which was endorsed by the Convocation of Canterbury, though by a small majority. The Metropolitan of Cape Town also declared him deposed from his See, but the deposition was declared by the Privy Council to be null and void; and Dr. Colenso was not only able to retain his office, but to compel the Council of the Colonial Bishoprics Fund to continue the payment of his salary. In South Africa Dr. Colenso chiefly distinguished himself by warmly espousing the cause of the natives, and if his advice had been taken there would have been no Zulu war. He has left behind him a Zulu grammar and dictionary, and a Zulu translation of the New Testament and of portions of the Bible and Prayer Book, as well as some educational works in the Zulu tongue. But over and above this he has vindicated the right to liberty of thought within the Eng- lish Church, and shown how confidently and calmly a great and Christiaß mind can withstand virulent perse- cution. _

THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES.—There was a good attendance on 'Change on Tuesday, with if anything a rather better feeling in the market. The weight of actual business doing is still not large, bat there are buyers. Where an advantage is to be gained in price and at a little under quoted rates, fairly good orders have been given out during the last few days. The business done has tended to give a little strength to the market, and makers are now less inclined to entertain low offers, although orders are still difficult to get at the full quoted rates. In Lanca- shire pig iron moderate sales bavelbeen made on the basis of 45s to 45s 6d, less 21, for forge and foundry qualities delivered equal to Maneheste? ; and in Lincolnshire iron business has been done in exceptional cases at as low as 445, but on an average at 445 4d for forge, and 45s 10d for foundry, less 21 delivered here. The finished- iron trade shows a slight improvement in some departments. There is more doing in sheets for shipment, and makers are stiffer in price, the average figures for delivery equatto Man- chester or Liverpnol bting now about 17s Gd to £8 per ton. Hoops, however, still meet with only an indifferent demand, at £6 10.3 to £6 12s 6d; and for bars the inquiry continues very slow, with orders difficult to get at the quoted price of £6 5s per ton delivered, and some under- selling to do business. The coal trade generally through- out the district continues very quiet, and it is exceptional where the pits are not working on a restricted output. Some of the collieries have been kept going about five days a week, but where this is the case a good deal of the coal is going into stock, and as the summer advances, the necessity for a curtailment of the get increases, many of the pits having already had to go on three to four days a week. House-fire coals move off very slowly, and although there is a fair de- mand for hard furnace coals, the common round coals gene- rally meet with only an indifferent demand. Except that some of the best qualities of slack are scarce, engine fuel generally continues plentiful in the market, with the common sorts a drug at some of the collieries. Quoted rates are without materiAl change, and colliery proprietors show a strong dis- inclination to enter into anything like forward engagements • at present rates, but for prompt sales prices are irregular, and where orders in bulk are to be secured, sellers in most cases are prepared to make some concession upon their list quotations. At the pit mouth pricesaverage about as under: Best coat, is; seconds, is to 7s 61 ; common round coal, 53 61 to 6s 3d; burgy, 43 6d to sa; good slack, 3s 9d to 4s 31, with some of the best sorts fetching 4s 6,1 ; but com- mon slack can be bought from 2s Od to 3s 3d per ton. In the shipping trade there has been a fair amount of activity but low prices are still taken to secure orders, steam coal . averaging is 3d to 7s 6d,tand seconds house coal 8s to 8s 6d per ton, delivered at Liverpool and Garston.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-MONDAY.

I MR. CHAMBERLAIN AT BIRMINGHAM. - The Royal ' assent was given by commission to several bills.—The Marquis of SALISBURY desired to know if the intimations of policy given by Mr. Chamber- lain at Birmingham were looked upon as the opinions of the Government.—Earl GRANVILLE replied that it was cbvious that the President of the Board of Trade stated, as he had done before, his own individual views and what he believed to be the views of his constituents. In no sense whatever was he stating those views as a member of the Cabinet, and still less as a member of Her Majesty's Government. Dur- ing the present Parliament the Government would present a bill or bills on parliamentary reform, and they would give in the most authentic and authoritative manner the views of Her Majesty's Government on the subject.

div.head: -HOUSE OF COMMONS.:-MaNney.
div.p: -HOUSE OF COMMONS.:-MaNney.
THE CRIMINAL CODE BILL.—The ATTORNEY GENERAL announced that it was the opinion of the members of the Grand Committee on the Criminal Code Bill that they ought to go on and do their best with it.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN AT BIRMINGHAM. The PRIME MINISTER informed Mr. Warton that in his speech at Birmingham last week Mr. Chamberlain expressed his own personal opinien on the questions of the payment of members and the formation of electorial districts, and he made it quite clear that he did not express the opinion of the Govern- ment, even reseryinz a certain amount of discretion as to the limits to which he should apply his own personal opinion on the questions should they come on for discussion. THE SUNDERLAND DISASTER.—The HOME SECRETARY stated that he had nothing new to communicate respecting the Sunde.rland dis tster, and that he had ordered a barrister to represent the Home Office at the inquest.—Mr. ASHLEY said that the rumour that Mr. O'Shaughnessy, M.P., had been ttppcinted to the governorship of Queensland was not true.

MR. BRIGHT AT BIRMINGHAM.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE called the attention of the House to some remarks made on Thurs- day last by Mr. Bright which appeared to him to amount to a breach of the privilege of this House. He read the pas- sage of Mr. Bright's speech in which he charged members of the Conservative party with being in alliance with the Irish rebel party. That was language which it was impossible to let pass, and he therefore moved that it was a breach of the privilege of the House.—Mr. BRIGHT said he was not sur- prised that passages in his speech had led to searching of heart among the Opposition. He was speaking to his con- stituents, and he found among them anxiety about the slow progress of business. He believed there was evidence. to show that on the part of the Opposition it Was considered the best way of damaging the Government to make it impossible for the Government busi- ness to succeed. The two parties against the Gavernment seemed to have the same purpose—to worry the Ministers and defeat the Government. With reference to the Irish members, the followers of Mr. Parnell, to whom he had re- ferred, if they would say they Were loyal to the Crown he would withdraw his charge, and make an apology if the House thought necessary.—After a long and animated de- bate, in which Mr. Gladstone. Sir Richard Cross, and others, took part, Sir Stafford Northcote's resolutioH was rejected by 151 against 117 votes. THE CLIMATE OF MADAGASCAR.—In the high interior districts it resembles tkat of the temperate zones, with no intense heat, and is quite cold during the nights in winter. These parts of the island are, therefore, tolerably healthy for Europeans. But the coasts are much hotter, especially on the western side; arid, from the large amount of marsh and lagoon, malarial fever is prevalent, and frequently fatal both to Europeans and to natives from the interior. The seasons are two—the hot and rainy season from November to April, and the cool and dry season during the rest of the year. Rain, indeed, falls almost all the year round on the eastern coast, which is exposed to the vapour-laden south- east trade winds, but it is much less frequent on the western side, being interrupted by the high interior land. No snow is known even on the loftiest mountains, but thin ice is very occasionally found ; and hail showers, often very destructive, are frequent in the rainy seasons. Terrific thunderstorms are also common at that period; water- spouts are sometimes seen, and hurricanes occur every few years, at very rare intervals ascending into the in- terior highlands.—Rev. J. Sibree, junr., in the Encyclopedia Britannia.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.-TUESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.-TUESDAY.

THE DECEASED WIFE'S SISTER BlLL.—Opposition to the Marriage with a Deceased Wife's Sister Bill has now spent itself.—On the motion te go into committee, Earl BEAU- CHAMP moved to strike out the clause legalisine, past marriages.—The LORD CHANCELLOR pointed out that re- trospection was an essential principle of the bill, but suggested that the necessities of the case would be met by legitimising the children of past marriages.—This compro- mise found acceptance, and it was decided that at a subse- quent stage a clause should be brought up embodying the principle adopted. The bill then passed through committee without further opposition, and is consequently in a fair way to become law this session. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY.

THE CORRUPT PRACTICES BILL.—The House of Com- mons spent the morning sitting in committee on the Corrupt Practices Bill. The second clause, which was fully dis- cussed on the previous evening, was adopted with little delay, and the committee proceeded to clause 3, which pro- vided that in cases where corrupt practices were reported to the speaker to have prevailed "by or with the knowledge and consent of any candidate," such candidate should be for ever debarred from representing the county or borough he had corrupted, and should he ineligible for a seat in the House of Com- mons for a period of ten years. This punishment was deemed too severe, and Mr. Lewis wished to exclude treating from the clause.—Mr. RATHRONE argued strongly against relaxation in this direction, and pointed out the de- moralising effect treating had had upon the freemen of Liverpool.--Sir R. CROSS thought the punishments all thiough the bill were too severe, and to meet this complaint the ATTORNEY-GENERAL agreed that the extreme penalty of the clause should only apply to candidates personally guilty of corrupt practices.—The concession gave the Tories satisfaction, but Mr. LEWIS insisted upon a division, and was placed in a minority of 47 to 306.—Mr. RAIKES then proposed not to for ever exclude a candidate found guilty under the clause from representing the county or borough in which he committed the offence, but leaving him subject only to the general exclusion from the House for ten years.—The discussion on this point was in progress when the sitting was suspended. VACCINATION.—On resuming at nine Mr. PETER TAYLOR called attention to the laws relating to vaccination, and moved a resolution declaring it inexpedient and unjust to enforce vaccination under penalties upon those who regard it as unadvisable and dangerous.—Sir LYON PLAYFAIR had the first place on the orders with an amendment declaring that "the practice of vaccination has greatly lessened the mortality from small-pox, and that laws relating to it, with such modifications as experience may suggest. are necessary for the prevention and mitigation of this fatal and mutila- five disease."--Mr. Horwoon having seconded Mr. Taylor's resolution, the right hon. gentleman rose to move his amendment. With him rose Sit Joseph Pease, who had another amendment proposing that "a Select Committee of this House be appointed for the purpose of assertaining whether a limitation of the accumulation of penalties for non-vaccination can be effected without endangering the practical efficiency of the Vaccination Acts."—There were calls for Sir Lyon Playfair, but the SPEAKER ruled that Sir J. Pease had precedence, and he moved his amendment accordingly.—Sir LYON PLAY- PAIR was thereafter precluded from moving his amendment, but he supported it in a speech of great force, research, and clear argument, which was listened to with profound atten- tion, and interrupted by repeated applause by an increasing audience.—Dr. CAMERON opposed the resolution.—Sir CHARLES DILKE, rising at a quarter-past twelve, observed, amid general cheering, that Mr. Taylor and Mr. Hopwood had been so completely and crushingly answered by Sir Lyon Playfair that it was scarcely necessary for him to devote further time to the task. He nevertheless proceeded to add a cloud of witnesses derived from official statistics in proof of the efficacy of vaccination as a preventative of smallpox. He did not see that any material end would be served by assenting to Sir Joseph Peese'e amendment, as a Select Committee of the House had already unanimously decided in favour of the proposition it contained. He suggested therefore that the amendment should be withdrawn, and the question of cumulative penalties brought forward on a subsequent oc- casion as a direct issue. If that were done he would be pre- pared to support Sir LlPlayfair's amendment.—Sir J. Pease thereupon withdrew his amendment.—On a division, Mr. Taylor's resolution was rejected by 286 to 16; and Sir L. Playfair's amendment, declaring that the practice of vacci- nation had greatly lessened the mortality from smallpox, and that laws relating to it were necessary for the preven- ion and mitigation of the disease, was agreed to. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WLDNESDA.T.

THE SEA FISHERIES (IRELAND) BILL. Mr. BLAKE moved the second reading of the Sea Fisheries (Ireland) Bill. The measure, he said, had this merit—that it im- posed no charge upon the Imperial Exchequer, and received the approbation of the majority of the Irish members. Its object was to secure the development of the Irish fisheries out of purely Irish resources. The estimated cost of £250,000 was proposed to be taken out of the Irish Church Fund. The bill would also give power to borrow money for providing public harbours, if considered necessary, and also to appoint four Irish Commissioners to be associated with the present inspectors.—Mr. FORSTER thought the case which had been made out in favour of the bill was a very strong one. In regard to the Irish Church Fund, be himself believed that there was a small surplus. If, however, there were none' the Irish fishermen had a strong claim for assistance, although he deprecated gifts from the State.—Mr. ARNOLD, speaking as a member of the Harbour Commission, said the impressions he had received from evidence given before the Commission had set his mind strongly against grants of public money and loans which were no better than grants, but in the bill now before the House the proposal was very different, and undor the circumstances he thought the House should pass the second reading.—Mr. Childers and Mr. Parnell followed, and the bill was read a second time amid cheers. THE VICEROYALTY (IRELAND) BILL.—Mr. JUSTIN WCARTHY proposed the second reading of the Viceroyalty (Ireland) Bill. He explained that the object of the measure was that the office of Lord Lieutenant should be abolished from the Ist of January, 1884. that the powers of the Vice- roy should be henceforth transferred to a Secretary of State, and that the Secretary of State should be a member of the House of Commons and should be elected by an Irish con- etituency.—Mr. Itlcatoosort moved the rejection of the bill.

—Mr. TREVELYAN said it was a measure which could only be proposed on the authority of the Government as a whole, and the Government certainly had not made up its collec- tive mind that such a strong step was required.—Mr. CAL- LAN described the bill as a sham, and said it never was either brou;ht before the Irish party or considered by them. He was talking at 5-45, when the debate stood adjourned.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—THUnSDAY. The bill proposing that grants should be made to Lords Alcester and Wolseley was read a second time.—Replying to Earl Dunraven Lord SUDELY stated that the reason why Professor .Tyndall had resigned was because he did not tnink that Mr. 'W'igham, the patentee of an invention for illuminating lighthouses, had received fair play, or that the Board of Trade had received fair play, or that the Board of Trade had sufficiently supported him—Lord COLERIDGE, replying to some observations of E trl Powis regarding the clashing of assizes and quarter sessions, said care would be taken in the future to prevent assizes being opened in the same week as quarter sessions.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Taunsney.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Taunsney.

MR. BRADLAUGH.—The PRIME MINISTER, who was questioned about the representation of Northampton, stated that he had received certain strong resolutions which pur- ported to come from largely attended public meetings, some asking hi-n whether if Mr. Bradlaugh was forbidden to take his seat he would support a motion for a new writ, to which his reply was that the seat was not vacant, and, therefore, no writ could be issued.

THE CRIMINAL PROCEDURE BILL. The ATTORNEY GENERAL announced that he had with great regret come to the determination to ask the Committes on the Criminal Procedure Bill not to proceed with the further concideration of the bill. He should submit a resolution at next meeting, and should endeavour to make it very simple and avoid all controversial matter.

ZULT:LAND,—Mr. Ashley threw some light upon the posi- tion of affairs in Zaluland. It is, it appears, true that a missionary named Schroder has been murdered, though by whom or under what circumstances is not yet known; but the Government have no news as to the reported' murder of Mr. Nunn, who is an aide-de-camp to the chief Ohatn. He further stated that the disturbances in Znluland are due to the refusal of Oham, who is in Cetywayo's territory, and therefore subject to him, either to go into the territory re- served for those who do not wish to be under Cetywayo or to submit to the restored King. Ths Government, he re- peated, had no intention of setting no a protectorate over Zululand, but would preserve older in Natal and on the Zulu frontier.

THE CORRUPT PRACTICES BILL.—On again going into Committee on the Corrupt Practices Bill, the consideration of Mr. Raikes's amendment in favour of allowing a candi- date who had corrupted a constituency to again offer him- self to the same constituency for re-election was resumed, and met with the support of Sir S. Northcote and the Op- position generally. But the Government stood by the clause debarring the candidate from ever representing the corrupted constituency, and, on a division, Mr. Raikes was placed in a minority of 131 to 180.—On the motion of Mr. WARToN, the period for which a candidate found guilty of corrupt practices should be excluded from the House was reduced from ten to seven years, and clause 3 was agreed to. On clause 4, Sir R. UROSS, on behalf of Mr. Gorst, moved an amendment to save a candidate from losing his seat if he were personally innocent of bribery and took reasonable means to prevent it, and if the result of the election was not affected by any corrupt practices.—The Tories and Mr. Cowen pleaded for liberty for agents to bribe, but the SOLICITOR-GENERAL pointed out that the bill did not pro- pose any alteration In the existing law, and it would be undesirable to relax existing provisions.—A second amend- ment by Sir R. CROSS was in favour of allowing a candidate found guilty of corrupt practices to again try his fortune at the next general election, but this proposal was rejected by 134 votes to 91.

div.head: STATE TM' IRELAND. REVELATIONS OF THE INVINCIBLE – ORGANISATION.
div.p: THE STATE TM' IRELAND. REVELATIONS OF THE INVINCIBLE - ORGANISATION.

A Dublin correspondent says the extraordinary state- ments given at Mullingar, on Wednesday, during the hear- ing of charges of murder and conspiracy to murder, form only a portion of the btartling facts which have come to light in the course of the police inquiries into the con- spiracy. All the evidence shows that the plot, which resulted in the murder brutal of Mrs. Smyth, at Berbaville, was the outcome of the conspiracy originated in Mullingar and neighbourhood by members of the Dublin Invincible organisation. As stated by the approver Patrick M-Keon, both Michael Fagan and Daniel Curley went down to Mullingar in the early part of 1882 and inaugurated a branch of the assassina- tion society. Not only did they assist in organising a local conspiracy, but it is stated that they tbemselves were also present at the time the murder was committed. To this fact is attributed the vigour with which the Crown pursued the prosecution of these two men in the Phcenix Park mur- der case. Shauld a prima facie case be proved against the Malinger prisoners, they will be brought to Dublin for trial at the next commission, to be held in August.

div.head: ILkFO:tNIER CARgY.
div.p: THE ILkFO:tNIER CARgY.

It is stated that Carey will shortly be removed from Kil- mainham Gaol and taken to London, from which he will be sent to a foreign country. It is also likely that an effort will be made to declare him a bankrupt, and thus remove him legally from the Town Council. It is argued that Carey oonfessed to be guilty of felony; that guilt of felony involves forfeiture of goods, and that forfeiture of goods in- fers bankruptcy. A question will be put in the House of Commons as to the circumstances under, which he wrote his recent letter to the Town Council.

A return was igsued on Wednesday showing that during May there were 93 agrarian outrages in Ireland, two being cases of firing at the person. Early on Thursday morning Messrs. Boucher and Co.'s wholesale oil, drug, and chandlery establishment, with the stores attached, in Waterford, was completely destroyed by fire. The damage is estimated at between £7,000 and £B,OOO. A parliamentary return issued on Saturday shows that the number of applications under the Arrears Act up to the end of May was 86,455, comprising 135,997 holdings. the estimated amount of money involved in these applications being £810,353 us. 3d.

The Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland and Lord Wolseley 'aro to receive the degree of LL.D. from the Dublin University. The degree will be publicly conferred on the occasion of Lord Wolseley's visit to Dublin next week, when he will be entertained at a banquet and presented with a handsonv.., gift by the citizens. " James Carey, T.C.," writing from Kiltatainham priaon to the Town Clerk of Dublin, intimates to that functionary his intention to attend the sittings of the Corporation• as soon as circumstances will admit. The astounded council- lors on Monday referred the matter to a committee. It appears that Dr. Wade, whose informal election in room of Carey was before the court last week, attends and votes in the Council as though he were legally a member. The Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland left Dublin on Saturday morning for Cavan, whence he will start upon his northern tour. He is guarded by detectives. In Cavan his Excellency inspected the militia, and was presented with an address of welcome from the townspeople. He left Cavan by live o'clock train, and joined the Countess Spencer at Clones. They arrived on Saturday night at Baronscourt, the seat of the Duke and Duchess of Abercorn, whose guests they were until Wednesday.

THE LORD LIEUTENANT: ALARMING INCIDENT.—WhiIst the Lord Lieutenant and Countess Spencer were being driven in the carriage of the High Sheriff of Derry to the railway station at Derry on Tuesday an alarming accident occurred. The carriage had to pass between two lines of militia, and as the men presented arms, the band, suddenly striking up, fri,ghteued the horses. They shied violently and plunged through the ranks, knocking down several men and seriously injuring one gunner. The horses were secured without causing further mischief. THE COST OF IRISH AGITATION.—A correspondent of the Times writes—" Mr. Patrick Egan has furnished Pre- sident Sulliven, of the Irish National League of America, with a detailed statement of the funds subscribed in Ireland for various purposes connected with the land agitation. Twenty-seven thousand pounds were subscribed directly to the central funds of the Land League, and, in addition, the Ladies' Land League received over £9,000. The con- siderable sum of £BO,OOO was subscribed and spent locally in the work of organisation and agitation, and £21,000 was specially collected fer the State Trial Defence Fund on the occasion of the abortive trial of Mr. Parnell and others. For the sustentation of the suspects imprisoned under Mr. Forster's righne £25,000 was collected, and a similar amount wag gathered in aid of the Dublin Exhibition of last year. In all, the Irish people themselves subscribed in less than three years a sum of over £228,000 for political purposes. The Irish in America in the same period forwarded to Ire- land for similar purposes £157,000, and about £lO,OOO was received from Australia, making a total of £837,000 sub- scribed in aid of the agitation conducted by Mr. Parnell. To this total must be added sums contributed for the relief of distress, of which £59,000 was 'sent from the United States. The financial statement was furnished by Mr. Egan in order to establish the fact that the greater portion of the money spent ia agitation was subscribed by the Irish in Ire- land."

WILLS AND BEQuEF-rs.—The following have been proved: —Of Mr. Francis Marcet, late of No. 13, Stratton-street, Piccadilly, the value of the personal estate in England amounting to upwards of £124000; of Mr. Hughes Francis Ingram, formerly of Halifax, Yorkshire, hut late of Poulett House, Lyme Regis, Dorset, over £113,000; of Mrs. Alex- andriue Gehier de St. Hilaire Archdeacon, late of No. 8, Rue d'Anjou, Saint Honore, Paris, over £54,000; of Mr. Robert Bowman, late of Springwell, Clapham-common, over £46,000; of Mr. Frederick Allen, formerly of Birmingham, but late of Llandudno, who died on the 10th February last at Erdington, was proved on the 10th ult. by Roland Felton Allen and Frederick Felton Allen, the sons, the executors, the value of the personal estate exceeding £37,ooo—the testator gives £250 each to his sisters Caroline Emma and Eliza, and his brothcr George, and the residue of the per- sonalty and all his real estate to his said two sons; of Miss Mary Selina Bathurst, formerly of No. 20, Grosvenor- gardens, but late of the Chateau Leader, Cannes, exceeding £3,000; of Sir George Alfred Arney, formerly Chief Jus- tice of New Zealand, but late of 17, Devonshire-place. Port- land-place, exceeding £16,000; of Sir Edwin Pearson, F.R.S., I formerly lieutenant of the Yeomen of the Guard, late of I "Road," &wayside, Wimbledon, was proved on the 4:h 1 ult. by the Hon. Alicia Aune Dame Pearson, the wilow and sole executrix, to whom he gives all his property,—lllgs- grated London NetC3.

div.head: FoREIGN •INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: FoREIGN •INTELLIGENCE.

A great tire occurred on Tuesday at some warehouses in Lyons, whereby damage to the extent of about 660,000 francs was done. Forty railway carriage's on an adjacent line were caught in the flames, and the railway service was interrupted. It is stated in Lisbon that the King of Dahomey, on hear- ing that Portugal contemplated ceding Whvdah to England, ordered the Portuguese commander to abandon the fortress within 60 days, and threatened to decapitate all Portuguese subjects in case of any resistance. Intelligence received from Getter° is to the effect that the Turks in the last engagement gained a decisive success, and occupied the enemy's positions. The Albanians were com- pletely dispersed, and, it is said, unless unexpected ob- stacles should arise, the handing over of the disputed ter- ritory to Montenegro will soon take place. It is reported that the Cantu pirty of Cetewayo's ad- herents have crossed the Pemvani tiiver, which forms the boundary between the Transvaal arid Zululand, and have been raiding on Transvaal territory, burning kraals and carrying off cattle. This violatittn of Boer territory has been reported by the Transvaal Government to the Governor of Natal.

The ceremony of annexing New Guinea does not seem to have been a very imposing affair. The .14Ie!bourne Argus says that Mr. Chester, in the presence of 300 natives and 13 Europeans, recognised Boa Vugi as the head chief of Point Moresby, and "gave the _British nag into his charge until such time as an official should be sent to represent the Imperial Government." OFFENCES AGAINST RELIGION IN PORTUGAL. Out Of the total of 9,267 crimes recorded in the criminal statistics of Portugal for the last year returmd, 15 are included under the head of "want of respect for relks,ion," which a note to Mr. Baring's reports states to include blasphemy. It ap- pears that there were 24 trials in all of this class, resulting in 12 convictions, the offenders being in all cases subjected to light-class punishments.

A.--Rome telegram dated June IA says: During the sitting to-day in the Chamber of Deputies, an individual named Giannellie, who was formerly employed in the prison administration, threw a number of papers from the-gallery into the body of the House. He w:is ;Entnediate!y arrested, and stated that he had been driven by misery to commit the act. The incident ha..ao political importanCe what- ever.

THE GERMAN ARIIIY.—The German army is at the pre- sent time distributed over 304 garrisons, 3) of whi3ll have an effective of over 2,000 men. Berlin, with 17,813, and Metz, with 14,441, are the only two towns w!.ich have gar- risons of over 10,000. The garrison of Strasburg numbers 8,968, that of Mayence 7,712, that of Cologne 7,655, that of Cohlentz 6,353, that of Konigshurg 6,383, and that of Mag- deburg 6.068. The garrisons or Potsdam (6,580) and Span- dau (4,339) are so close to Berlin that 28,732 troops could be concentrated upon the capital at a few hours' notice. The Capetown journals are satisfied with Lord Derby's declarations in regard to Basutoland, but protest in advance against the Cape being called upon to contribute towards the expense of the new arrangement. From Durban it is announced that Mr. Schroedef, a missionary, has been murdered at his station in Zululand ; and another mission- ary is reported to have been killed some ten miles from Oham's kraal. The Natal Caffres are not allowed to mom into the Reserved Territory, which is alleged to be intended for the Bechuanas.

The French Admiral who bombarded INlajunga has sent a report of the exploit to his Government. iNo loss was sus- tained by the French, and it is recorded that the accuracy of the fire from the fleet prevented the cominercial part of the town being damaged during the bombardment. In the night, however, a fire broke out in the town. When the news reached Tamatave, "a certain agitation" was observed among the people, and fears were entertained of mischief to the European population. The French Commissioner, however, says that he made representations to the Governor which produced the immediate restoration of tranquility. The accounts received in Paris from abroad respecting the Tonvin expedition represent China to be busy pre- paring for war, while the reports emanating from French sources, as well as semi-official notes that have arrived in that city, represent her as being resolved to keep the peace, and as anxious for friendly negotiations with France. French official papers, indeed, continue to represent the negotiations between M. Tricou and Li Hung Chang as having taken a most favourable turn, though a correspon- dent hints that the French Government are very much in the dark as to the exact state of affairs, and that a brisk exchange of despatches has taken place between Paris and St. Petersburg, where the Chinese Envoy, Marquis T'Sing, has been staying, but who left that city en 'route for Paris on Friday morning last. THE REPORTED MURDER OF MISSIONARIES IN ZULU- LAND.—A Daily News telegram, dated Cepetown, Saturday, states:—" Die reported murder in Zululand of the German missionary, Mr. Schroeder, is believed to be true. The news of the late murder of Mr. Hoerman, another missionary, is still unconfirmed." The Durban correspondent of the same paper telegraphed on Saturday :—" The Rev. Mr. Weber,the superintendent of the German missions in Zululand, writes that the missionary Schroeder was murdered on the 6th just, and the body interred on the Sth. It had six assegai wounds and the stomach had been cut open. The deceased lived quite alone. Mr. Doerman, another German missionary, living near Ohatn, is reported to have been murdered. This news is very startling, the German missionaries being in no way partisans in Zululand, and the murder is a very bad sign. THE BOMBARDMENT OF TAMATIVE.—AdmiraI Pierre has reported to the French Government that he has captured Tamative, the chief port of Madagascar, an taken posses- sion of the Custom House, mad that he has destroyed three villages. Referring to this news, the Malagasy Embassy in London states that some time ago the Malagasy troops were almost all withdrawn from Tamative to the capital of the island, situate 200 miles inland, and that orders were issued by the Queen that the fire of the French was not to be returned. If these orders were adhered to, the capture of the port would not be a very difficult matter. The Embassy ' adds that at the capital there are about 6,000 troops, mostly armed with Remington rifles, and that it will take an army five months to penetrate to the capital and reduce it to sub- mission. Within this period it is hoped that England or some other power or powers will be able to arrange a pease. The Malagasy Ambassadors are at present in Paris, and had an interview with M. Jules Ferry, oa Tuesday, before this news was received.

EAnTIIQUAKF, IN ANTiocirota.—A strong earthquake was felt throughout the state of Antioquoia at six p.m. on the Sth ult. Little damage was done in Medellin, although much alarm was caused and the walls of the cathedral were injurPd. In the town of Antioquoia the facade of the cathedral was thrown cut of plumb, many of its columns were thrown down, and all the houses suffered more or less. In Santa ItKta the church steeple was injured and a number of hons,s rendered uninhabitable. In Aquadas the town hall was d,stroyed. and at Abejirral the church and a number of houses were injured. It was feared more disasters had oc- curred in districts which bad not been heard from. The shock lasted more than two minutes, and appeared to move _

from the north to the south. This same shock was felt all over the isthmus, all along the Atlantic coast of Columbia, doing damage only at the mouth of the Atrato, so far as reported up to the present, and in the Magdalena Valley. It appears t 4 have been the sharpest and ,nost widely ex- perienced sine, the great one of September 7 last year. A TRAGIC ROMANCE.—In the winter of 1875-6 a young Russian, a member of the Orthodox Church, and a young Jewess named Umjanskv, desired to marry. She must he baptised before a legal. union could be contracted, and her father was furious at the bare suggestion of her becoming a Christian. At last the young people ran away to Kiev, where the girl was formally received in the Christian Church. A day was fixed for tho marriage, and the bride- groom went into the city from the village where they had taken up their abode, in order to make the last purchases. On his return, the bride had disappeared. After a vain search, the distracted lover applied to the police, but they could not discover the least trace of her. He became re- served, moody, and at last hanged himself. When the ice melted with the spring the waters of the Dneiper bore to the bank a heavy sack, in which were the fragments of a dis- membered female body, which, with some difficulty, was identified as that of the missing Jewess. One of the chief police-officers at Kiev set himself to unravel the mystery; and, after years of patient inquiry and toil, he has lately succeeded in doing so, Her father bad traced the fugitive to Kiev, and, discovering that she had betome Christian, resolved that she should die. He secured the assistance of six men, who, during the fatal absence of her lover, carried her off, killed her, chopped the body into pieces, and, having put them into a sack, tumbled them into the lmeiper. The winter's ice secured them from discovery for months, at least. Five of the murderers have been found, and, with the father, tried, and condemned to death. Search is being made for the tnizsiDg sixth man.

At the Sheffield Bankruptcy Court, on Thursday, Mr. J. C. White, a local stock and share broker, was adjudicated a bankrupt. His liabilities are stated to be about £25,000. The bankrupt left Sheffield several weeks ago, and has not since been heard of. Mr. John Morley and Mr. P. Stewart Macliver are about to introduce into the House of Commons a bill at the in- stance of the Provincial Newspapers Society to relieve pro- prietors of country newspapers from a disability which now ' renders many of them liable to penalties if they except advertisements from local boards or other public bodies of which they may happen to be members. In the case of borough newspapers. proprietors who are members of town councils are already freed by the Municipal Corporations Act from any such liability. CHARGE OF STEALING £27.000 WOHT/I or BONDS.— Edward Guerlain and Lon Dandin were further charged before Sir Charles Ingham at Bow-street, on Thursday, with bing concerned in stealing laonds' value £27,000, within the jurisdiction of the French Bcpublic. Mr. Poland, instructed by Mr. Michael Abraham", prosecuted. M. Tail- lefer, appointed by the French Government, Mr. Bosley, and Mr. Forest Fulton defended Daudin, and Mr. Tatham defentled Guerlain. The bonds were stolen from the Socia6 do Dopots et Cornptes-Courants by a clerk named Repoteau, and were afterwards negotiated in London. It was alleged that a portion of the proceeds could be traced to the defen- dants, and that Daudin had been in comp my with a man , named Chah.iron and another, when two £5OO Bank of Eng- , land notes, proceeds of the sale of the bonchz, had been changed at the bank. It w.lF+ further proposed to show that both defend.,nts were at Paris at the time of the robbery. • Evidence in this direction was given, and prisenum were again remanded,

A GIRL CHARGED WITH ASSAULTING HER FATHER.— Ellen Lavelle, described as a bad character, residing at 11111- street, was charged at Warrington Police Court on Satur- day, with having at five minutes past one that morning as- saulted John Lavelle, her fatber.—Prisoner, who had only left gaol on the previous day, went at the time stated to he' fati,er's house and demanded admittance. Her father refused to admit her, whereupon she struck aid kicked him yen violently. P.C. Baxendale, who was near by, saw prisoner's violent conduct, and brought her to the lock-up. As the father, who was said to ba of drunken habits, did not appear, the prisoner was discharged.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JUNE 23, 1883.

THE speeches of Mr. BRIGHT and MT CHAMBERLAIN at Birmingham last week have attracted a considerable amount of attention, but we are surprised that on Monday evening they should have tormed the theme of discus- sion in Parliament. Time there is precious, and we think our legis- lators might have been b,tter employed advancing useful measures, still the reference to these speeches will not be with- out advantage, for it is not difficult to per- ceive that it will cause them to be more ex- tensively read and their conclusions, we hope, will be more generally adopted. Mr. BRIGHT and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN were, it must be ad- mitted, unusually free, bold, and incisive in their utterances—Mr. BRIGHT, in criticising the past, the present, and to some extent the future policy of the Conservative party, and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN in promulgating a mea- sure of electoral reform which shall be more in accord with the political views and aspira- tions of the constituencies than that which now obtains. We believe that the deliver- ances of both gentlemen were exceedingly welt-timed ; we cannot help thinking Mr. BRIGHT'S denunciation of obstruction was not one whit too severe and fully justified by the conduct of the Opposition ; and we are con- vinced Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S declarations on the question of reform will go a long way in guiding public opinion in the direction he has indicated. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN was, of course, careful to observe that he spoke his own individual opinions only and not by any means the views of his colleagues on this im- portant question, and, therefore, there was the less necessity to quarrel about them. He was well known to be far in advance of many members of the Liberal party in this regard long before he had a place in the Liberal Cabinet, and we have yet to learn that jr. ac- ceptingthat position he was of necessity bound to abandon his opinions or to desist from ad- vocating them when convenient opportunities offered. To put the matter briefly, what Mr. CHAMBER LAIN contends for—and what we believe we shall one day have —is manhood suffrage, equal electoral districts, and the pay- ment of members of Parliament. A measure of such a Radical character is probably a long way off, yet, as education, and more especially polictical education advances, it is bound to come. It may be and no doubt is distaste- full to the opponents of all reform, but we have not forgotten the loud outcry there was when it was first proposed to extend the fran- chise from ie. to £7 householders, and that the agitation at that time resulted in a very much wider diffusion of electoral power than was at first sought. So it may be again. What Mr. CHAMBERLAIN now advocates is but a very liberal extension of the principle long since conceded, and though the Tories may be alarmed at his proposal we are not without hope even they may be led to see that it is not so revolutionary as at the first blush it appears. Lord Sa-LiSBURY gained nothing by his question respecting the speech, but the answer of Lord GRAN- VILLE proved that the idea of a divided Cabinet which the noble Marquis so fondly nurses exists only .in his own fertile imagina-

tion. Sir S. NORIHCOTR'S handling of Mr. BRIGHT'S speech was as unfortunate as Lord, SALISBURY'S criticisms of Mr. CHAMBER." LAIN'S. The right hon. baronet is aware that obstruction is rampant not only in the House, but in the grand committees; he is himself powerless to prevent it, for the very good reason that his followers will not follow his lead; at the same time he is not unnaturally anxious to clear his party from the "soft impeachment." That Mr. BRIGHT'S philippic had gone home was abundantly proved by the eager: ness of Sir STAFFORD to resent it, ye' the righteous indignation which he and some of his colleagues affected was of no avail, the result of the division testifying to the justice of the accusation. The bringing of the matter forward, however, gave Mr. BRiGia the opportunity of substantiating in Parlia- - ment his statement out of it. As Sir STAY' FORD admits, Mr. BRIGHT is always clear and forcible, and his charge, which we repeat his own language, was this, that the Con' servative party "in not a few of its member! appears willing to repudiate the authority or a majority of the constituencies. A NEW MAGISTRATE FOU Itmconx.—Mr. James Hand- ley, of Runcorn, has been placed on the commission of the peace for the county of Chester by his grace the Duke of Westminster, and will probably qualify to serve at the quar- ter sessions on the 4th July. We believe Mr. Handley is the first gentleman placed on the commission since his Grace accepted the Lord Lieutenancy of the county. THE WATERLOO HOUSE ARRANGEMENT3.—On Thursday evening a committee of the Commissioners met the over- seers at Waterloo House, with reference to the removal of the offices of the latter to that place. The overseers offered no objection to the rooms offered for their use, and the pro- posed removal will be submitted to the ratepayers' meeting on Thursday next. If the sanction of the ratepayers is ob- tained, the assent of the Local Government Board will be all that is necessary to the removal.
