Postance, Vicar of St. Barnabas, Liverpool, preached a sermon in Farnworth Parish Church, on Sooday morning, and in the afternoon in Bold Schoolroom. On Sunday evening, the Rev. J. Hirst, organising Secretary for the Liverpool district, preached in St. Ambrose Church, on behalf of the same object. The collections realised a good sum. RUNCORN AND THE SHIP CANAL.—A deputation from the Runcorn Commissioners went to London on Monday, for the purpose of submitting several clauses which had been drawn up by the Board to the promoters of the Ship Canal. The members returned to Rnncorn on Thursday night, and we understand that previous to leaving the metropolis they had an interview of several hours duration with the promoters, who granted them several important concessions. Further communications are likely to take place, and early next week a special meeting of the Com- missioners will be held to consider the matter.

EXCURSION FROM WIDNES.—The employes of the Desota Alkali Company had their first annual excursion on Satur- day last. To the number of about 400 they started from Widnes London and North-Western Station at seven o'clock and arrived at Southport, their destinaticn, about nine o'clock. Favoured with fine weather the excursionists spent a most enjoyable day in visiting the various places provided for the amusement of visitors, and in the evening the work- men sat down to a substantial tea at the Commercial Hotel. After the repast, Mr. Parnell delivered a short speech, and Mr. Bray, the foreman, also addressed a few words to the med. The return journey was accomplished by ten o'clock. Carracif ThIfFERANcis WP"s BlitAxcii,—A Meeting oi tills society was held in Waterloo- road school, on Thursday evening, when the Farnworth Teniperance and Total Abstinence Society paid a fraternal visit and gave a miscellaneous entertainment. There was a large audience, and the Rev. J. Wright-Williams presided. The Farnworth glee party rendered several glees in good style, and the following ladies and gentlemen contributed songs: J. Wright, Miss Bond, Miss Ida Bond, Mr. F. S. Lee, and Miss Hibbert. Recitations were given by Mr. J. T. Lowe, Mr. A. Carter, Mr. J. Davies, Mr. T. Knowles, and Miss Fogg. A sketch entitled " The evils of intemper- ance" was given in a capital manner, the characters being well sustained.

Veppgrur4 ScAT...T,Cf6 leciDENt AT WIDNES.—On Sun,. day eVehillg, Peier ilurgess, 35 years of age, living in Grove. isireet, Widnes, was most seriously injured at Messrs. Brock and Sullivan's chemical works, where he was employed. About seven o'clock, Burgess was scraping out a caustic liquor pan. when his foot slipped, and he fell into the vessel. There was no person near the spot to render any assistance, and Burgess had to scramble out of the vat him- self. The corrosive liquor into which he fell, WS of con- siderable strength and very hot, and he was very badly scalded all over the body, from the neck to the heels. His skin hung in shreds from his body. When assistance arrived, the injured man was conveyed to the Accident Hospital in a cart, and Mr. Heffernan, Surgeon, (Assistant to Dr Robinson, of Runcorn), and Dr. McDonnell's assistant, were quickly in attendance. A Derentertelef FATIiER 8-ENT TO GAOL—Robert Harrop lnboifter, was summoned on Monday at the Runcorn Petty Sessions, to show cause why he should not pay the SUM of £2 17s 6d due from him to Mr. Superintendent Williamson for the maintenance of his child in the Stockport Industrial School.—Superintendent Williamson said an order bad been made upon the defendant to contribute a certain sum to- wards the support of his son, but after paying a few shill- ings he ceased altogether. In January last he was summoned before the magistraces, and he was ordered to pay arrears amounting to £7 2s 6d. The defendant was in full work and earning £1 per week, but he had never shown any desire to pay anything towards the support of his child. He was one of that class of people who made a practice of getting rid of their children in order that they might be kept by the ratepayers.—The defendant said he was un- able to pay the money. He had suffered very much from ill-health, and had in consequence contracted many debts. He stated that he received 19s per week. Superintendent Williamson remarked that the defendant's wife kept a shop, and in order to nullify these proceedings conducted the busi- ness under an assumed name.—The Bench said the defendant had received no less a sum than £23 from his master during the months of January to June, and he was perfectly able to pay the money. He would be committed to gaol for 14 days. LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE POOR-LAW EXPENDITURE. —With a view of future legislation as soon as possible, a return bai been called for and just issued for the purpose of showing those sums expended out of the poor rates entirely foreign to the object originally contemplated in the I' enactment of the rate, and which have greatly increased since the passing of the Poor-Law Amendment Act in 1834, in consequence of the imposition of new and the angmeeta- tion of old charges. The return is for the last half of 1882. div.head: BREAKING AN OLD MAN'S LEG AT WIDNES. BRUTAL ASSAULT.
div.p: BREAKING AN OLD MAN'S LEG AT WIDNES. BRUTAL ASSAULT.

At Widues Police Court on Monday, Timothy Leonard, labourer, was charged with unlawfully wounding William Barran, clogger, of 5, Barn-street, Widnes, en Saturday night. In consequence of his serious injuries the prosecutor was unable to appear. Inspector Barnett said the prose- cutor was an old man 73 years of age, and followed the occupation ef a clogger. About 10 o'clock on Saturday night the prisoner called at the prosecutor's shop for a clog he had left to be mended. The clog was ready, and Barran handed it to the prisoner, who, without trying it on, said it appeared to be too small, and did not offer to pay for the repairs it had undergone. At this time the prosecutor went to the door for the purpose of driving away some boys who had congregated there, and while he was standing there the prisoner attempted to rush past him. The old man pluckily seized the prisoner to prevent him leaving the shop, when the prisoner turned upon him, kicked him, and violently threw him into the street. The prisoner then said "Take that;" and ran away. Thenoise of thedisturb- ance attracted the attention cf the neighbours, some of whom came to see what had occurred, and assisted the injured man into his houee.—Mr. Pattison, assistant to Dr. Cooper, was called in. He said Barran's leg was broken, and subse- quently the injured man was removed to the Accident Hospital.—Ann Quinn, wife of Christopher Quinn, living at 4, Barn-street, said about ten o'clock on Saturday night, when in her own hoase, she heard someone calling "Police, police." In consequence she went to the door, and saw a struggle going on at the other side of the street. She saw the prisoner give Barran a push. Barron fell down and the prisoner ran away. It was dark, and she could not very well see what took place. When the prisoner had gone, she went to Barran and helped him to rise. He could not get up without assistance.—The prisoner asked if she saw him kock the prosecutor down, and witness replied that she saw him lift his hand.—Dr. O'Keeffe said on Sunday he was called to see the injured man at the Hospital. He examined him with Mr. Pattison. He found that he was very seriously injured, his right hip bone being fractured at the thigh, which was a very serious matter for a man 73 years of age. —ln retoy to the prisoner, the doctor said there was ne wound, bur the thigh was very badly swollen.—By Inspec- tor Barnett : The prosecutor was quite unfit to appear in court to give evidence. It would be some weeks before he esem appear.—On the application of Inspector Barnett, the inagistrate remmded the prisoner to Wednesday, when the pr eecutor was Unable to appear, and Superintendent Barker .spplied for o remand.—Mr. Knowles, who appeared for the prisoner, strongly objected, and said sufficient evidence had not been produced to justify a charge of assault. He there- fore asked for the prisoner to be discharged.—Mr. Gibbon said such a course was altogether out of the question. The Bench remanded the prisoner until Monday, when the else will be beard in the Accident Hospital.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 23,1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 23,1883.
RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COM-
MUTER

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Thursday, the Rev. Canon Barclay, the chairman, presided, and there were present—Messrs. W. Handley, F. A. Lake, T. Riley, W. Brook (secretary), and J. D. Jones. (librarian) —The LIBRARIAN (Mr. J. D. Jones), reported that 1,257 books were borrowed from the lending libraty during the month of May last, classified as follows :—Theology 27, philosophy, political economy, S:c., 5, history, travels, bio- graphy, &c., 170, science and art, 44, poetry and drama, 21, prose fiction 916, miscellaneous 74. During thesame period £1 3s was received in fines for undue detention of books. A number of books were presented during the month, and the thanks of the committee were ordered to be conveyed to the donors.—Bills amounting to £26 were passed for payment on the motion of Mr. F. A. Lent,seconded by Mr. HANDLEY. —The SECRETARY informed the committee that the auditor had completed his examination of the committee's accounts and had made two surcharges—one of £5 in respect of pay- ment to Mr. Jones for extra labour in preparing catalogue last year; and another of lOs in respect of a portion of the secretary's salary.—Mr. HANDLEY observed that Mr. Frith and himself were the members surcharged with the item, and had appealed to the Local Government Board.—lt was decided that the Library, which was closed on Tuesday last, should be re-opened on the sth July, the anniversary of the opening ceremony by Sir J. A. Picton.

RUNCORN COUNTY COURT- Before Mr. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge. The cause list contained 106 original plaints, and 24 original judgment summonses. . A Curexous COW-DEALING CASE.—This was a case in which George Bromley, farmer, of Trafford, near Chester, claimed £l2 purchase money which had been paid to Mies Lewis, of Bank House farm, Alvanley, for a cow which had been returned, and £3 damages.—Mr. W. H. Churton, of Chester, appeared for the plaintiff ; and Mr. A. Fletcher, of Northwich, for the defendant.—lt appeared that Thomas Spruce, cattle dealer, carrying on business at Frodsham, was instructed by the plaintiff to purchase a cow from defendant, and the purchase was effected about the latter end of March, defendant being aware that the cow was for plaintiff. On the day of the purchase Spruce asked the defendant if the cow was sound, and she replied that it was as sound as he was with the exception that it had an abscess on one leg, and she added that it gave five quarts of milk at a "meal." A day or two after the purchase was effected Spruce and plaintiff fetched the cow away, the latter pay- ing defendant £l2 for it. The morning after the cow had been taken to plaintiff's it was found to be ailing, and it gradually grew worse. Spruce was informed of this, and he went several times to defendant's about the animal. On one of these visits he told her that plaintiff intended returning the cow, and she said she was sorry the cow was ill, and she would bear part of the loss, but she would not have the cow brought back as plaintiff would be able to make more out of it than she would, The cow growing worse, plain- , tiff sent for Mr. Storer, veterinary surgeon, of Chester, to examine it. Mr. Storer found it to be suffering from lung , disease and chronic bronchitis, and he gave plaintiff a certi- ' ficate to that effect. Plaintiff then, after the lapse of several weeks from the day of the purchase, took the c,7/W back to defendant, NMI tfbowed her the Certificate he had received from Mr. Storer. beierie,; ant, however, refused to have the cow back, saying that she would have nothing whatever to do with it. The cow was then left in the yard with no one to attend to it, and defendant subsequently informed the police of the fact, and sent a note to spruce to the same effect. No action, how- ever, appears to have been taken by anyone, and the cow after rambling about in the croft for some time died.—The judge, after hearing evidence on both sides, did not think ehere was any evidence to show that there bad been any false r!nresenta.tions op the part of the defendant in dispos- ing of The cow, Or kf any recision of the contract. And although defendant had made a warranty in saying that the cow was sound, unless plaintiff reliedopon that warranty he could not recover upon it. That the warranty was not re- lied upon was clear from the evidence of Spruce, plaintiff's agent, who admitted that he was well acquainted with the defendant's stock, that he had known the cow a long time, that he having been in the cattle trade all his life relied upon his own judgment in buying the cow, and that he said to defendant when he bought it if plaintiff would not have it he would.—A verdict was given for the defendant._

DISPUTE BETWEEN RUNCORN TRADEEMEN.—Lnke Holmes, auctioneer, High-street, Runcorn, claimed from Charles Houghton, fruiterer and fish dealer, of the same locality, the sum of 18s 6d for work done. Defendant, who had. paid 8s 6d into court, set up a counter claim for 6s, the value of six packs of cards entrusted to the plaintiff for sale. At the last court Mr. Holmes brought the claim against John Houghton the father of the present defendant; when the Judge, after hearing the evidence, gave judgment for the defendant. The plaintiff now sought to recover against tho son. It seems that after leaving court on the last occasion, some words passed between the plaintiff and the present de- fendant, which resulted in Mr. Houghton summoning Mr. Holmes to the petfy sessions on a charge of using threaten- ing language. Before the summons was called on, however, the parties agreed to leave the matter in dispute to Mr. Bur- ton, solicitor. Mr. Burton drew upon an award, which Mr. Holmes objected to; hence the action. His honour said he considered Mr. Burton's award a very just one, and gave judgment for the plaintiff for 133 which included the Ss 6d paid into court ; but declined to allow costs. He gave a verdict for the plaintiff for the whole amount of the counter claim, with costs.

div.head: SHOCKING FATALITY ON THE RAILWAY NEAR WIDNES.
div.p: SHOCKING FATALITY ON THE RAILWAY NEAR WIDNES.

A terrible accident occurred ou the Cheshire Lines Rsil- way at Hough Green, near Widnes, on Saturday, and Robert Oscar, a young man 18 years of age, employed as a porter at the railway station of the former place, was killed and shockingly mangled. It seems that three parcels for Mrs. Elallows, of Ditton, had been left at Halewood by mistake. Oscar went for them by the 9-25 p.m. train from Hough Green, but there being no train by which he could return that night, he was compelled to walk. Ha started back along the line, and when within half z mile of his destination a heavy shower of rain came on. One of the parcels Oscar was carrying contained green peas, and it is surmised that the paper cover, becoming wet and torn allowed these to escape, and were scattered about the line. Oscar then ap- peared to have placed the other two parcels on the four-foot, and to have taken his handkerchief out for the purpose of placing the peas into it. While he was thus occupied a goods train passed in the direction of Manchester, the driver of which perceiving a passenger train travelling in the oppo- site direction, realised the peril of Oscar, and endeavoured to attract his attention. He failed, and in another instant the midland express due in Liverpool at five minutes past ten rushed past at the rate of 60 males an hour. The driver of the goods train on arriving at Hough Green station, informed Wm. Ranft, a companion of the deceased, that he thought a dreadful accident had occurred, and the two walked down the line together. In the ditch by the side of the line they found the body of Oscar frightfully mutilated, life being quite extinct. The back of his head was cut away, the scalp was torn off, and the shoulders were completely shattered. The rest of the body also presented a dreadful appearance, and the poor fellow's blood and brains bespattered the metals. It is sug- gested that the noise made by the goods train prevented Oscar from hearing the approach of the express, which evidently struck him on the head and carried his body about 60 yards. The deceased lived with his parents in Ditton. He was a member of the Wesleyan body, and a zealous worker as a teacher in the Ditton Wesleyan Sunday school ; and his untimely end is much lamented by his fellow teachers, and scholars, who held him in high esteerre—The inquest on the deceased was held at the Hammer and Pincers Inn, Hough Green, on Tuesday, before Mr. T. W. Barker, the coroner. Mr. F. Simpson, chief of the Cheshire Lines Police, was present on behalf of the railway company. The evidence went to show that the facts narrated above are correct.—lt was stated by Joseph Oscar, the father of the deceased, that his son previous to com- mencing work for the railway company, seven weeks ago, had been employed at Messrs. W. Gossage and Sons. He had had no experience of railway work.—Mr. G. S. Ham- brook, stationtnaster at Hough Green, deposed that the deceased voluqteered to fetch the parcels from Halewood, and promised to return across the fields and along the lane, but he seemed to have returned all the way from Halewood on the line —Evidence having been given by Edward Moore, engine driver, in the service of the Midland Railway Com- pany ; Frederick Maskwell, stationmaster at Halewood; and Joseph Robinson,. engine driver for the Midland railway, the Coroner observed that so far as he could see no one was to blame, and the jury returned a verdict of " Accidental I death."

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The annual meeting of this Board, for the purpose of ap- pointing a chairman for the ensuing year, was held at the Town Hall, on Wednesday afternoon. Dr. Steele presided, and there were present Dr. MacDougall, Messrs. J. Dobson, J. Williams, J. J. Speakman, P. .Speakman, W. Rhodes, F. Lake, P. Briscoe, W. Shaw, b. Taylor, W. Brookes (secre- tary), and M. Barker (surveyor).

div.head: THANES TO DR. STEELE.
div.p: THANES TO DR. STEELE.

The CHAIRMAN said: This is the annual meeting for appointing a chairman in the place of myself, who retires. In retiring from the position of chairman, I have to thank the members of the Board for the courtesy and the general kindness and co-operation I have received from them. It is with mixed feelings of regret and pleasure that I retire, because I regret that my term as chairman is now at an end, but I am glad to lay aside the cares, and anxieties, and troubles of office. (Hear, hear.) I shall be glad if someone will propose a chairman.—Mr. DossoN Mr. Chairman, I have great pleasure in moving that the best thanks of this Beard be given to you for the very able, efficient, and gentlemanly manner in which you have pre- sided over the proceedings of this Board during the last two years. I hope your life may be long spared, and your good health continue, that you may in future be useful to the town in which you live, and a benefit to the Board.— Mr. SPEAKMAN : I have great pleasnre in seconding the pro- position proposed by Mr. Dobson. The chairman has rather forestalled some of the remarks that I might have made up- on the subject, particularly with reference to the difficulties that he has had to deal with during his term of office. Taking that period as a whole I think we may congratulate ourselves that we have had such a chairman as Dr. Steele has made.—No other member rising to offerany observations, the motion was put to the meeting and carried unanimously. —The CHAIRMAN: I thank you gentlemen. It is always pleasant to feel that when one does retire he leaves good will behind. I certainly have tried to do my duty as chair- man during the time I have held the office, and worked for the interests of the ratepayers ii every way that I could do. If we have not done everything exactly as everybody wished it has not been our fault. I shall be glad to:receive a proposition.
TIiE ELECTION.-DOCTOR'S ADVICE AND ITS RECEPTION.-
PERSONALITIES.

Mr. Slum: I beg to move that Mr. Meadowcroft be ap- pointed chairman of the Beard for the ensuing 12 months. We have some knowledge of Mr. Meadowcroft's abilities. He has had considerable business experience which will fit him, 1 am sure, for the discharge of the duties which will devolve upon him; and I feel convinced, in proposing Mr. Meadowcroft, that he will be able to discharge those duties to the satisfaction of the Board, and I believe to all con- cerned.—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN seconded the motion.—Dr: MeecDouciaaa said before a proposition of this importance was accepted, he should like to say one or two words. He was not going to throw the apple of discord, nor would he, under any circumstances, take that opportunity of making any ungracious or personal observations about the propriety of appointing Mr. Meadowcroft as chairman of the Board; but they would pardon him if he diverted the attention of the Board for a moment to what seemed to him the cardinal principle in the appointment. Mr. Meadowcroft was not a representative of the ratepayers, but of the Bridgewater Navigation Company, which had inherited its rights from the Bridgewater trustees. This rfasan aHOnISIOns condition which must b::PilArent to everybody. W6ti a gentleman Wea appointed to occupy the post of chairman of a public body, that individual should represent the ratepayers. He did not think that there was anything personal against Mr. Meadowcroft, He should be very glad to see him occupying the chair which Dr. Steele was about to vacate, if he were to occupy it as a repr.?.senta- tive of the ratepayers. But Mr. Meadowcroft had the mis- fortune of representing an interest—a powerful interest. lie Cur. MacDougall) was not aware of any other body consti- tuted like their own, and it therefore seemed to him that as a matter of principle, at all events, it was not wise nor dis- creet to appoint the representative of a private company to be the chairman over a public body with functions like their own. They might unfortunately have questions arising between that powerful interest represented by Mr. Meadow- croft, and the Board, which would necessitate Mr. Meadowcroft taking sides either one way or tke other. That was one of the points which seemed to him to be of interest if not absolute importance in the appointment of chairman, such as they were about to do that day. They must go a little further back in the history of the Board than they had done on former occasions. The Board, which was instituted by Act of Parliament, had been in existence 31 or 32 years, and the chairman had generally been of a representative character up to a certain period. About seven or eight years ago it was thought that the chairraanship should "go round" the senior members who were generally supposed to be competent to occupy that post. About 11 years ago Mr. John Linaker Wright occupied the chair with credit to him- self and advantage to the ratepayers generally. He was succeeded in that post by th:ir resp?cted friend Nit.. Briscoe, who wa still a member of the Boar,i, wlio was in his turn succeed by the late Mr. Lyon, a gentleman whose departure fro as the town they all regretted. Mr. Lyon was succeeded by Mr. Norman, who, if he (Dr. MacDougall) mistook not, was succee led by Dr. Stele. It was generally supposed that the chairmanship should go round in that way, and be took it that there must be some special reason why it was considered necessary on this occasion to deviate from the course which seemed to have answered at all events tolerably well, and given satisfaction to the ratepayers. He did not say one word with regard to the propriety of appoint- ing any individual person to the chairmanship, but he cer- tainly did demur to the appointment of any individual who represented an interest without there were some special rea- sons. These reasons did not seem to have prevailed up to this particular thne,for during the exiatenctof theßridgewAter , Trustees,and their excellent representativeS at that Board, in the persons of Mr. Forrester, Mr. Farrell, Mr. Timmins(who had been a member of the Board for a great number of years, with special knowledge on special subjects), down to the present time, it was not thought wise to appoint them upo that very ground. He must take the opportunity of saying as a representative or the ratepayers, that had Mr. Meadowcroft been a representative of the old Bridgewater Trustees he should have oppbsed his appointment with any power he might possess. He took it that they intended to do honour to the Bridgewater Navigation Company in the person of Mr. Meadowcroft because they had treated Ruacorn very much more favourably, and certainly with greater consi- deration than the old trustees had d6ne. He could only refer to the discussions which took place with respect to the treatment that Board and the public generally met with from that particular body. He had no intention to fall back upon what Mr. P. SPEAKMAN : I 'rise to a point of oider. I consider Dr. MacDougall has no right to bring the intentions of any private firm into the appointment of a chairman of this Board. I think he should be called to order for doing so.—The CHAIRMAN: I think you are out of order, doctor.—Dr. MacDouciatn,: That is only a ma( ter of opinion, sir. We have usually been allowed a great deal of latitude on occasions of this kind.—The CHAIRMAN : No latitude should have been allowed and the business of the Board would have been conducted better. Dr. MACDOUGALL : Just so. lam perfectly aware. lam not a party man in any way; I am identified with no cliques, and you will excuse me, Mr. Chairman, if I use my tongue somewhat freely. It is the only occasion I venture ever to do so. If it is unpleasant to any mem- ber of this Beard to refer to that company, I have no desire to pursue the question any further. I am here to give a vote. I vote in favour of Mr. Meadowcroft's ap- pointment, but I am going to vote with a certain amount of justification, and I take it that a person is peefectiv justified in explaining here why he does so. I give it simply on Mr. Meadowcroft's account, but I decline to vote for him on the principle that Mr. Meadowcroft is the re- presentative of a large body who really do not represent the ratepayers, but who are ratepayers themselves. There- fore, I consider it my duty to make these observations. I can only express my deep regret that I should touch the corns of any member of this Board in anything I have said, but I trust Mr. P. Speakman, who feels so acutely anything I say with regard to the Bridgewater Trustees, and feels called upon to call me to order upon a point which, of course, is in your discretion to say whether it is, or whether it is not, in order.—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN : But the chairman ruled you out of order.—Dr. MACDOUGALL : As a matter of principle, I think it only right to make these observations.—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN: I should like to say that what Dr. MacDougall has said in the remarks he has thought fit to make on private indivi- duals has not touched me one bit. It is to keep Dr. Mac Dougall to the point, which he is so very fond of wandering away from at all times; bat as far as lam individually con- cerned it does not make great difference—Dr. MacDouGataa It made great difference to you at the time.(laughter.)—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN : I don't know how Dr. l'ilanDOW44ll is going to vote in favour and also veto against Mr. Meadowcrolt'a election. We shall see how the performance goes on as time goes on.—Mr. &Lew said he did not think it needful to enter into any elaborate discussion as to why he moved Mr. Meadowcroft to take the position which the Board would be asked to vote upon. He had no fear in his own mind as to any chairman whoever he might be being the Board. The Dr. seemed to take it very much to heart that the chairman be- comes the Board, and might do something that was radically wrong /or his own interest or for the interests of those he represents. He took it that the Board need not fear any- thing of the kind. He hoped that gentlemen with sufficient intelligence and straightforwardness would at all times, whenever questions came before the Board, be able con- scientiously to give their vote as they believed right and proper. So ferns Mr. Meadowcroft not being the represen- tative of the ratepayers was concerned, be took it that he represented the largest ratepayer', they had in Runcorn. [The CHAIRMAN: Hear, hear.] That certainly should not be a disqualification. If the doctor had referred to the Act of Parliament he would have found that any gentleman having a seat at that Board was eligible for the post of chair- man.—Dr. MecDonaaaa I referred to that, sir.—Mr. SHAW (continuing) said he did not want to argue the ques- tion as to the peculiar round-about way in which the office might have been given before. That was not before them. ft was for the present Board--as it would be for future Boards out of their own members—to elect whoever they might think fit and proper to occupy the position of chair- man. He had, therefore, great pleasure in feeling that Mr.

-M---e;"dou7c-roit ;as entitled to their confidence. Ifthe mem- bers believed that he was a person of sufficient ability to conduct the work of the Board they would place that con- fidence in him, and give him that assistance which every chairman must expect. and must receive if there was to be that harmonious working. in connection with the business transactions of the Board, which would reflect credit upon the members. (Hear, hear.) He was glad that the doctor would, notwith-

standing the remarks be had made, vote for the chairman that had been proposed.—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN said the Law Clerk bad informed him that Mr. Meadowcroft could legally accept the office.—The CHAIRMAN observed that before put- ting the motion to the meeting he cou!d not help regretting that Dr. MacDougall should impute motives to anybody at the Board, and have used word "clique."—Dr. 2.le.cDorr- GALL : I said I was not a member of a clique.—The CHAIR- MAN: Thereby inferring that others were, and implying that nothing is done at any time but wiiat is under- hand work. I never met a truer saying than that "We judge others by ourselves "—(laughter)--- and I hope Dr. MacDougall will remember my parting words as chairman, and try to be more charitable and more amiable towards his fellow-members. Dr. MAC- DouGALL (with temper) : Mr. Chairman, I must protest against your observations. I will really not take advice from a chairman who, in my opinion, has utterly failed as one—( Mr. SHAW: Put the resolution, Mr. Chairman; put the resolution)—and, therefore, when that chairman chooses to give me advice I must pointedly tell him'that I decline to receive his advice.—The CHAIRMAN then put the pro- position, which was carried unanimously, Dr. MacDougall voting for it.—The SECRETARY pointed out that Dr. Steele had held a seat on the various committees ny virtue of his office as chairman, but these would now be vacant. He sug- gested that the Board should now appoint Dr. Steele on the committees.—Dr. MecDoucteLL said it was incompetent for the Board to do so, because the sole business was to elect a chairman.—Dr. STEELE said it was a matter of no mo- ment, and might very well be left over.—The members then separated.
RETIREMENT OF THE REV. T. PETERS, OF WIDNES. PRESENTATION BY THE CONGREGATION.

On Thursday evening the Sunday school teachers of the Milton Congregational Church had a social tea party, and subsequently an ordinary church meeting was held. The Rev. 12. Peters, the pastor, had previously made known his intention of retiring from his charge, and the members of the congregation took advantage of the opportunity to pre- sent him with a sun) of money and an address to mark their appreciation of his Christian character and untiring labours whilst among them. The presentation was made by the Rev. G. Lord, of Stanley,Liverpool, who was supported by the Rev. J. D. Thomas (of Runcorn) and the Rev. Hudson. The ad- dress read as follows :—" To the Rev. Thomas Peters. Dear sir,—We, the members of the church and congregation meet- ing in Milton Congregational Chapel, Widnes, having been apprised of your retirement (after 30 years' labour) from the regular pastorate, desire to express to you our earnest prayer that the closing years of your life may be made bright and happy by the Master's presence. In relinquishing the charge which was committed unto you more than six years ago as our pastor, you do not purpose to retire altogether from the work of the ministry. You hope to find many opportunities of service. May you have much joy in that service, and may the 'joy of the Lord be your strength.' Your ministry here has been marked by evn?stness and fidelity to the car- I dine] truths of the Gospel of Christ. We also recognise with gratitude the valuable service which you rendered in the liquidation of the debt (Z 1,550 which had so long crip- pled our energies. We feel that kindly reference is also due to one who is 'gone before,' and who was, for many years, associated with you in every good work. She was ever to the front in every effort to further the Kingdom of God. It is a poignant grief that you no longer feel the touch of a vanished band,'-nor hear the seund of a voice that is still.' But let us assure you that her memory will long remain fragrant in our midst. And now, sir, permit us to express to you our fervent desire that wherever yeu reside you may enjoy the peace of God,' whom you have served -with the strength of youth and manhood.—WidneS, btu) 21st, 1883." (Signatures follow.)—The Rev. T. PETBRS acknowledged the gift in an appropriate speech, and the pro- ceedings terminated.—The retirement of Mr. Peters will excite feelings of regret in the minds of all the Christian workers in Widnes, and the good wishes of all who know him will follow him into the new sphere of life which he in- tends to enter in Liverpool. Since he came to the town in 1877 a debt of £1,550 has been cleared off the Milton Congrega- tional Church, which has also during that period been greatly improved by an artistically constructed wall which was built around it about two years ago. This work was accomplished to a great extent through his persistent and energetic labour, but while thus mindful of the temporal welfare of his church, he was always in the van of every philanthropic and social effort in the town. He was an earnest advocate of Sunday schools, and he, along with his son, Mr. T. J. Peters, was one of the chief organisers of the Widnes Sunday school Union, an institution which has been attended with marked success. Mr. Peters was an ef- fective speaker; he invariably commanded the attention of his audience and was at ease on any platform. His depar- ture will leave a gap which it will be hard to fill.
MURDEROUS ASSA.ULT ON THE
WIDNES SPAVRRAGE CONTRACTOR.

At Widnes rutty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. E. K. Muspratt (chairman) and Mr. E. Gibbon, hales Morris was brought up, on remand, charged with ,aeing drunk, and also with asstulting Mr. R )bert Jeffries.—P.U. Griffiths stated that about three o'clock on Thursday after- noon, the 14th instant, he found the prieoner lying down on the Widnes Marsh in a state of drunkenness, and he brought him to the police station and locked him up.—Mr. Jeffries said he was contractor for the Widnes sewerage works, and the prisoner had been in his employ. On the 14th instant, he was on one part of the works when the pri- , sonar, who appeared to be in drink, walked up to the &de of the cutting. He wieriess) was afraid the prisoner would tumble in head first, and in consequence sent a man to ask him what he was doing there. Mr. Griffiths was also walk— ing up to the prisoner, when the latter picked up an iron bar four feet long and an inch and a half thick, and said "If you don't pay me for my half-day on Saturday I will split your skull open." He then run one end of the bar right on the middle of Mr. Griffith's back.—Mr. Lewin: Did you give the prisoner any cause to do this? Never.— Did you give him any provocation? I only asked him what he wanted to do with that bar, and told him Trot to talk in t)at way.—By Mr. Gibbon : lie sufflred pan from the blow for some days. He was now all right. Mr. Lffries added that he did not want to runish a workman severely, but still he wanted protection.—Mr. Lewin,. You said the other day that you being a large employer of labour, brought this case as a warning to other men,—Mr. Jeffries: I Yes, that is so.—The Bench caused the -charge of drunken- ness to be withdrawn, and for the assault fined the prisorter 20s. and nests, or in default a month's imprisonment.

div.head: WILD WIDNES BOY.
div.p: A WILD WIDNES BOY.
A YOUNG JACK SHEPPARD.

On Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, John Roberts, 11 years of age, was charged with stealing half a sovereign, belonging to Henry Coppock, a greengrocer's assistant, re- siding at 21, Wellington-street, Widnes.—On the 11th inst. the prosecutor was hawking vegetables in a handcart. He sold ton pounds of potatoes to a woman, who gave him half a sovereign. He was unable to change it, and asked •the prisoner, who was riding in the cart, to get it changed. He went away for that purpose, but did not return with the money, and the prosecutor had not seen him until he was in custody on Tuesday last.—Supt. Barker asked the magistrates to send the prisoner to a reformatory school. His parents could not get him to attend school, and for several nights after committing this robbery he had been sleeping out. The boy, in fact, ran about the streets wild.— Mr. G. H. Danby, the clerk to the School Board, observed that he had summoned the parents before the magistrates with the object of having the prisoner sent to a truant school, because the School Board could d no good with him. He frequently slept in the works. The Bench intimated that they would hear the summons issued by the School Board before dealing with the prisoner.—lt was stated that the boy had made 11 attendances out of a possible 40.—Mr. Danby said the parents had been fined by the magistrates for not sending this boy regularly to school, and they had been before the -committee of the School Board nine times. The mother bad had a great deal of trouble with him. She had frequently taken him to school, but when she put him in at one door he managed to escape by another. He often stayed away from home for a week, sleeping in the works during that time. He (Mr. Danby) was instructed to ask for an attendance order to send the prisoner to a truant school for a few months, but if their worships desired to send him to an industrial school he should have no objection.—Mr. Gibbon : We think it better for him to go to an industrial school.—The prisoner was then formally committed to the Beacon Lane Industrial School until he is 16 years of age.

OFFENDING BICYCLISTS. —At Present Petty Ses- sions, on Tuesday, Herbert Savage, Croateth Lodge, Huyton' who did not - appear, was fined 28. 6.1. and ' costs far riding a bicycle after sunset without a lamp in ' Knowsley-lane. A young man, named Henry Thewlis, was fined Is. and costs for a similar offence on Warrington-road, Rainhill ; and Edward Woods was similarly fined for a like offence on St. Helens-road, Prescot. STATE OF 'TUE CROPS AT ECCLESTON AND WINDLIL—A correspondent writes :—Hay crop will in most places be very light on account of the very dry season. Oats have looked very well up to about a week ago, when they began to show that they were suffering for want of rain. Wheat crop, what little there is, is looking very well, and so also are po- tatoes. Turnips and marigolds are fair, but want rain badly. , Pastures are looking very bad. Sacatth HEART CHURCH, Sr. HELENS.—The annual charity sermons in aid of the building debt fund were preached in this church on Sunday, in the morning by the Rev. Father Dorran, Croft, and in the evening by the Rev. Father Haza de Radlitz, Ditton Hall. On both occasions, but particularly in the evening, there were large congrega- tions. The music was rendered by a special choir and orchestra under the leadership of Mr. J. Dennett. TRANSFERS OF LICENSES.—At Present Petty Sessions on Tuesday, the magistrates granted the following transfers of licenses:—Beerhouse at Widnes, from James Concannon to Joseph Thomson; Original Farmers' Arms, Horn Smithies, Huyton, from Peter Ashcroft to Joseph Atherton. Wilbra- ham Clough applied for the transfer to him of the license of the Engine Inn, Sewell-street, Prescot. Superintendent Barker objected, as he had an information to lay against the applicant for permitting drunkenness, and the magis- trates refused the transfix.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

In the chess tournament, yesterday, the drawn game be- tween Rosenthal and Englisch again resulted in a draw. Amongst those who will be present at the banquet of the Constitutional Union, under the presidency of the Marquis of Salisbury, on the 27th inst., will be Earl Jersey, Earl Cadogan, Lord Valentia, Lord Francis Hervey, and Sir John Mowbray; Messrs. E. Stanhope, E. Gibson, Beresford Hope, Chaplin, Balfour, Clarke, and other members of Parliament.

Yesterday morning a four-lined whip, marked "special and important" was sent out to Conservative members of Parliament,urging the extreme necessity of a full attend- ance in the House in the afternoon, when the Committee on the Corrupt Practices Bill would be resumed, and the clause dealing with the punishment of candidates again con- sidered.

An alarming fire broke out at Partick, near Glasgow, yesterday morning, resulting in four valuable horses being burned tO death. The premises were occupied by Mr. M•Meekin, florist, and so rapid was the progress of the flames that everything was consumed before the animals could be rescued. Five sets of harness, and a large number of agricultural implements were also burnt. The property is insured.

The Queen, accompanied by Princess Beatrice and Prin- cess Elizabeth of Hesse, left Balmoral this afternoon, and drove in open carriage to Ballater Railway Station. The Royal party left for Windsor at 20 minutes past three. It was noticed Her Majesty seemed much better in health and spirits than on her arrival at Balmoral, and she had so far recovered as to be able to walk from her carriage to the train.

div.head: SUNDERLAND DISASTER.
div.p: THE SUNDERLAND DISASTER.

The Mayor of Sunderland has again received a large num- ber of letters expressive of sympathy with the parents of the children killed in the recent disaster. They come from Father Ignatius, Secretary of the Order of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, from Mrs. Fenwick, widow of a former nember for the borough, from Admiral How, Mr. W. Ward, London, with cheque for ten guineas and subscription, and a loving letter from a number of children. In accordance NI ith a resolution passed at a meeting of the Relief Committee on Thursday night, the wants of bereaved parents are being I inquired into. A very large quantity of flowers and wreaths Ito be placed on the graves continues to arrive. To carry out ; the intention of the committee to erect and endow a con- valescent home in memory of the children £lO,OOO or £12,000 will be required. Contributions continue to flow steadily in. Atari open-air concert in the pain on Thursday night £7 133. was realised.

div.head: STRUGGLE FOR THE POSSESSION OF PROPERTY.
div.p: A STRUGGLE FOR THE POSSESSION OF PROPERTY.

I lively contest to obtain possession of property is taking place at Flint. A woman, named Catherine Hughes, claims a certain cottage and tillage land, held by the repre- sentative of the late Thom es Lewis, Bryn Edwyn, and in order to enforce her claim sire caused a wooden shed to be erected on the land and took up her residence therein. The servants of the Bryn Edwyn estate stormed the shed, bundled Mrs. Hughes oat, and co npletely demolished the building. Mrs. Hughes obtained the assistance of several sympathetic nelp,hbuurs and returned to the attack, but the servants also had been reinforced, and Mrs. Hughes failed after a struggle to retake her position. As a last resort she has caused a notice to be put up near at hand warning all trespassers that they will be dealt with as the law directs.
CONVICTION OF AN INNOCENT MAN.
RELEASE BY THE HOME SECRETARY.

An extraoldinary case of accusation and conviction by mistake through the resemblance of two brothers has just come before the notice of the liome Secretary. On the 9th of June Alfred Weaver, of Birmingham, was convicted be- fore Messrs. T. Avery and J. .liffray, Birmingharh magis- trates, for stealing sign boards and was sentenced to two months' imprisonment with hard labour. The man, who declared [lie innocence, was taken handcuffed to the borough gaol. It was afterwards shown hoyond the shadow of a doubt that tho man was perfectly innocent of the charge, land the next day the following letter was sent to the Home ! Secretary :—" Police Court, Birmingham, June 10th, 1883. Sir, we have the honour to inform you that Alfred Weaver, was convicted yesterday of stealing six sign boards, and was sent to prison for two months. It was proved before the justices that the prisoner disposed ! of the sign boards shortly after they were stolen to Sidney WilliamTarratt. The identity of the prisoner was posi- tively sworn to by Tarratt's wife and father, the latter stat- ing that he had known the prisoner by sight for a long time. We are now desired by the committing justices to forward I you the statements since made by those two witnesses, wherein they admit that they were mistaken, and that the person referred to was prisoner's brother. These are con- firmed by the statements of other persons also sent there- with. rider these circumstances we are desired to ask you to be good enough to forward to the governor of Her Majesty's prison, with as little delay as possible, an authority authorising him to discharge Alfred Weaver. —J. B. Hebbert, W. Barradale (signed), Clerks to the Justices." The innocent brother has now been set at liberty by order of the Home Secretary, who a few thys since wrote to the governor of the gaol. directing his immediate discharge.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.

Upon the resumption of the inquiry into this bill by the I Select Committee of the House of Commons, yesterday, the cross-examination of I Mr. T. R. Foster, a witness called on behalf of Sir , Humphrey Trafford in opposition to the bill, was continued. He said he coald not understand where the engineer of the canal got the six million gallons per day that he said would come down the river from the Salford sewers when the total amount of water supplied to Salford by the Manchester Corporation was only 1,750,000 gallons per day. Mr. Wm. Henry Watson. analytical chemist, of Bolton, gave the result of his analyses of samples of water taken from various points on the river Irwell on the 12th of April, and from the Ist to the 12th of May. The result of those analyses was that he found a large amount of organic matter in suspension, especially in the samples taken from the river at a point below where the Manchester sewage entered the river, and at a point opposite Trafford Hall. He had kept some of the samples for three days with the result that they became putrid and gave off a very offensive smell. As the result of his experiments he concluded that the water of the river was very highly pol- luted with sewage matter, and that if a large quantity of the water was stored in locks it was certain to become offensive and injurious to health. Dr. Sidz, professor of chemistry at the London Hospital, produced samples of water taken from various points in the River Irwell on the 12th of the present month, and also submitted tables shlohwe- ing the results of his analyses of these specimens. ._ effect of his observations was that the river Irwell was abominally polluted with sewage matter. Large black pieces of sewage were floating in the stream, and bubbles were rising all over the surface of the water. In his opinion any diminution in the velocity of the flow of the river, such as would be caused by storing the waterinaalocvkes, d and tlalsti would cause the water to become very off si he likely to be injurious to health. Mr. Stephenson, chief engineer to the L. and N.W. Rail- w4, Company, was next called and examined by Mr. Pope upon the Railway opposition. He stated that he had had considerable experience in harbour dredging and deck work. He agreed with Mr. Fowler's calculation of two tons per cubic yard of the matter to be dredged for this scheme, but he was satisfied that the eseimate of 9d per cubic yard Nv ould not he sufficient, judging from lrie own experience. The distauce which the dredged matter would have to be carried was a vital element in the question of cost, and upon that point no comparisons could be made between the Tyne, the Tees, and the Clyde and the Mersey, because in the latter case the distance would be much greater than in the former. On the Clyde dredging could be carried on nearly all the year, but that was not so in the Mersey, which was very much more exposed. He believed that not mare, but rather less, than seven hours dredging per tide would be practicable on the Mersey, and that each hopper would not make more than 103 trips on an average in 24 hours Ghat was upon the two tidk s). He estimated the working days of the year at 200, that 30 hoppers, capable of carrying 400 tons of dredged matter, including water, would be required for this work, to-

gether with two dredgers. Each hopper, he calcu/ated, would cost at least £B,OOO, and each dredger, £25,000, while the working expenses et the dredgers would be £3,500 per annum each. Each hopper could make 333 trips per annum to discharge the dredged matter, and each would dispose of 960,000 tons aye 'The total tons of matter, taking it at two tons per cubic yard, would be 30,000,000 tons. Turning next to the ques- tion of gradients, Mr. Stephenson said that the alteration of the levels of the line over the proposed canal to 1 in 114 would necessitate the use of extra assistance to get the greater part of the goods traffic over, although.nerhaps not for the passenger traffic. As to the deviation fur the pro— posed tunnel, he believed the result would be a constant in- flow of water unless special means were adopted to pre- vent it, and that in consequence it would be necessary to carry the inverto and training walls up to the level of the high water in the canal. With respect to the excava- tion of hard rock in the tidal portion of the c mat, he esti- mated from practical experience that it would cost 35 per cubic yard at least, as against the 2s 6d suggested by the promoters, and that for soft cutting the cost would be is. 6d., as against is. id. per cubic yard. The cost of cement concrete he put down at 13s. per cubic yard, as against Bs. to 10a. estimated by the promoters; and upon other points of cost he dif- fered from. the estimates of Mr. Leader Williams. Mr. Stephenson also expressed his conviction, from his own experience, that the landowners would not be at ail willing to receive the " spoil " upon their land, but that the promo- ters would have to buy land for the purpose. The committee adjourned to Monday.

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The LORD CHANCELLOR moved the second reading of the Pawnbrokers' Bill, the object of which wastop_rorfdt,ermeoi,..re effectual means of recovering stolen property cussion the Bill WRS read a second time.—Lord ALCESTRR informed Lord Sidmouth that the Admiralty would c sider any representation from warrant officals in the Navy, provided they were forwarded in a proper manner. Any combination among these officers was contrary to regula- tions.—Lords Alcester and Wolseley's Grant Bill passed through committee. HOUSE OF COMMONS. SIR R. PEEL'S SETTLED ESTATE BILL.—Mr. ARNOLD ob- jected to the third reading of Sir Robert Peel's Settled Estate Bill, and said it proposed to keep ten thousand acres of the most fertile land of England in embarrassed hands rather than allowing them to pass into the possess:on of persons who would make better use of them.—After a short discussion, the bill was read a third time. DROWNED OR MURDERED ?—Mr. ASTLEY said it Was the opinion of many that the five gentlemen who had disap- peared from the sea coast of New South Wales had been drowned, not murdered. NEW WRIT.—A new writ was issued for Hastings. CORRUPT PRACTICES BILL.—The House went into cont- mittee on the Corrupt Practices Bill, and resumed considera- tion of Mr. Gorst's proposed addition to clause four for giving the election court power to deal with the disqualifica- tion of candidates when it was proved such corrupt practice had not been committed with their know- ledge or consent.—Sir W. BARTELLOT said that without ' concession was made the bill would altogether fail.— After a long discussion the proposal was wididrawn as was also the proviso standing in the names of Mr. Lewis and Mr. E. Clarke.—Mr. H. FOWLER then moved his proviso, which set out if the election court reported that a candidate and his election agent had taken all reasonable means to prevent corropt practice, and no corrupt practice had been committed with their consent, and also that if trivial corrupt practices were proved, then the election should not be declared void. The AT- TORNEY-GENERAL said he would as a concession adopt the middle course. He would accept the principle of Mr. Fowler's proviso, provided it was agreed that it should nut apply to bribery and personation, but only to is influence and treating. He could not accept the para..* r words as they stood, but he would bring up a new clause on the subject.—Mr. GORST blamed the Government for nct announcing the decision earlier.—A long discussion ensued on the proposal to withdraw Mr. Fowler's amendment.— MR. CHAPLIN said the concession or the Government amounted to nothing, as it did not ,touch bribery.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE objected to close present discussion on the bare promise to bring up their new proposal in the shape of a new clause.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL said his proposal was in fact the embodiment of the suggestion of Sir R. Cross, and he was surprised Sir S. Northc.,te should object to it.—He thought it sharp practice that the Government should be driven into the lobby to vote against the proviso. —Sir R. Cross, Mr. Ritchie, Mr. Cowen, and Mr. Labouchere objected to the withdrawal of the proviso.—Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN defended the course adopted by the Government. He condemned the opposition raised and the withdrawal of the proviso, and said it was a course of action that would have an effect in the constituencies.—Mr. lIENEanE approved the Iproposal of the Attorney General.—Mr. PLUNEETT urged the Committee to adopt the proviso.—Sir W. HARCOURT said it was impossible for the Government to adopt the proposal which relaxed the securities against bribery. He trusted the Committee would reject all proposals having action in that direction.—Mr. A. BROWN moved to amend the first section of Mr. Fowler's proviso by inserting the words " other than bribery " after the words "corrupt practice."—Mr. LABOUCHBRE thought it extremely clever that the Government should have induced members to with- draw a variety of amendments in crder that they might ',lake a concession which amounted to Inning—which was io f set asking for a shilling and getting a halfpenny If Government made no further concession when they brought forward the new clause, he should move its amendment so as to include bribery.—Eventually, Mr. Brown withdrew his amendment, and a division was taken on Mr. Fowler's proviso.—For, 180; against, 200.—Sir H. Gil-YARD then moved an amendment in the same direction as Mr. Fowler's.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL Opposed. He promi,ed to give the proposal full consi 'era.ion whin he was 7 drawing up the new clause. The amendment was withdrawn and clause 4 was agreed. Clause 5, which provided for the punishment of persons convicted on indictment for corrupt practice, was next considered. Mr. BIGGAR moved an amendment extending the clause to charges of undue in- fluence.—Mr.CaLnere talked out the amencin-.ent.—The sit- ting was suspended.
WESLEYA.N METRODIST QUARTERLY MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

The June quarterly meeting of the Warrington Wesleyan Methodist Circuit was held on Monday. The proceedings commenced with the meetieg of local preachers in the vestry of Bold-street Chapel, under the presidency of the superin- tendent minister, the Rev. John Eglinton. when the usual order of business special to this meeting was transacted. Afterwards the stewards, leaders, trustees, and local preachers, with the Revs. J. A. Beet and Thomas Rippon, met in the large room of the chapel for the consideration and discussion of matters having reference to the welfare and interest of the circuit in general. The superintendent Minister officiated as chairman. The society's numerical status was reported as 830, and on trial for membership el. The financial condition was satisfactory, aud showed a balance in hand of £43. This being the last time the Rev. Joseph Agar Beet would be present before leaving the circuit in August next for Wrexham' it was unanimously resolved that the thanks of the meeting be presented to him for his three years' valuable services. This resolution was spoken to by several gentlemen who were representative of the different departments of Methodism in the circuit, all of whom spoke very highly of Mr. Beet as an expositor of God's word, a preacher of the Gospel, and as one deeply in- terested in the welfare of younz people. Mr. Beet, in reply, spoke of Ids deep regret in hafing to leave the circuit. He had spent nearly three years in Warrington. ;His colleagues had been brotherly and faithful, the members of the society had been friendly and pleasant, indeed, he had not had to his recollection a cross word with any one. His thanks were due to them for bearing with him in his peculiar circum- stances, for while lie had wished to be faithful to the circuit as a minister, he felt he had other work to do which was rnost important, and which he could not lay aside. The position of Mr. Beet is well known as a learned, critical. and trustworthy commentator on the Epistle to the Romans, and the Epistles to the Corinthians' and he has expressed an intention to write similarly with respect to the rest of the Pauline writings. Mr. Beet will quit War- rington witti the satisfactory reflection that none wish hits more success in his future expositions or ministerial wcrk than the people he will ehorrly leave and among whom he has laboured so earnestly. The meeting had also to say farewell to Mr. Alfred Lamplugh, who for 38 years has been connected with the Wesleyan church in the Warrington cis - cuit, and who has filled with honour and credit the office of local preacher, Sunday school superintendent, class leader, trustee, society and circuit steward at various periods during his residence in the town. Special mention was made of Mr. Lamplugh's services in connection with the Bold-street Mutual Improvement Society, his leadership of an im- portant society class, his willingness to -render help Personally and financially to circuit effort, and his constant attachment and valuable assistance in the services, more particularly of the sanctuary of Bold-street Chapel. Mr. Lamplugb, in responding to the expres ion of warm-hearted feeling so unanimously given by the meeting, was deeply affected, and spoke in encourag- ing, terms respecting the position of Methodism in Warring- ton. We believe it is Mr. Lamplugh's intention to dwell at South Kensington, London. A letter of condolence was directed to be sent to Dr. Smith, J.P., in his bereavement through the death of Mrs. Smith. The meeting very feel- ing referred to the virtues and services of the deceased lady, and expressed their deep sympathy with the worthy and afflicted husband and family. Reference was also made at the first meeting to the fact that several local preechers are at present unable to work through ill-health, and a hope was entertained tbat scon their health might be re-established We must not omit to state that during the afternoon tea was provided by Mesdames Bowden and Guest, in a manner which reflected upon those ladies much credit, and at the tables a large number of persons sat down and did justice to a substantial repast. —Communicated.

A CARELESS FATFlER.—Superintpmlent Johnston applied at the St. Helens Police Court, on Friday, for an order to pay Is. 6d. per week towards the support of a daughter, in a reformatory school, to be made out against a labourer named John Ford. It was stated that when the girl was first sent to the reformatory school defendant promised to I ay is. per week, but sinca then he had fallen into arrear a. He earned over 20s, per week in wages when he was work- ing, but he lost time owing to being addicted to drink.—The order was made.

GOOD TEMPLARS' MEETING AT EAULESTOWN.—The usual weekly meeting of the members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars, was held in the lodge-room, Bridge-street, on Monday evening. There was a very good attendance, and Sister M. Allison, W.C.T. presided. Several items of lodge business were discussed, after which Brother T. 0. Roberts read an interesting paper on the temperance movement, in which he alluded at some length to its past Progress, and spoke with pleasure of the fact that many of the temperance soaieties were based on Christian principles. An instructive discussion afterwards followed, and a hearty vote of thanks waa accorded to Brother Roberts for his emay. The meeting concluded about 9-30. Tra GOSPEI TENT, PRESCOT.--For the last seven years religious services have been conducted in this place of worship under the auspices of the Liverpool Evangelisation Society. That society having „„w discontinued its con- nection with it, the tent has been acquired by the Baptist denomination, who have not hitherto had a chapel in Free- cot. The services under the new regime commenced on Sunday, when sermons were preached by thaenßev.? G.a. Green, of tl.: ictoria Mission Hall, St. Helens, d iar of the Baptist Church, Park-road, St. Helens. On Tuesday evening Mr. J. Bennett Anderson, of Byrom Hall, Liver- pool, preached in the tent, and also connucted an open-air service. PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD.—The morAhly meeting of this Board was held on Monday evening. The only members present were Mr. Goldsworth and Mr. Fogg, with Mr. Cross (clerk), and as these did not constitute a quorum, no business was done. The monthly return of attendance in the Board schools showed that there were on the roll of the schools 231 boys, 124 girls, and 86 infants, as compared with 210 boys, 104 girls, and 108 infants in the corresponding month of last year. The average attendance was 201 boys, 102 girls, and 63 infants, as against 140 boys, 78 girls, and 52 infants in the corresponding month of last year. The fees received during the month amounted in the boys' school to £ll 7s. 10d.; girls,l6 lie. Id.; infants, £2 12.5. 2d. In June last year the fees received were—from boys, £6 I.os. 241; girls, £4 19s. 441. ; infants, £1 les. 6d.
