div.head: DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.
ASHTON.

ODDFELLOWS' MEETING AT A SIITON.—The usual monthly meeting of the members of the Loyal Triumphant Lodge of the Independent Order of Oddfellows, M.U., was held at the Gerard'a Arms Hotel, Ashton, on Saturday evening last. There was a good attendance, and Prov. C.S. John Hodg- kinsen presided as N.G. Several matters affecting the lodge were discussed, and a delegate was appointed to represent the ledge at the next quarterly district meeting to be held at Golborne on the 30th'inst. The receipts and contributions amounted to over £26, while the disbursements were About £3B.

Assetrur AT ASHTON. -At the Wigan County Police Court, on Friday last, Edward Clark was summoned for as- saulting Thomas Sumner.—The men are colliers, and live at Stubshaw Cross, Ashton. On the night of the 10th inst., chey were in a public-house at Stubshaw Cross, and on the defendant going into one of the rooms complainant told him that there was no seat for him. Defendant then seized Sumner, threw him down, strack him in the eye, and kicked him.—Defendant alleged that as be was passing complain- set, the latter struck him several times, and called witnesses to support his statement—Defendant was fined 5s and costs.

SINGULAR ROBBERY OF A COAT FROM AN ASHTON MAN. —At the Wigan County Police Court, on Tuesday, two men named James' Dawber, Chapel-lane, and Caleb Hilton, Spring-gardens, were charged with stealing a coat from the person of John Harkell, painter, Ashton. The previous day prosecutor, who is a stranger to the town, met the prisoners at Spring-gardens and treated them to some drink. Prose- cutor got advanced in liquor, and on leaving the house the men took him on to some waste land where they all sat down. Whilst there the prisoners took Harkell's coat from him and made off with it, but went they got to Lime-street, Police- constable McFay met them, and seeing Dawber with the coat suspected them and took them to the police station. Dining the evening McFay made a round of several lodging houses .and found prosecutor in one of them without his coat. He afterwards identified the coat found on pesoners as his property. Both men had been previously convicted, Dawber being a returned convict. They were commited to the sessions for trial. ADDRESS AT THE ASHTON CAVE-BROWNE PROTESTANT INSTITUTE —A very impressive address was given by Walter Roughton, Esq., of Livetpool, in the Cave-Ercr.vne Protestant Institute, Heath-lane, Ashton, on Sunday afternoon last. There was a crowded attendance of the teachers, scholars, ard congregation, and the most earnest attention was mani- fested in Mr. Roughton's remarks. He founded his remarks upon the words "She bath done what she could" (Mark xiv. 8), and drew therefrom an instructive lesson. He ex- plained that Mary had done all she could for her Master's sake, and brought the question home to his hearers by ask- ing if they had, or were they willing to imitate her example by doing what they could. He commendably spoke of the work they had accomplished in that neighbourhood by raising that institute for the service of their Master, and said he would always pray that the blessing of the Master might rest upon them. • -Mr. Thomas 'Jameson presided at the harmonium. 'The service throughout was a very earnest one. We might mention that Mr. Roughton was accom- panied by Mr. W. Richardson, of Rose Cottage, Newton, whose guest he was for the day.

div.head: BOLD.
div.p: BOLD.

ALLEGED ASSAULT ON A WOMAN. A young married man named William Pritchard was, on Monday, charged At the St. Helens County Petty Sessions with having assaulted a married woman named Margaret Livingstone, at Bold, on the 27th May. Mr. J. 0. Swift defended.—The complainant, in a somewhat rambling and obscure statement, asserted that on the day in question the defendant had taken hold of her and put her down in a ditch, and after that she "did not know what took place." It appeared, however, on cross- examination that there had been nothing of a very serious nature about the assault, and the case was dismissed. CHILD WALL.

RURAL DEANERY OF CRILDWALL.—The first conference of the New Rural Deanery of Childwall was held on Friday last, in the Diocesan-rooms, Lord-street, under the presi- dency of the Rural _Dean (the Rev. J. W. Diggle, M.A.) There were present the Revs. E. Snowdon Smith, C. 1 Stephenson J. Cassels Brown, J. Wright Williams, J. 11. F. Henson, H. Vernon, H. C. Beeching, and D. W. Mounfield ; Messrs. Stolterfoht, C. Langton, Lonsdale, A. Book, W. D. Jeans, Domville, and Fletcher Rogers. After a-communication from the Bishop had been read and by- laws framed, the Rev. Snowdon Smith was eleded secretary, and Mr. F. Rogers treasurer for the year.—Mr. Agnew then introduced the question of forming a Sunday School Asso- ciation for the Deanery. He thought there was great need of organisation, but a danger of making it too formal. The teachers themselves ought to be consulted as to the kind and number of meeting required, and as to the election of officers. There was a difficulty in forming an association for a large district, but the larger the district the more ne- cessary was some means of union. He knew of a place where two gentlemen friends had been both 6unday school teachers for a quarter of a century without each other's knowledge. The association should aim at reaching children of all classes and by all possible agencies. In Philadelphia, there were not only several children's services on Sunday, 1 but on week day evenings as well. Another good effect that weuid result from an association would be to keep the same teachers longer by wakening a deeper interest in their work. In arswer to questions from the chairman (the Rev. C. Stephenson), Mr. Agnew explained that it would be the work of such an association to promote some central devotional service, to hold special services as at the opening of s;ssions, and _ to have meetings for dit:cussion either on training lessons or on some paper to be read. He thought that two centres would be sufficient for the deanery, and that the movement might be best set on foot by a general meeting of teachers held after some central service. As points of detail he thought the effect of training lessons given by a competent teacher could scarcely be overrated, and he expected that superintendents, on whom the success of, the schools so much depended, would derive very great advantage from conference with each otker.—Mr. Doraville, who spoke from 40 years' experience of Sunday schools, thought that the proposed association would smooth away many difficulties, and he knew that the idea would be cordially embraced by the teachers of Sankey.—A motion embodying Mr. Agnew's proposal was then movid by the Rev. Wright Williams, seconded by Mr. Domville, and car- ried; and a sub-committee was appointed, consisting of the hon. secretary,.Messrs. Domville, Forster. and E. W. Bird, ,and the Vicars of Farnwortb, Ditton, and Widnes to consider the form the association should take.—A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Agnew, and the conference soon after broke up. HAXDOCK.

INgrEST ON A COLLIER AT LIATDOCK.—On Monday, Mr. T. W. Barker, the district coroner, held an inquest at the RAM'S Head Hotel, Haydock, on the body of Thomas Ley- land, 20 years of age, a collier, residing in Lyme-street. The evidence showed that on the oth November last the deceased was trorking in the Ram pit belonging to Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., and a fall of the roof occurred. He was in a stooping position at the time and some of the stones fell upon him. When he was released he told a fellow-collier that he thought he was "done for." It was found that he had received severe injuries to his back, and he was at once re- moved home, where he was attended by Dr. Hayward up to his death, which occurred between four and five o'clock on Friday morning last. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

div.head: HOUGH GREEN.
div.p: HOUGH GREEN.

THE FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAH HOUGH GREEN. —On Tuesday afternoon Mr. Barker, county coroner, held an inquest at the Hammer and Pincers public-house, Rough Green, on the body of Robert Oscar, aged 18, lately em- ployed as a porter at the railway station at that place, who was killed on Saturday evening under circumstances pre- viously reported. Mr. Frederick Simpson, detective super- intendent, was present on behalf of the Cheshire Lines Railway Company, and Mr. Tetley, of the locomotive de- partment, represented the Midland Company. The evidence showed that the cause of death rested entirely with the de- ceased, and the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

div.head: HUTTON.
div.p: HUTTON.

FIGHTING HIS BITTLES O'ER AGAIN.-011 Monday, at the St. Helens Police Court, a man named Charles White- head, who came from Huyton, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly, and also with assaulting Henry. Penketh, a tram-ear conductor. on Saturday night.—lt ap- peared that pi isoner bad been on one of the Present tram- cars, and when requested to pay his fare by Penketh he re- fused to do so, swearing that he had already paid it. A companion, however, paid it for him, but prisoner still con- tinued to make a disturbance, and wanted to fight with another passenger. Penketh and the driver interfered, and got him out of the car, but when on the road he got hold of Penketh by the neck and struck him. He also got in between the horses in trying to get at the driver. A pclice- man at length appeared on the scene and book prisoner into custody, bat he continued to be so violent that the officer had to call upon two civilians for assistance before getting him to the police office.—Prisoner, who said he had just come from Egypt and was now in the Army reserve, offered no7defence, and was fined 10s. and Is. costs for-the assault. and ss. and Is. 6d. costs for having been drunk and disorderly, or in default three weeks' imprisonment.

HITYTON QUARRY. FUDDIIIN DEATH AT HUTTON QUARRY. Mrs. Price, widow of the late George Price, Seel-streot, !futon Quarry, died suddenly on Tuesday night. The late Mr. Price was an engine-driver at one of the pits of the Wigan and Whis- ton Coal Company, and was much respected. He died on Sunday morning, after an illness of only three or four days, and the sudden death of Mrs. Price is ascribed to the shock caused by her bereavement. She was about 35 years of age, and has left four young children. ASSLULTING A. CONSTABLE AT HUTTON QUARRY.—At Prescot, on Tuesday, Henry Hirst was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and assaulting P.C. Hall. On Satur- day night, the 9th inct., prisoner was making a disturbance at Huyton Quarry when P.C. Hall and P.C. Hewitt tried to pacify bins. As Hall was turning away, the prisoner came behind and gave him two or three kicks on the leg.—For the drunkenness prisoner was fined 5s and costs, and for the atsault lOs and costs. A man named Frank Worall, who had attempted to rescue the prisoner when in Hall's custody, was fined 5s and costs for being drunk on licensed premises—the Engine Inn, Sewell-street, Prescot. GIRL HOUSEBREAXERS AT lirtrroN QUARRY—Two girls named Catherine and Mary Ellen Leach were charged at Preecot, on Tuesday, with breaking and entering the dwell- ing-house of TiIOIIIAS Mounslow, labourer, Huyton Quarry. It was stated that on Monday afternoon Ml 3. Moultslow went to Liverpool, and when in Huyton Qizarry ttatiou saw the

div.head: LEIGH.
div.p: LEIGH.

NOVEL Form or SIVWDLINO.—On Tuesday, at Leigh, before Mr. T. T. Hayes, a smart-looking young fellow from Manchester, who gave the name of William Harcourt, was charged with obtaining money by false pretences. On the sth inst. the prisoner prevailed on the wife of Thomas Harrison, grocer, Hindesford, Atherton, to purchase three dozen envelope packages of his vermin killer, which was described in print on the address side as "the only powder which is not poisonous to human beings or domestic animals. Manufactured only by J. H. Harford, London and Glasgow." A short time after Mrs. Harrison had been induced to part with 12s. to the prisoner she called at a chemist's shop in Tyldesley, and there saw him buy a pound of yellow ochre for threepence. Information was given to the police, and Harcourt was found in the taproom of a beerhouse preparing packages of powder. When charged, he admitted that the powder consisted only of ochre and plaster of Paris, and stated that he had made a "good thing" out of it since Whitsuntide. On the 25th April last the prisoner obtained 12s. 6d. in a similar manner from Emma Derbyshire, wife of Richard Derbyshire, Blackburn-road, Bolton. In April of last year he obtained 245. from Henry Ince, grocer, Tyldes- ley, and in each case he appointed the purchasers his agents for their districts. The prisoner, who had now nothing to say, was committed- for trial on the three charges.

div.head: LY MISL
div.p: LY MISL

LIMIIt POLICE COUE.T.—Patrick Haverty, who said he had just come from Ireland, was brought before Mr. G. C. Dewhurst, at the Lymm Police Court, on Monday, charged with being drunk and disorderly at Broom Edge, on Satur- day night.—The case having been proved, Mr. Dewhurst said it was intolerable that a man like the prisoner should disturb the peace of what was well known as a quiet and orderly neighbourhood.—The prisoner was fined ss. and costs, and in default of payment Ile went to prison for seven days.

LIVERPOOL EXCURSIONISTS AT LYMIL—The annual reunion of the office staff of Messrs. Cope Brothers and Co., Liverpool, took place on Saturday. As heretofore, the party consisted of the office staff, together with the repre- sentatives from other branches of the establishment, to whom invitations hal been extended. After having lunched in one of Messrs. Cope'sspacious dining-rooms, the company availed themselves of the 12-40 train from Lime-street, on which an elaborate saloon carriage had been kindly placed at their disposal. Warrington was soon reached, and here a well-appointed coach, horsed by four handsome, valuable steeds, was, agreeably with a pre-wrangement, waiting the arrival of those on pleasure bent. This vehicle was speedily on its way over hill and dale, *id Latchford and Grappen- hall, towards Lymm, where, at the Plough and Railway Hotel, light refreshments were partaken of. After a short interval a re-mount was made, and the four-in-hand was again en route for Bowdon, afterwards returning by another route to Lymm. At the Plough and Railway Hotel, Lymm, dinner was served at six o'clock. Leaving Lymm by 9-50, after an unusually enjoyable excursion' the train at War- ington for Liverpool was reached in good time.

div.head: RAINFORD:
div.p: RAINFORD:

STRAYING lionsEs.—Joseph Owen, a farmer, was, on Monday, charged at the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, with having allowed four horses and three colts to stray on the highway. A police officer stated that at 20 minutes to twelve on the night of the 9th inst. he found the animals straying along Rainford-road, and a few hours afterwards he saw them again at Denton's Green. Defendant said the horses must have been let out of his field by some one dur- ing the night. He was ordered to pay the costs of the summons, 43 od._

DAMAGE TO the St. Helens County Petty Sessions on Monday, two youths named John Smith and Jas. Prescott were charged with having wilfully damaged shrubs, the property of Mr. Pennington, Muncaster Hall, Rainford, on the 3rd inst. Mr. J. 0. Swift prosecuted, and said that Mr. Pennington had suffered a great deal from injury being done to his shrubs in the plantation surrounding his house. It appeared from the evidence that Mr. Pennington's son and another young man had been concealed in the plantation on the day in question and saw the defendant Smith break a rhododendron, Prescott sitting on the wall at the time, ap- parently keeping watch. The damage was estimated at id.' —Each defendant was fined '2B. 61. and is. 6d. col ht. A Sus Pinions CHARACTER.—At the St. Helens Police Court on Tuesday. a man named James Ashurst was charged with being on enclosed premises for an unlawful purpose.— It appeared from a statement by P.C. Parker that that officer had visited the farm buildings of Mrs. Elizabeth Tinsley, near Rainford. about 12 o'clock on the previous night and found the prisoner lying wide awake on some straw in a shed. He apprehended him, and on arriving at the police office the prisoner was searched and a black mask was found upon him. Adjoining the shed in which prisoner was found was a poultry cote. Prisoner asserted that he had permission to sleep on the premises, but the officer said he bad inquired of Mrs. Tinsley if that were so and she said it was notralthough the prisoner had done labour- ing work for her before —Superintendent Johnston said As- hurst lived with his brother at }Lanford, and had been five times convicted.—He was sent to gaol for 14 days. DRUNKENNESS AT RAINFORD.—At the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, on Monday, Richard Cowley was fined ss. and costs for having been drunk and disorderly at Rainford on the 2nd inst.—William Hurst was fined 10s. and costs for a similar offence on the same day.—Edward Higginson, an employ 6 at the Rainford brewery, was also charged with having been drunk and disorderly at Rainforde on Sunday, the 10th inst.—On being charged defendant said: If a basin of broth will snake me drunk at ten o'clock in the morning I am done for.—P.C. Dutton spoke to having seen defendant drunk on the highway.at ltainford at half-past ten on the morning named. Defendart would not go away when told,and N%itnrss was consequently under the necessity of locking lam up.—Defendant (to the officer) : If I had bad a half-barrel in the kiln you would have said nothing about this.—P.C. Duerdan was called, and corroborated Dutton's statement. Defendant: That officer, I believe, was lying concealed in the frame but if I had known he was there I would !Ave drowned him. (Laughter.)—A fine of 55. and costs was imposed.
RAINHILL.

PIGEON STEALING AT RAINHILL.—A miner named Thomas liankey, was charged at Prescot on Tuesday, with stealing a pigeon, the property of William Thirlwall, Bridge Inn, Rainhill. Mr. Mackenzie appeared for the prosecutor. The offence dated as far back as Easter Mon- day, when the defendant, with some companions, was drinking in prosecutors's house, and on leaving, took with him a pigeon from a cote in the back yard.—Mr. Earle (to prisoner): I suppose the real truth of the matter is that you were drunk when you took the pigeon—Defendant: Yes; we were all drunk together.—Mr. Earle: A nice party. You will have to pay 20s, and 2s. the value of the bird, or go to gaol for one month. ASSAULT BY A RAISHILL BEERHOUSEKEEPER.—WiIIiaIII Thirlwall, landlord of the Bridge beerhouse, Itainhil!, was charged at Frescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, with assaulting William Rabinson, cab driver, Rainhill.—Mr. Mackenzie appared for the defendant. It appeared that on ths sth instant, when complainant was in defendant's house defendant and he had a quarrel about complainant's children, and about is. 6d. which defendant alleged com- plainant owed him. The upshot was that defendant slapped complainant's face several times, and gave him a blow which cut him across the nose.—For the defence, it was alleged that camplainant had refused to give defendant some information which would have led to the conviction of a man who had stolen some of his fowls, and that in the heat of passion and under provoking circumstances, he had struck complainant slightly.—Mr. Earle said defendant had committed an assault, which he had no business to do how- ever much avgravated, and he must pay 20s. and 103. 6d. costs.

div.head: SOUTFIWORTH-WITII-CROFT,
div.p: SOUTFIWORTH-WITII-CROFT,

SCHOOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Board School on Tuesday evening. Present— the Rev. I'. P. Kirkman (chairman and clerk), and Messrs. Richard Turner (vice-chairman), James Hatton, Lewis Bir— chall, James Gooden, and Alfred Dixon (school attendance officer). The school attendance officer presented his report, which stated that he had visited the various schools in the district during the past month, when he found that 27 children had been away sick, and that he had warned several parents that unless their children attend school more regularly they would be summoned to appear before the Board to show a reasonable excuse for such absence. He also reported that he had summoned six parents to ap- pear before the Board for neglecting to send their children to school in pursuance of the bye-laws, all of whom ap- peared. Five were being cautioned, and the other will be summoned before the magistrates. The attendance officer further stated that he had visited all the children siek, and those who had been attending school irregularly, and that be desired to call the Board's particular attention to the fact of so many children being kept at home one and two half-days per week. The teachers of the various schools in the district had frequently called his attention to this re- peated irregularity. The bye-laws require that children must attend school every time the school is open. and far breach of this bye-law a parent may be summoned before the magistrates and fined. The report having been un- animously adopted, the Board directed the attendance officer to prepare a list of the number of children remaining at home wee or two half-days per week, and to report the same at the next Board meeting, after which their parents would be summoned before the magistrates if they continued to keep them at home. Several accounts having been passed, the proceedings terminated.

div.p: WESTON.

TRIAL TRIP OF THU CLARLssA.—Aboat three months ago, at Weston Point there was launched an iron steam tug,which recieved the name of "Clarissa," it being intended for the Weston Point Steam Tug Company. Since then the vessel has been sold to Mr. John Datton, of Cardiff, and will be used in the Bristol Channel, between Cardiff and Sandy Island for towing purveses. It is 92 feet long, and 18 feet across the beam, and has a depth of ton feet two inches. Tho engines, which have been supplied by r4r. Edwin Foden, of Sandbach, are compound surface condensing with an indicated horse-power of 300. The boiler loan ordinary marine multitubular of 10 feet diameter, havilog, two furnaces with a pressure of 801bs. The vessel, as wiv have previously stated, was built from the lesigns of Mr. Ritchie. Oa Sa- turday morning last the vessel went on a trial trip to the Nt,rrh-west lightship, and behaved ahlyl the Intasulta mile being run in very quick time..

WHISTOX. WESLEYAN SUNDAY ECHOOL, WHInON.-014 MORdaY7 the scholars attending the Wesleyan Sunday School, Whiston, enjoyed a field day in Halsnead Park. which was kindly placed at their disposal by Mr. Willis. The scholars walked. in procession from the school to the Park, under the guidance of Mr. Molyneux, the superintendent, and the teachers; and were accompanied by Mr. Mason and the choir of the Wesleyan Chapel, of which he is leader. The scholars, aided by the choir, sang hymns at the residence of Mr. 0. Ward, where they were refreshed with a copious supply of milk and cakes, and after their arrival at the Park an abundant tea was served in a large building. After tea the scholars and their friends devoted themselves to a variety of amusements, and the weather being fine an ex- tremely pleasant afternoon was spent. UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH -BAND, WHISTON.— The brass band in connection with the United Methodist Free Church, Whiston, the auspicious formation of which was recorded a fortnight ago, continues to make satisfactory progress. In acknowledgment of the valuable services ren- dered by Mr. J. Leatherbarrow, of Roper's Farm, when the band was projected about four months ago, the members bad intended that the first public exhibition of their skill should take place at his residence, but owing to the serious illness , of Mr. Leatherbarrow's father this intention had to be aban- doned. The elder Mr. Leatherbarrow having since partially recovered from his illness, the band on making their second public appearance on Saturday last made Roper's Farm their first stopping place, and testified their regard for Mr. Leatherbarrow and their gratification at his father's im- provement in health by playing several tunes. After this they paraded a great part of the township, passing through Huyton Quarry and returning by Tarbock-road, pausing on their way at the residences of several gentlemen, and receiv- ing not only hearty welcome, but gratifying contributions to their funds. On this occasion they joined to the harmony of their instruments harmony of appearance by donning a uniform of blue with gold facings. PILFERING COAL AT WilieToN.e—Annie Lyon appeared before the Prescot magistrates, on Tuesday, to answer a charge of stealing coal at Carr's colliery, Whiston. On the defendant coming forward it apfteared that she was a well- dressed little girl, seven years of age.—Mr. J. 0. Swift, who prosecuted, said he had had no idea the defendant was so young, and he would take the responsibility of with- drawing the charge. He believed, however, that the child's parents had encouraged her, in spite of repeated warnings, to steal coal. The father worked at Halsnead colliery, and made a practice when he did buy coal to buy it there, and all the coal he had bought since September last was 3s. 41 worth-10 cwt., and since September his three children had been in the habit of going to Carr's colliery and taking coal.--A middle-aged woman named Sarah Birchall was charged with stealing coal from Carr's colliery, Whiston.—Mr. J. 0. Swift prosecuted.—lt was stated in evidence that on the 25th May, at a quarter-past seven in the evening, P.C. Kay, and Jonathan Watkinson, a fitter employed at Carr's colliery, were on the engine house of the colliery, having been set there to watch in consequence of frequent robberies of coal, and saw the defendant and the little girl (Lyon) come to a coal heap and pick up some coal. As soon as they saw the watchers the woman and girl ran away, and in her flight defendant dropped 601 h. weight of coal, worth about 3d. Both defendant and the girl had been previously :warned.—Mr. Swift stated that many people had been brought before the court for similar offences, and penalties had been inflicted, but still the thefts continued. The defendant was a widow, and she had been warned on the 24th May. Some time ago, at the suggestion of the magistrates, a fence had been put up round the coal heap, and notice boards had been put up, but without much effect.—The magistrates said they were deter- mined to put a stop to the pilfering of coal at Whieton. They did not like to send a widow to gaol, but in future they would send persons who so offendei to gaol.—Defen- dant was fined 405., in default, one month's imprisonment.

div.head: EARLFSTOWN PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL. INTERESTING SERVICE OF SONG.
div.p: EARLFSTOWN PRIMITIVE METHO- DIST CHAPEL. INTERESTING SERVICE OF SONG.

A most interesting service of song entitled, "Little Minnie, or the sunshine of a sister's love," was given by the United Primitive Methodist Choirs of Earlestown and Parr in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Leg,h-street, Earlestown, on Sunday evening, in aid of the circuit fund. There was a crowded congregation, and their interest in the service was sustained to the end. The Rev. M. Dickenson was the reader, and after the congregation had sung a hymn and prayer had been offered up, he remarked that he did not think it necessary to say anything at all by way of intro- duction to that service, as by the time it was concluded he presumed they would all feel that they had been sufficiently long in the chapel with such a crowded congregation and the night air being so Warm. The united choirs conducted by Mr. Binton then gave the opening hymn " Glory be to God." The " reading " next introduced to the congregation 1" a pretty rural village," on the borders of one of the western states of America, which for distinction's sake was called Rockville. The deacon of the only place of worship in the village was Richard Owen, who had two children— 'Frank, a stalwart fresh-looking young man of twenty-ene years," and "Minnie, a pretty fair-haired, blue-eyed girl, , of thirteen." There had been others whose feet had crossed the threshhold of the door, and the dark angel of death had I • entered in at that cottage porch more than once. Minnie yearned for a mother's love, but its sunshine was gone. "That beautiful throne" (a piece which was sung by the choir) was a special favourite of hers, as the verses seemed to bring her into closer communionship with that dear departed mother whose dwelling was in the angel land. Abraham Lincoln had not long occupied the presidential chair of America when the horrors of a civil war broke out, and the Northern and Southern States struggled hard for the mastery. Rockville was in one of the Northern States, and consequently its inhabi- tants were favourable to justice, freedom, and unity. Among the gallant young men who left that peaceful se- questered village to draw the sword upon the battlefield, was Frank Owen, who, in an unguarded moment and full of ex- citement, enlisted for a soldier. This rash step the poor young man regretted almost as soon as it was taken. This was in the spring of the year 1862, and at Eastertide a farewell service was held in the little church or meeting house. The choir then sang" Easter hymn," and shortly afterwards the Misses Smith sweetly gave a duet entitled "Good-bye." The connective readings next depicted the teuching scene at the railway station, where Frank promised an old widow , named Wilton, whose only son Tom had also joined the ranks, that whenever it was in his power he would look after the lad. "Are we sowing" was then given by the choir, after which the story was resumed with the depar- ture of Frank and Tom for headquarters. They were subsequently sent to the seat of war, and marched side by side, fought side by side, and slept under the cover of the same tent. Tom gradually grew weaker, and Frank, according to his pro- mise, helped him with his knapsack, anti twize saved .him from being cut down by the sword. The Misses Smith again sang a duet, entitled "By and by." After a heavy march, in which Frank had bravely assisted his friend Tom, the latter was called out as one of the sentinels for the night. Frank, however, persuaded the captain to allow him to go in his friend's place, but when he was performing the duty he felt that he had overtaxed his own strength, ' and be felt an irresistible desire to lie down and go to sleep. lie knew it would be a gross negligence ot duty, and liab'e to be followed by the severest punishment if he was found out. A quartette, entitled "Lift the Heart" was then sung by the Misses Thompson, Mr. H. Smith and Mr. R. Spros- ton. Frank bravely resisted the natural but dangerous desire to sleep, but at length exhausted nature could bear up no longer, and he gradually fell asleep against the trunk of a gigantic tree. For a short time his sleep was intensely sound, and he passed into a state of I slumber, and dreams of a varied character passed before ! him. Miss Susan Smith at this point sang "Angels evey bright and fair," The story continued to the efect that happy in his dreams and thinking of no 111, Frank was sud- denly startled by a heavy hand being rudely placed upon his shoulders, and starting to his feet he beheld in the ruddy ' glare of a lantern held in his face, his commanding officer. He was subsequently condemned to be shot for the offence. During the reading of this part the Dead March was played on an harmonium in the vestry, and gave the service an impressive effect. It was succeeded by the choir singing a.' chorus entitled "Peace." Frank wrote home to his sorrow- ing father and sister acknowledging the justice of his sen- tence, and detailing bow he had assisted his friend Tom. After the choir had sung "Father, I am worn and weary." the connective reading was proceeded with. Minnie at once hurried to the railway station and by train proceeded to New York, and then to Weshington, for the purpose of having an interview with the President Abraham Lincoln. Miss Sarah Smith sang " Minnie'a prayer," after which the touching interview between Minnie and the President was depicted. The President carefully read the letter of Frank, and ordered the immediate release of the condemned soldier. "Zion's King" was then sung by the choir. News of the glad tid- ings quickly spread, and everywhere were signs of rejoicing and gladness. The President personally decorated Frank, and commended him for assisting his sick comrade. When Frank and his sister arrived heel the whole village came forth to meet and welcome them back, while the bells of the little church chimed out a merry peal. The choir sang "Will the angels come to me ?" and the service concluded. —The Rev. M. DICKENSON then said: I may perhaps say with all honesty and candour that the circuit is considerably deficient in its finances, and therefore the united choirs of this place and Parr have very generously given their ser- vices in connection with this service of song for the purpose of replenishing the circuit exchequer. The managing com- mittee of this meeting once thought, and for a considerable time deliberated as to the best means and method by which to secure what we so ardently desired. In the first place, it was thought that the admittance should be not exactly by ticket but by payment at the door, and it was thought that 6d. each would be a very small, or at any rate a very reasonable sum for admittance. But there were two objec- tions against that, the first being that it was Sunday, and the other that some of our friends contended that if the charge was 6d. they would disappoint somebody who would like to give is. Therefore it was thrown open so that those who prefer to give more than 6d. will be at liberty to do so I have stated the object and the whole of the concern, snd I am sure if the service of song—so beautifully and effi- ciently rendered by the united choirs—be appreciated, it will be by a very good collection.—The collection was then made.

ALLEGED THEFT BY A DOMESTIC SEILYANT.—A respect- able-looking young woman, named Annie Kelly was on Tuesday charged, at the St. Helens Borough Police Court, with having stolen two towels and seven yards of cloth, the property of Mr. Thompson, tailor and draper, Westfield-street. Mr. Thompson said that prisoner had been in his employ for four weeks as domestic servant. On the 14th instant he gave her notice to leave, the notice to expire on the 23rd instant. He found that yesterday she had removed her box, and on suspicion he had it searched, and the four towels were found in it. The cloth, however, had not. yet been found. The whole of the articles were worth 255. On the application of Superintendent Johnston, prisoner was remanded till Monday.

Tnivien ASSAULT CAsns.—At the St. Helens Police Court. on Friday, a young man named Charles ;lolland was summoned by Hairy Crich, also a young man, for having assaulted him.—Complainant stated that on the Sunday evening previous he had been coming down Crop- per's Hill, when defendant struck him deliberately twice in the face without any provocation whatever.—Defendant and one or two witnesses said that no assault had been committed. All that defendant did was to rub complainant's cheek with his hand in fun.—The magistrates thought a trivial assault had been committed, and fined defendant Is and costs.—Elizateth Aston was fined ss. and costs for assaulting Jane Pilkington, at Parr, on the 12th inst.—Tbe evidence in this case was also somewhat contradictory, and much bad language had evidently been exchanged between the two parties.

CASE r's CLOWN CRICKETERS AT ST. HRLENS.—Tbis team of cricketers visited St. Helens on Friday and Saturday last, and on each day played against a team of fourteen St. Helen's cricketers, in the cricket ground, Denton's green. There was a fair attendance of spectators on the Saturday afternoon. The play of the clowns was net of a particularly impreseive kind,thongh considerable amusement was caused Iby some of the mere comical members of the team. TI e re- sult of the two days' playing was that the St. Helens players made in their first innings a score of 110, and in their second, 156. The clowns, of whom there were only 11 batsmen, made a first innings of 87 ; their second innings being scarcely begun before the stumps were drawn. On the evenings of each day they gave an entertainment in the circue, North-road, the programme of which comprised comic songs, feats of agility and strength, dances, itc. The attendancea were only moderate. The bind of the 2nd LEN. was engaged on each day Wth at the cricket field and at the circus.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

THE TEMPERANCE WORK AT WINSFORD.—The Sal- vation and Blue Ribbon Armies, especially the former, have not becOme defunct with the advent of fine, long days, Lut both have been seriously weakened, espccially the latter. Of the Bands of Hope, none have been more active than the Wesleyan, under the active pilotship of Mr. Stocks and tbose who have assisted him.

div.head: WO OLTON.
div.p: WO OLTON.

ALLEGED TFIEFT OF A SUGAR CRIFSFIER.—A respectably dressed young man named Jos!pb Callighan was brought up in custody at Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, on a charge of stealing a sugar crusher, value 6d, from the Derby Arms Hotel, Woolton. Mr. Spence, of Liverpo)l, appeared for the prisoner.—Arthur Buckley, landlord of the hotel, stated that on the 16th June the prisoner, with two other men and a young lady, came into his house and called for ttree pints of ale and a glass of port wine. The sugar-crusher was put in the wine glass, and when the party had left the house Buckley missed it. He fol- lowed them down All erton-street. and saw the sugar-crusher glittering in prisoner's hand. He:shouted to him to stop, but the prisoner and his companions took no heed. They were, kswever, overtaken by P.C. Steele, who came on the scene just in time to see the prisoner toss the stolen article over a wall into a field where it was found.—The defence was that the prisoner and his friends, being on a visit to a relative, named Glover, at Woolton Convalescent Hos- pital, called at Buckley's house. One of these, named Davies, stirred up the young lady's wine, and then put the crusher on the table alongside his pipe. After leaving the house he found the crusher in his side pocket, having apparently put it there inadvertently along with his pipe. He handed it to prisoner, expresaMg surprise at what be had doge, and the prisoner' remarking that it was of no value, threw it over the wall. Immediately afterwards Buckley and the policeman appeared—The prisoner was discharged. ' ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.

THE CHESHIRE YACHT CLUB —A. sailing match for local five-ton yachts took place on Saturday, the course being from the Royal Mersey Yacht Club Slip in the Mersey, op- posite Tranmere, to the Southport Pier. The prizes amounted to 15 guineas, and were divided as follows : First, 12 125.; second, £3 3s. Six yachts competed, namely, the Zazel, five tons, owned by Mr. C. Jamieson; the Elaine, four tons, owned by Mr. A. Nickels ; the Nautilus, four tons, owned by Mr. W. Scott Hayward; the Tyro, three tons, owned by Mr. G. H. %Vintner ; the Sheila, yawl, three and a half tons, owned by Mr. F. J. Fownes ; and the Litra, yawl, three tons, owned by Mr. J. Heap. The start was at twelve o'clock. The Tyro passed the winning post at 4-48, followed by the Sheila, which arrived at 5-10. This is the first time the Tyro had been to Southport, but'owing to the channel being now efficiently buoyed, she had no difficulty in finding her way in. The prizes were the gift of. Lieutenant S. Crowley, of the Southport R.N.A.V. . CHESHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.—A general meeting of the members of this society, was held at the Royal Hotel, Crewe, on Wednesday, Mr. T. Cliffe (Crewe Gates) pre- siding. Messrs. W. Fair (Aston) and.Bahner were appointed judges of farms and cottages at the forthcoming show at Crewe. A long discussion took place on a motion by Mr. Fair to give £l5O. in prizes in the dog and poultry class, and an amendment by Mr. Coomer reducing that amount to £lOO was carried, a committee being appointed to make out the lists. The secretary (Mr. William Beckett) announced that Colonel Talbot, of Preston Brook, had become a vice- president of the society, and that he expected Earl Shrews- bury to be in the same list.—A suggestion was ordered to be conveyed to the Crewe Horticultural Society to hold their annual show in conjOnction with the society's. A vote of thanks to the chairman terminated the proceedings ; and the meeting then accepted an invitation to visit the Crewe abattoir premises,

THE FATHEH OF PRIMITIVE METHODISM IN CHESHIRE. —At (Thorley, Cheshire, on Thursday, there was celebrated the golden wedding of Mr. Thomas Bateman. About SOO persons were present, and the event excited deep interest in the local religious world. The Mayor of Newcastle presided over the gathering, and there were also present two clergy- men of the Church of England—the Rev. T. W. Norwood, of Wrenbury, and the Rev. T. H. Sparshott, chaplain to the Marquis of Cholmondeley, and ministers belonging to the Primitive Methodist, Wesleyan, Congregational, and Baptist denominations. Mr. Bateman was born in 1799; and will be 84 years of ago in October next. He still officiates as vice- chairman of the Nantwich Board of Guardians, and also acts on the committee of the union. But it is in connection with Primitive Methodism, its rise and progress in Cheshire, that Mr. Bateman is honoured throughout Cheshire. In 1851 Mr. Bateman was elected a permanent member of the Pri- mitive Methodist Conference, and twice subsequently he was elected president of the conference. Although he has reached his 84th year, Mr. Bateman is still hale and vigor- ous, and generally takes service at one of the places of wor- ship in the county.

MUNIFICENCE OF CHURCIIMEN.—At the presentation of prizes at Belle Green School, Ince, near Wigan, on Thurs- day, Canon Fergie, the vicar of Ince, in commending the liberality of the people of Ince, stated that, as announced at their recent sale of work, £s,ooo,bad been. promised to him for the building of a church, and £2,000.f0r the erection of a school and other purposes, and that a few days ago another gentleman had promised him another 25 000, mak- ing E12,000‘ of unsolicited donations in a few weeks.

PUBLIC-MUSS ETIQUETTE.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, a man named Michael Ran was charged with having stolen ss. from the person of Wm. Simpson.— It appeared that the prisoner and prosecutor along with another man had been in the Sefton Armapnblic-house on the afternoon of the 12th inst. Simpson fell asleep w hilst there,,and on awaking found that ss. which he had had in his pocket was gone, and the prisoner was also missing. The next day he accused prisoner of having taken the fawner, but he then denied it. Information was given to the police, and after being apprehended the prisoner practically admltted the charge, but said, in exause, he only took the mow out of Simpson's pocket to pay for some ale, which he said. was quite a common thing for people to do in pc:alic-houses under such circumslances.—He was fined 10s. and costs.

A "No RENT" ASSAULT A.,T PRESCOT.—At :trescot I,etty Sessions on Tuesday, Malgaret Murphy wa& charged with assaulting Isaac: Hignett. Complainant, a. young man, gated that he. was agent for some proper-by belonging to Mrs. Tyrer, mar the King's Arms, Present. On the 25th May ho went to collect the rent, and defendant struck him on the ehes4 and seizing a poker threatened to strike him with it. Had it not been for the intervention of her hus- band she would have assaulted him with the poker. He retired for safety into Mrs. Tyrer's house, and as he was going; away defendant came to tbe door of the house- with her apron full of stones, threatened him, and us,-dd very ktbusivo and obscene language.—Mrs. Tyrer stated that de- fendant came to the front of her house and threatened to smash the windows.—Difendant was tlned 111}P,. and costs

div.head: NEWTON ANNUAL RACES.
div.p: NEWTON ANNUAL RACES.
NEwroli, Wednesiay.

Vespite the fact of the weather being dull and overcast, there was a goodly muster at this popular riunion. The general public was well represented, and not only were the denizens of the city on the banks of the "Inky Trwell" pre- sent in strong force, but the large towns in the vicinity contributed their quotas to swell the muster. While the Northerners were well represented, there was a fairly good sprinkling of Southern turfites, who had resisted the attrac- tions of Bibury in order to assist at the Lancishire gather- ing. Under these circumstances, as may be supposed, the ritsgs and stands were well filled, and the *sleeting may be considered as most successfully inaugurated. lhe recent moisture bad largely benefited the ground, and consequently the going was of a good description. Six items made up the bill of fare, and the ball WAS set rolling at two o'clock, with the All-aged. Welter Plate. Half-a-dczen can- didates came to Me post for this event, and Protector was thought to have so good a chance that he was backed energetically, and closed at G to 4 on. However, the winner turned up in Juniper, who defeated the favourite by a head, and landed the nice odds of 12 to 1. The next item, the All-aged Selling Plate, resulted in another rebuff for backers, Bumblepuppy, who was the most fancied, being nnplaced, while Little Duchess secured the winning brackets. Stonectop, who ran second to Lucerne in the Twenty-first New Biennial Stakes at Ascot, was the most in demand for the Manor Cup, but the son of Winslow and Wallflower was relegated to third place, and the moderately- scked Nerida proved successful. The Golborne Park Stakes resulted in favour of Campanile, who was the most in demand, and then another good favourite in Lady Hamp- ton won the Makerfield Handicap Plate. An interesting day's sport was brought to a conclusion with the Copeland Welter Handicap Plate, in which Hesperian proved success- ful. In this race Harcourt fell, and Hill, the jockey, was hurt—it is feared somewhat seriously. GAMING AND POCKET-PICKING AT NEWTON RACES. It has been a common remark that a number of "card- sharpers" and other swindlers to be met with on the road to the Common and in the neighbourhood of the race-course has far exceeded that of previous years. The police have been unusually vigilant and energetic, however, and a goodly number of the' law-breakers' fell into their clutches. At six o'clock last (Wednesday) evening a special court for the trial of prisoners was held at the Police Station, Market-street, Earlestown. The magistrate present was Robert Houghton Esq. The following persons were charged, and were fined 211 e. and costs each for gaming by performing the "three card trick," yesterday afternoon : Richard Scott, of Liverpool ; Daniel McFadyers, Scar- borough; Thomas Johnson' Oldham; George Smith, Leeds; Harry Kirk, Ashton; James Leonard, Manchester; and John Calder, Manchester. The following persons were also fined 20s. and costs for ether forms of gambling :—John Winstanley, Atherton; Joseph Matthews, Manchester ; Eliza Clough, Ma.ncbester ; Harry Walker, Bradford; John Bennett, Manchester; Robert Doughty, Manchester. Thomas Jones, a young man, was charged with stealing a gold watch from the person of Thomas Davies, on the race course.—The prcsecutor stated that lie was standing near to the rails speaking to a friend on the opposite side, when the prisoner came up between him and the rails. The prisoner pushed againet him, and he (prosecutor) immediately felt that his watch had gone. He seized the prisoner by the arm, and saw that the watch was in his fist. He had broken it off from the chain by "twitching" it. He tried to ren away, and he (prosecutor) straggled with him for some moments, and the prisoner, seeing he could not get away, threw the watch to the around. A gentleman picked it up. —Mr. Houghton: There can be no mistake about it, be- cause it did not go out of your sight.—The prosecutor: There is no mistake about it —The prisoner was remanded until the sessions to be held at Newton on Saturday week. William Jones, a young man, who said he came from Dublin, was charged with attempting to steal a purse con- taining £5 from the person of Edward Yates, at Eerlestown I Railway Station.—lnspector Sturgess, of the London ard North-Weetern Railway Company, stated that while he was at the railway station that afternoon, he saw the prisoner ;n company with a number of other men. From the prisoner's appearance and movements he suspected there was something wroug, and he watched them very minutely. He saw him make two or three different attempts to steal gentlemen's purses as the persons were entering the train. He saw him go near the prosecutor and put his hand in his pocket, and at that moment the prosecutor felt his hand in his pocket, and he shouted out "Take your handout of my pocket." With that he seized the prisoner by the throat, and witness then went to his assistance. The prosecutor would tell them distinctly that he felt the prisoner's hand in his right handl trousers pocket, and he seized hold of it.—The prisoner (ex- citedly) : Oh, you scamp.—Mr. Houghton: You must not talk like that here.—P.S. Commins : Silence, don't talk like that here.—The prisoner: I cannot help it —you are lying.—lnspector Sturgess explained that the prisoner carried a macintosh on his left arm, which he pushed against those whom he intended to rob, and then put his right hand into their pocket.—The prisoner: Oh, wait, L don't say that. Let me speak.—Mr. Houghton: Your L turn will come.—The prisoner again essayed to speak, and was told to.be silent.—The prisoner : It would reeke me cry to hear what is coming out of his iroath now.—P.S. Commins : Be silent, will you.—The prisoner: When you saw me on the station was I getting into the train? —lnspector Sturgess: No, you were not.—The prisoner: I say I was —lnspector Sturgess: No, you were not, and the prosecutor will tell yen—The prosecutor was then sworn, whereupon the prisoner exclaimed: I will do no more now ; I'll not say anything else; do as you like.—Edward Yates, the prosecutor, said he came from Fallowfield, near Man- chester. When the train came up at Earlestown station he was looking for a place where he could sit, when the pri- soner put his hand in his (witness's) pocket. He seized him by the throat while he had his hand in his pocket. He would have taken the purse if it had not been for a handkerchief and while prisoner struggled with him Inspector Sturgese came up.—The prisoner: Is it true that I put my hand in your pocket ?-The prosecutor : It's as true as there is a God in heaven that he had hold of my purse.—The prisoner : Did you feel my hand in your pocket P—The prosecutor: Yes. —The prisoner: Did you take my hand out ?—The prosecu- tor : Yes, I did.—The prisoner: I'll say nothing more.—The prosecutor: You had your hand in my potket when I seized :rota by the throat.—The prisoner was then remanded until the sessions to be held at Newton Town Hall, on Saturday week,

div.head: LYMM LOCAL BOARD
div.p: LYMM LOCAL BOARD

A special meeting of this }hard was held in the Bard. room on Monday evening. There were present—Messrs. Cameron (chairman), Dewhurst, R.)gers, Gibbon, Appleton, Thomason, Taylor. Bayley, and Mallard (assistant clerk).

div.head: MR. TAYLOR'S MEMBERSHIP QUESTIONED.
div.p: MR. TAYLOR'S MEMBERSHIP QUESTIONED.

Mr. ROGERS said before the business was proceeded with, he would like to ask if a person who was not a ratepayer had A right to sit as a member of the Board.—The Cuata MAN : It is a question for the clerk.—Mr. TAYLOR thought the question ought to be put in tome other form; it ought to he put openly. Did it apply to him ?—Mr. ROGERS : It does.—Mr. TAYLOR asked the reporters to take note of the fact that he was both a ratepayer and a member of th tt Board.—Mr. RoGEns : Is that right, Mr. Chairman.—The CHAIRMAN said he cluld not tell whether Mr. Taylor was a ratepayer or not.—Mr. TAYLOR said he had the keys of his house his possession, and he had paid all his rates.—The CHAIRMAN : You can answer as to the latter, Mr. Clerk ? —Mr. TAYLOR : The clerk is not here.—The ASSISTANT CLERIC : Mr. Taylor has not paid his rates.—Mr. TAYLOR said he bad paid his rates up to the current one. This dis- cussion he said, was out of order, and as a member of the Board he was very grieved that it had been raised. He could put on the table letters, very sharp letters, that had been written to him, and he had received one only that morning. He believed he got his notice before anyone else got his. The discussion was of a personal character and it ought not to be brought up in that way. His house was in his pos- session, and he paid a person to look after it, and he, his wife and children came and slept there occasionally.—The CriktardaN thought it was a question entirely for Mr. Taylor, as the responsibility would rest upon him.—Mr. Tnorrasmi thought so long as Mr. Taylor's name was on the rate book, and he acknowledged the rate it was all right.— Mr. TAYLOR: Ido acknowledge the rate.—Mr. RoGEns I have been informed that the house has been let, and that Mr. Taylor has not paid his rate, and as a matter of fact the law—Mr. TAYLOR: I know the law as well as Mr. Rogers. I object to this as irregular.—The CHAIRMAN: I think it is a question for Mr. Taylor himself.—Mr. RooEns: If Mr. Taylor has paid his rates I am quite willing--Mr. TAYLOR: I think this is quite irregular. If the Board had Eiven me proper notice of it I could have produced papers that would have as- tonished the Board.—The Chairman then proceeded with other business, and the matter was allowed to drop.

div.head: CLERK'S SALLEY.
div.p: THE CLERK'S SALLEY.

Mr. RooEns said he was about to make a proposal, but before he did so, he begged to offer his apology to the mem- bers of tha Finance and Gas Committees for not mentioning it to them beforehand. What he was about to do he did entirely on his own responsibility. He was going to pro- pose an increase in the clerk's salary. He saw more of the clerk's work than any member of the Board, and he thought the clerk was very much under paid. He had not consulted any no nber of the Board on the subject, neither had he said one word to the clerk further than giving him notice of his proposal. He proposed that an addition of £55 be made to the clerk's salary—£3o to be charged to the gas account, £5 for postage and circulars, and £2O to the general account. The increase would not affect the rates in the smallest degree. The amount collected in the pre- vious year was £3,200, and if they were to have an ordinary collector they could not get that amount collected for £l6O. Besides, most of the money was collected in small amounts, some as tow as a shilling. They required their clerk to attend every meeting, and give advice on questions of law, and he (Mr. Rogers) estimated the attendance at each meet- ing at £2. The clerk got £lBO per year, and £l5 per year for postage and circulars, but the latter could not be reckoned in his salary as he was out of pocket by it. The AsslsraNT-CeEux said that list year the account for postage and circulars was close upon £lB.—Mr. ROGERS, continuing, said the gas accounts were very complicated, and he had noticed that it had been necessary for two clerks to attend at that room once or twice a week, and they had to be paid out of that magnificent sum of £lBO a year.—Mr. GIBBON thought the matter ought to go before the Finance Committee. Mr. Decvrt nese' said he was very much against any expenditure they could possibly avoid, and he thought they ought not to go lute this question hurriedly, as it was hardly a matter they could consider publicly. It would be bqter if it first went before the Finance Committee.—Mr. ROGERS said he was perfectly satisfied. He had an object in bringing the matter forward in the way he had, and that object had been accomplished.—The subject was allowed to drop with the understanding that it would be brought before the Finance Committee to be dealt with in detail, after which it would be again brought before the Board.
There was no other business of interest. . ea..are.40.1.111.1.11

There have just been re-valuations of lines on the Nantwich side, and on the Prescot aide, and I have followed the proceedings in those Unions, and know the totals. UNITARIAN PROVINCIAL ASSEMBLY.
REV. E. ST A. DUKE'S VALEDICTORY
SERMON 3.

The Rev. E. St. A. Duke, who has officiated as curate at St. Paul's Church, Warrington, for nearly seven years, preached his valedictory sermon on Sunday morning. There was a large congregation, and the rev. gentleman took for his text, Ecclesiastes xii. 7, "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it." At the close of the sermon Mr. Duke said: [have now preached my last sermon as curate of St. Paul's Church. You may say I have chosen a somewhat gloomy subject about which to address you this morning, but I have done so for this reason. I have tried to make it one of the seliant points of my teaching to constantly bring before you the great fact of death, and the need there is for us to . . prepare for it, because it seemed to me when I came here that all of you led very busy lives—lives from which religion seemed to be greatly divorced during the week—and Sunday was, therefore, a good time to remind you of the terrible reality of which I have been speaking. So I would have the last words I shall say to you as a minister of this church, ring in your ears as the echo of my former teaching—about the certainty of death and thk need of preparation for it. I now want to say a word or two to you of quite a personal character. My de- parture is a great deal more hurried than I expected it would have been, and I have,therefore, had no time to go round and say " good-bye " to my friends. Now about another mat- ter. I know that some of you have felt very much dissatis- fied with my ministry here, but, my friends, if you will bear in mind that when I have come here on a Sunday evening to conduct the service and preach I have had a very great deal to do at the other end of the parish, namely, at St. &amebas. having often acted as superintendent, school teacher, and choirmaster. I am sure you will forgive me. I have often preached in weariness and painfulness, but I can tell you that you have not been more disvatisfied with the manner in which I have conducted the services than I ' have been. I have known my deficiencies very well, and I think you ought to have a little consideration for me. I ask you to try to think kindly of ma when I go away, for I assure you I have done my best. I have very tender asso- ciations connected with this church. It is within these wails, in the old church, that I first officiated as a clergyman of the Church of England. Here I preached my first s,rmon, here I first administered holy baptism, here I had to celebrate holy communien for the first time, and ought not these associations to be very tender to me? Yes. I tell you that I have always tried to do my best, but it has not been my fault if that best has been very poor. And now I make one request to you this morning. I feel very much my separation from the people in this parish. There is one matter I cannot trust myself to speak about, and that is my connection with my dear vicar and his wife. I cannot say anything more about that, but Ido ask you to pray most earnestly that I may have success—though it is a word I hate to use—in Liverpool. I hope God will give me strength lo go on with my work, that I may raise the standard of the Gospel, and that many souls may be given to me in the last great day. My friends, I promise that I shall always re- member you in my prayers as Sunday morning after Sunday mm fling comes round. and on week days too I shall try to think of all my dear friends at St. Paul's, Warrington. The rev, gentleman preached in the evening at St. Barnabas Church, and at the close of his address took his farewell of the congregation.

At the close of his sermon in the evening, the Vicar Drisay referred to Mr. Duke's departure. He pointed out that that gentleman was leaving the parish to undertake a most important and responsible work in the parish of Liver- pool, and he asked for the prayers of the congregation on his behalf. The same request he would make on behalf of Mr. Duke's successor, the Rev. W. B. Pratt, who was a man of great piety and man attainments. The Archdeacon of Warrington, on Friday, congratulated him upon having ob- tained Mr. Pratt's services, and spoke of him in the highest terms. He (the vicar) did not want a curate who was here to-day and gone to-morrow, but one who, like their friend who was leaving them, would stay with them till be got preferment. Let them pray for the one who was leaving them, and for the one who would shortly reside amongst them.
GOSSIP OF TIIE LONDON CORRESPON-
DENTS.

A new misery is in store for poor Mr. Irving Bishop. Mr. Labouchere intends now to prove that he was for some time a Spiritualist medium ; and he took to exposing the me- diums when their game was found not to pay. I hear the Czar has given Lord Weiseley a magnificent souvenir of the coronation. It is a splendid gold sauff-box, with the Czar's portrait set in brilliants on the lid. A number of other fine diamonds are fixed in the box.

Those of your readers who take in the Times will notice a bold piece of advertising. One whole page of the leading journal is covered with the advertisement of the first issue of the new series of the Cornhill Magazine, which is re- duced in price to sixpence. This means a cost of not lessl than from .£lBO to £2OO for one day's advertisment. The first of the innocents went on Thursday. The Criminal Code Bill is abandoned. It has occupied two Governments, two Parliaments, a committee of sage judges, and a grand committee; but it is again shelved. Sir Henry James made a good fieht for it, but when Mr. Henry Labouchere joined Mr. Warton and Mr. Parnell, there was no help for it. The Attorney-General surrendered on the spot. The other night, Mr. John Bright quoted in the Houee.of Commons a letter of the late Mr. Dillon, father of the retired member for Tipperary, to the effect that the only hope for Ireland was in uniting with the Liberal party. In his attack upon Mr. Bright which followed, Mr. T. P. O'Connor denied that his friend ever wrote snch a thing. I hear that Mr. Bright intends to publish the letter as a proof of his absolute adherence to fact, and also as evidence of the changed tone amongst trusted lOsh leaders The election of Profeeaor F. W. Newman to an honorary fellowship of Worcester College, Oxford, will give great satisfactien to the many friends and admirers of that sound scholar and steuech Liberal. Worcester College has done well to remember in his ripe oil aee the brilliant student who entered its walls in 1822. Four years later he was elected a Fellow of Balliol, but resigned in 1830, rather than sign the Thirty-nine Articles. This is the reason why, not- withstanding his eminence as a student of mathematics and philology, he never went beyond the B.A. degree. Lord Sudeley is building a large jam manufactory on his estate at Toddiegton, in Gloucestershire. Two years ago he planted there 93,000 gooseberry trees, 167,000 black cur- rant, 20,000 plum, 3,000 apple, 900 pear, 9,000 damson, 500 cherry, 10,000 red currant, 25,000 raspberry, and 100 cebnut, and 52 acres were planted with strawberries At the same time 100 Scotch firs and 10,000 poplars were planted for sheltering purposes. I wish him every success, for most of the jem now sold in shops is horrid trash. It may not be pernicious, but it is as different from the old-fashioned home- made j am as chalk is from cheese Why suddenly the Scotch peers should come to the con- clusion that tire Duke of Buccleuch wants to be testi- rnonialised, I don't know. He is not just now reaching any particular anniversary. He has been among men for 77 years; he has been among English peers for 134 years; he has sat in the House of Lords for 56 years, having come of age eight years after his father's death in 1827. There is nothing mystic about these figures—no lustrum nor majority nor jubilee. Perhaps it is felt that as he presided over a banquet to Lord Beaconsfield something ought to be done for him. For until the Berlin Congress the Duke of Buc- clench maintained his obstinate Scotch prejudice against the Tory leader, and hit conversion was rewarded by the Midlothian election. Even that cannot be an anniversary which the Scotch peers are keeping, for it was four years ago, and there is nothing about four that excites any par- ticular feeling. Doubtless, however, the Scotch peers are grateful. The Duke of Buccleuch elects all of them who are representative; and they have a reason for showing that they can feel gratitude. Some anxiety is felt about the election at Hastings on I both sides. A Tory has made the vacancy, and ha headed I the poll in 1880. Sir Thomas Brassey was then returned as touch for his personal popularity as because his views were those of his constituents. The Tories did not attempt to attack his seat, and, in consequence, Hastings is one of those boroughs which, in Mr. Chamberlain's opinion, dis- franchise themselves by the one and one compromise. Since then there has been some movement of opinion in Hestings not yet very clearly defined. So far as Hastings is a watering place it is Tory; but it is also a fishing place, and the fishermen are usually Liberal ; and it is in sympathy with agricultural interests, and the farmers are feeling some I gratitude for the Tenant Right Bill. On ihe other hand, a I quiet Own like this is just one where what happened in I Ireland will seem particularly horrible, and nobody can pre- diet the result of the contest. At present the Tories are more hopeful than the Liberals.

The Channel Tunnel Committee finished the taking of evidence on Thursday with a stormy episode. Lord Aber- dare, who all through the inquiry has shown himself im- patient of every witness who has ventured to suggest the undesirability of constructing the tunnel, quite lost his temper with Lord Wolseley because the great Egyptian hero spoke of the possibility of an enemy surprising the defences of the tunnel, and the probability of a "peace government" being in power who under no circumstances would order the destruction of the tunnel. This expression of opinion seemed to creatly incense Lord Aberdare, and he cross- examined Lord Wolseley very severely as to the common- sense and reasonableness of his views. I have heard the evidence all through, and I estimate the great bulk of it to be against the construction of the tunnel. I believe, how- ever, if Lord Lansdowne, the chairman, votes in favour of the project the committee will be equally divided for and against. Colonel Harcourt, Sir Massey Lopes, and Sir Hussey Vivian have indicated strong objections to the pro- ject ; apd Mr. Arthur Peel and Lord Barrington, in a milder degree, have also displayed an adverse feeling. Lord Rowton is spending a few days in town, and looks very well. Much notice has been given to the remarkable article in the Times the other day, from its still more remark- able Paris correspondent, apropos of the anniversary of the Berlin Conference, retailing a good deal of personal gossip about Lord Beaconsfield and Prince Bismarck at the Con- ference. The despatch was the outcome of a breakfast con- venation the great M. Blowitz had with Lerd Rowton in Paris the other day. Lord Rowton, with the fastidiousness of a literary man, is disappointed at the way in which some of the circumstances are set forth in the glowing language of M. Blowitz. In particular, there is a long sentence in which Lord Beaconsfield is described as having expressed his preference for assassination as compared with imprison- I ment. I have heard Lord Rowton tell the story in crisper form than lt is retailed by M. Blowit4. When Lord Beacons.

div.head: REV. R. PILCHER ON "THINGS NEW AND
div.p: THE REV. R. PILCHER ON "THINGS NEW AND
OLD."

The annual meeting of the members of the Provincial Assembly of Presbyterian and Unitarian ministers and con- gregations of Lancashire and Cheshire was held on Thurs- day at Altrincbam. Divine service was conducted in the Dunham-road Chapel during the forenoon, when a sermon was preached by

The Rev. R. PILCIIER, of Warrington on "Thing new and old." He stated that the most marked departure in the Christian Church from the spirit of the Master, and the one most fraught with evil, was thetaking, as the test of a man's acceptableness to his Maker or to his fellow-men, his belief about divine things insteed of his faith in them; in a word, a correct creed—orthodoxy—instead of a correct life. The resultant evils in life were 'shown in all their intensity by ' the corruptions which gave such force to Luther's revolt against the church of his day, and were still too painfully clear to-day in the slackness, not to say deadness, of con- science shown by many whose professions of orthodoxy were the loudest. The resulting evils in the realms of mind were shown in the intellectual suicide of myriads who, un- able to believe the Church creeds, vet afraid to doubt, sought refuge from the necessity of thinking in the ceaseless round Of a symbolical worship, or in the attitude towards religion of thousands whoAorced to deny, passed on into indifference or into open hostility. "All or none" was the challenge of the Church. Then "none" was the reply. Nor were things much better among so-called Protestants. Although they claimed the right of private judgment, in matters of faith they failed to see or at least to own, that the recogni- tion of conscience as the final court of appeal, in thought as well as in deed, shut out the claims of an infalliable book as logically and as peremptorily as those made made by an infallible church. To those who frankly made conscience the final court of appeal, and whose bond of union was their religion rather than then' theology, the criti- cisms so frequently passed on Christianity caused no misgivings or fear. Their attitude towards the great problems of theology was one of expecta- tion, not of certainty ;of tentativeness, not of finality. For inasmuch as every newly known fact must alter their point of view, and therefore their mode of thought and speech, there could be no" finality in theology any more than in politics. To "rest and be thankful" was only possible to a true man or woman in the deep weariness of age or in the deeper hush of death. The disowned heretic of to-day, who in a spirit of son-like sympathy lifted soul and life alike to the great Father, was more truly a follower of the Master than myriads of the infallible fold who bowed before God in fear but had no thought of love. In the afternoon a business meeting was held under the presidency of the Rev. William Gaskell. An address in favour of a wider application of the principle of religious equality was delivered by the Rev. J. Wright, and the re- port of a Special Committee was submitted in which it was stated that the committee had witnessed, with sincere regret, the rejection of the Affirmation Bill. The only subj-ct of congratulation in connection with the matter was the noble speech of the Prime Minister, which they remarked was rendered all the grander as a vindication of civil and reli- gious liberty by the fact that there was probably not a man in England who had more aversion than Mr. Gladstone has to Mr. BracilauA and all his works. The committee also ex- pressed the opinion that the day was past when blasphemy should be punished as a criminal offence. They also stated that they cordially approved of the Cemeteries B'll intro- duced by Mr. H. Richard, and expressed their conviction that religious equality would not be secured until fellowships and posts in connection with the Universities of Oxford an Cambridge are thrown open to .Nonconfi.rmists. and not con- fi,v-d to Churchmen as they now are. A petition in favour of the rupeal of the blasphemy laws was afterwards adop`ed, as was also one to the Home Secretary praying for the re lease of the persons recently committed to prison for blasphemy.

One day he entered the room where Lord Rorrton (then Mr. Montague Corry) was seated, and to the great surprise of his faithful secretary, he bad on his hat and gloves, and carried his walkingstick. "Come, Monty," he said, "let us go for a walk. I've tried imprisonment, and I prefer assassination." This is, of course, a parody upon Lord Derby's famous declaration that he had tried a certain sherry and preferred the gout.
DR. FOX ON INFANTILE MORTALITY

div.head: AND MILK SUPPLY.
div.p: AND MILK SUPPLY.

Dr. Fox, medical officer of health for Mid-Cheshire, writes as follows with reference to this subject :—Dr. Borchardt, in his recent interesting address, is right in con- necting undue infant mortality rather with the absence of milk than with its presence of one quality or another. And, therefore, the logical sequence of "infant mortality and milk supply" is not apparent. Dr. Borchardt speaks very mach of general ignorance respecting the dairies, the cows, and the general sanitary arrangements of the places from which milk is imported into Manchester. It might be well if some kind of official supervision could be devised by means of which customers and vendors could be brought into acquaintance with each other. So far as my knowledge ex ends, I may say there would be no hindrance or obstacle on the Cheshire side. But in regard to public security it ought to count for something that rural districts as well as urban are under sanitary supervision. The water supply and general sani- tary arrangements of the farms that supply Manchester with milk have been for many years receiving due attention from responsible sanitary authorities and their representatives. It is not contended that thera is no defect anywhere. But I affirm most positively that There is no connection whatever between the phenomenal infant mortality of Manchester and the dairy farms of Cheshire; and it betrays an ignorance which is puerile and ludicrous to place the two in any kind of relationship. It is remarkable that, in the vital statistics of Mid-Cheshire, of which I have been the castodian for five years. it is each year apparent that it is the aged that die in excess there and not the infants. Can it be asked what constitutes the difference? Air, light, and milk present in Cheshire, and absent from the slums of Manches- ter; and gin the reverse. And if the milk is in it at all as a disease-producing agent, if Dr. Borchardt does not know the condition of our farms, we know the condition of the low- class milk shop and cottage pantries of Manchester. Milk is an absorbing fluid, capable of imbibing and propagating within itself germs from the surrounding air, from flies, &c. Need more be said?
